IN NO EVENT SHALL THE +AUTHORS OR COPYRIGHT HOLDERS BE LIABLE FOR ANY CLAIM, DAMAGES OR OTHER +LIABILITY, WHETHER IN AN ACTION OF CONTRACT, TORT OR OTHERWISE, ARISING FROM, +OUT OF OR IN CONNECTION WITH THE SOFTWARE OR THE USE OR OTHER DEALINGS IN THE +SOFTWARE."},{"sha":"97690daf8243586b46257fd8953d291a7f0710fb","filename":"README.md","status":"added","additions":142,"deletions":0,"changes":142,"blob_url":"https://github.com/udayallu-ml/Lightfoot-GraphRAG/blob/fbba969e73eaeaf45e1e8a8ad33a96cfeadbb66d/README.md","raw_url":"https://github.com/udayallu-ml/Lightfoot-GraphRAG/raw/fbba969e73eaeaf45e1e8a8ad33a96cfeadbb66d/README.md","contents_url":"https://api.github.com/repos/udayallu-ml/Lightfoot-GraphRAG/contents/README.md?ref=fbba969e73eaeaf45e1e8a8ad33a96cfeadbb66d","patch":"@@ -0,0 +1,142 @@ +# Lightfoot + +GraphRAG with exact, model-free document deletion. + +Lightfoot builds a knowledge graph from documents with one language-model call per passage, retrieves with no model calls, and deletes documents as a database operation with no model calls. After a deletion, the graph is identical to a fresh index of the remaining documents, verified on the full 11,402-passage MuSiQue corpus. + +This repository holds the reference implementation, the benchmark harness used for the paper, per-question results for every run, and the paper source. + +Paper: [paper/main.pdf](paper/main.pdf) + +## Results + +Recall@5 is the share of gold evidence passages in the top 5 retrieved. EM is exact-match answer accuracy. Index cost is normalised to list prices. + +| System | MuSiQue R@5 | 2Wiki R@5 | HotpotQA R@5 | HotpotQA EM | MuSiQue index cost | Delete 10% of docs | +|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| +| **Lightfoot** | **0.646** | 0.884 | **0.943** | **0.630** | **$1.64** | 0 model calls, exact | +| HippoRAG 2 | 0.616 | **0.905** | 0.930 | 0.553 | $2.23 | 0 model calls | +| LightRAG | 0.480 | 0.722 | 0.902 | 0.543 | ≈$9.5 | 2,187 model calls, 3.7 h | +| fast-graphrag | 0.412 | 0.838 | 0.732 | 0.517 | $4.89 | not supported | + +Against HippoRAG 2, Lightfoot is significantly better on 5 of 15 paired comparisons, significantly worse on 2 (both on 2WikiMultiHopQA), and tied on 8. Full tables, intervals and caveats are in the paper and in [docs/design/05-results-all.md](docs/design/05-results-all.md). + +## How it works + +```mermaid +flowchart LR + subgraph Index + P[Passage] --> X[One LLM call:
entities + facts as JSON] + X --> F[Per-chunk name forms
with provenance] + F --> E[Entities = linked groups of forms
cosine >= 0.92] + E --> G[Graph: entities + passages
fact and synonym edges] + end + subgraph Query + Q[Question] --> S[Seed from top-2 matching facts
+ top-100 dense passages] + S --> W[Personalized PageRank
damping 0.9] + W --> R[Cross-encoder rerank of top 30,
fused with PageRank rank] + R --> A[One answer call
top 10 passages + facts] + end + subgraph Delete + D[Document] --> DF[Remove its forms and fact assertions] + DF --> DR[Recompute only touched groups
no model calls] + end +``` + +Every stored record is a function of the live per-chunk forms only, never of insertion order, batching or history. That is what makes deletion exact. The design and how it changed during benchmarking are in [docs/design/01-architecture.md](docs/design/01-architecture.md), section 11. + +## Repository layout + +| Path | Contents | +|---|---| +| `lightfoot/` | The Lightfoot package: extraction, resolution, provenance ledger, graph, retrieval, answering, stores (SQLite, PostgreSQL), optional Elasticsearch channel | +| `harness/` | Benchmark harness: dataset builders, metrics, cost ledger, runner, answer-only rerun, LiteLLM proxy config, adapters and subprocess workers for each baseline | +| `tests/` | 82 tests, including the exact-erasure tests | +| `runs/` | One YAML per benchmark run | +| `data/` | The question and passage subsets used in the paper (parquet), built from the public datasets | +| `results/` | Per-question predictions, scores, cost ledgers and summaries for every reported run (index stores are not included) | +| `scripts/` | Diagnostics and validation scripts, plus dataset download | +| `docs/design/` | Architecture, evaluation plan, results write-ups, paper draft notes | +| `docs/frameworks/` | Source-code reviews of 17 open-source GraphRAG frameworks | +| `paper/` | LaTeX source and PDF | + +## Setup + +Tested on macOS 14 (Apple M3 Pro, 18 GB) with Python 3.14 for Lightfoot and 3.12 for two baselines. + +```bash +python3 -m venv .venv +.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt +cp .env.example .env # then put your OpenRouter key in .env +``` + +Lightfoot's tests need no API key: + +```bash +.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests +``` + +### Datasets + +The `data/` folder already holds the exact subsets used in the paper. To rebuild them, or build other sizes, download the raw datasets into a sibling `datasets/` folder: + +```bash +./scripts/download_datasets.sh +.venv/bin/python -m harness.datasets build musique 1000 +``` + +### Baselines + +Each baseline runs in its own virtual environment under `envs/`, driven by a worker process: + +```bash +./envs/setup_baselines.sh +``` + +This installs LightRAG (lightrag-hku 1.5.7), HippoRAG 2 (2.0.0a5) and fast-graphrag (0.0.5, commit 23b3a1b). LightRAG runs on PostgreSQL with pgvector; see the script for the database setup. + +## Running the benchmark + +Lightfoot alone (calls OpenRouter directly): + +```bash +./lf_v2.sh lightfoot_v5a_musique_1000 +``` + +Baselines (start a local LiteLLM proxy and embedding server, then run each system): + +```bash +DATASETS="musique_1000" ./run_all.sh lightrag hipporag2 fastgraphrag +``` + +Summary tables from saved results: + +```bash +.venv/bin/python -m harness.report musique_1000 +``` + +Models used in the paper, set in `.env` and `harness/proxy.yaml`: + +| Role | Model | +|---|---| +| Graph building (extraction) | meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct | +| Answers | openai/gpt-5.6-luna, reasoning off | +| Embeddings (local) | BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5 | +| Reranker (local) | BAAI/bge-reranker-base | + +The MuSiQue benchmark for all four systems cost about $35 at list prices on OpenRouter. Expect actual bills to run about 1.45 times list price, depending on provider routing. + +## Citation + +```bibtex +@article{allu2026lightfoot, + title = {Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion}, + author = {Allu, Uday}, + year = {2026}, + note = {arXiv preprint} +} +``` + +## License + +MIT for the code in this repository. The datasets keep their original licenses (MuSiQue CC BY 4.0, HotpotQA CC BY-SA 4.0, 2WikiMultiHopQA Apache 2.0, MultiHop-RAG ODC-BY); see [docs/datasets.md](docs/datasets.md). The baseline frameworks are installed from their own repositories under their own licenses."},{"sha":"3993ca720e829ab6361a0ad85013360378c0a928","filename":"README_elasticsearch.md","status":"added","additions":36,"deletions":0,"changes":36,"blob_url":"https://github.com/udayallu-ml/Lightfoot-GraphRAG/blob/fbba969e73eaeaf45e1e8a8ad33a96cfeadbb66d/README_elasticsearch.md","raw_url":"https://github.com/udayallu-ml/Lightfoot-GraphRAG/raw/fbba969e73eaeaf45e1e8a8ad33a96cfeadbb66d/README_elasticsearch.md","contents_url":"https://api.github.com/repos/udayallu-ml/Lightfoot-GraphRAG/contents/README_elasticsearch.md?ref=fbba969e73eaeaf45e1e8a8ad33a96cfeadbb66d","patch":"@@ -0,0 +1,36 @@ +# Local Elasticsearch for Lightfoot's hybrid channel + +Elasticsearch 8.19.21 (official darwin-aarch64 tarball, released 2026-09-01), single node, localhost only, +security disabled, heap 1-2 GB. No Docker, no sudo. + +- Install dir: `~/opt/elasticsearch-8.19.21` (tarball kept in `~/opt/dl/`) +- Data: `~/opt/es-data`, logs: `~/opt/es-logs`, pid file: `~/opt/es-data/es.pid` +- Config appended to `~/opt/elasticsearch-8.19.21/config/elasticsearch.yml` + (`network.host: 127.0.0.1`, `discovery.type: single-node`, `xpack.security.enabled: false`, `xpack.ml.enabled: false`, + `path.data` / `path.logs` as above); heap in `config/jvm.options.d/heap.options` (`-Xms1g -Xmx2g`) +- License: Basic. The native `rrf` retriever is NOT available on Basic in 8.x (403 "current license is + non-compliant for [Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)]"), so `lightfoot/hybrid_es.py` fuses a BM25 `match` query and + a `knn` query client-side (RRF, k=60). With `es_native_rrf="auto"` it tries the retriever once and falls back. +- Python client: `elasticsearch` 8.19.x in `bench/.venv`. + +## Start (background) + + ~/opt/elasticsearch-8.19.21/bin/elasticsearch -d -p ~/opt/es-data/es.pid + curl -s localhost:9200 # wait until it answers (~15 s) + +## Stop + + kill $(cat ~/opt/es-data/es.pid) + +## Use from Lightfoot + +Set `hybrid_backend: es` in the run YAML `models:` block (or `LightfootConfig(hybrid_backend="es")`). +`es_url` defaults to `http://localhost:9200` (env `LIGHTFOOT_ES_URL`). The index name is derived from the store +path plus the tenant (`lightfoot--`), so runs never share an index; on open the index is reconciled +with the store's chunks (stored vectors, no model calls). + + curl -s 'localhost:9200/_cat/indices?v' # list indices + curl -s -XDELETE 'localhost:9200/lightfoot-*' # drop all Lightfoot indices (needs action.destructive_requires_name: false) + +Tests: `tests/test_lightfoot_hybrid.py` runs without Elasticsearch (fake client); its integration test is skipped +when `LIGHTFOOT_ES_URL` is not reachable. Light to build, light to run, and it leaves no footprint when a document is removed. + +Status: design proposal, 2026-10-17. Nothing here has been benchmarked yet. Every performance claim is a hypothesis to be tested under `02-evaluation-plan.md`. + +## 1. What the 17 frameworks taught us + +The survey in `../frameworks/` gives us a short list of mechanisms that demonstrably buy accuracy per dollar, and a short list of mechanisms that burn money without paying for themselves. + +| Keep, because it pays | Evidence | +|---|---| +| One structured extraction call per chunk, no gleaning | fast-graphrag indexes in minutes at 1 call per chunk and still outscores nano-graphrag on 2Wiki retrieval. Microsoft's own docs attribute about three quarters of cost to extraction, and gleaning doubles it. | +| Facts (triples) as first-class retrieval units, not just entities | HippoRAG 2's largest gain over HippoRAG 1 comes from matching the query against fact embeddings and seeding the walk from facts. | +| Personalized PageRank from query seeds to passages | HippoRAG 2 and fast-graphrag get multi-hop retrieval in milliseconds with no LLM in the loop. Planner-based systems (KAG, Youtu) need 6 to 15 calls to do the same job. | +| Original chunks as the answer payload, graph as the router | 16 of 17 frameworks do this. Summaries hallucinate and cannot be erased. | +| Provenance counts on every node and edge | LightRAG's delete-by-document works only because it stores which chunk produced each entity. HippoRAG 2's delete works because facts carry source counts. | +| Content-hash sync at document level | GraphRAG-SDK's update path is the only one that is crash-safe and proportional to the change. | +| Embedding-based entity canonicalization with an LLM judge only in the ambiguous band | fast-graphrag's identity edges and GraphRAG-SDK's double-vote judge are the only resolution strategies better than string equality. 14 of 17 use string equality. | +| Local cross-encoder reranker instead of an LLM filter | TrustGraph uses flashrank; HippoRAG's DSPy filter is an LLM call per query that mostly drops facts. | + +| Drop, because it does not pay | Evidence | +|---|---| +| Leiden communities plus LLM report per community at index time | Microsoft and nano-graphrag spend one LLM call per community per level, then either never re-cluster (stale) or re-cluster everything on insert. Youtu builds communities and discards them at query time. | +| Map-reduce global search over all reports | Dozens of 12k-token calls per question. | +| LLM summarisation of merged entity descriptions | LightRAG, Microsoft, nano all do this. It is an extra call that produces text you cannot attribute to a chunk, so it cannot be erased when a chunk is deleted. | +| LLM query planner by default | KAG and Youtu pay 4 to 15 calls per question. Use it only as an escalation path. | +| Exact-string entity resolution | Universal weak spot. | +| Research-code shortcuts | Hard-coded sleeps, whole-corpus re-extraction, positional parsing of delimiter strings. Use JSON mode or constrained decoding. | + +## 2. Design goals, in priority order + +1. **Erasable.** Deleting a document is a database transaction: zero LLM calls, zero embedding calls, bounded by the number of chunks in that document. The graph after deleting document D must be byte-identical to the graph that would exist had D never been indexed. This is the invariant that makes the system enterprise-safe (GDPR erasure, contract expiry, retracted documents). +2. **Cheap to index.** Target one LLM call and one embedding batch per chunk, with a small model. No second pass, no summaries, no community reports. +3. **At least as accurate as HippoRAG 2 on multi-hop QA, and better than LightRAG on domain QA.** The accuracy levers are facts as retrieval units, hybrid dense plus sparse seeding, entity canonicalization, PPR, and a local reranker. +4. **Cheap to query.** One embedding call, one PPR, one local reranker pass, one answer call. An optional second retrieval round only when a confidence gate fails. +5. **One database.** Postgres with pgvector for truth. An in-memory sparse matrix per tenant for PPR, rebuilt incrementally from the database. No Java server, no message broker, no separate clustering service. +6. **Global questions without index-time cost.** Topic summaries are built lazily at query time and cached with a content hash of the chunk set they cover, so they invalidate automatically on delete. + +## 3. Data model: the ledger + +Three node kinds and four edge kinds. Every node and edge carries `prov`, a map from chunk id to count. A record exists if and only if its `prov` is non-empty. + +``` +Document(doc_id, content_hash, tenant, metadata, created_at) +Chunk(chunk_id, doc_id, ordinal, text, tokens, embedding, bm25_tsv) + +Entity(entity_id, canonical_name, type, name_embedding, prov) + Alias(alias_text, entity_id, prov) -- every surface form ever seen + Mention(chunk_id, entity_id, description, prov) -- per-chunk description, never merged by LLM + +Fact(fact_id, subject_entity_id, predicate, object_entity_id, sentence, embedding, prov) + FactSource(fact_id, chunk_id, evidence_span, prov) + +Synonym(entity_a, entity_b, score, prov) -- embedding-derived, recomputed from Mentions + +TopicCache(topic_key, chunk_set_hash, summary, created_at) -- lazy, invalidated by hash +``` + +Why this shape: + +- **Mentions instead of merged descriptions.** LightRAG joins all descriptions with a separator and asks an LLM to summarise once there are eight. That summary cannot be attributed to a chunk. We keep one description per chunk per entity. At query time we show the top-k mentions by PPR score. Nothing to summarise, nothing to un-summarise. +- **Facts carry their sentence and evidence span.** This is what gets embedded and matched against the query, following HippoRAG 2. The evidence span lets the answer prompt quote exact text and lets a reviewer verify the extraction. +- **Aliases are kept forever while they have provenance.** When chunk 17 called the entity "IBM" and chunk 42 called it "International Business Machines", both aliases point to one entity. Delete chunk 42 and the alias loses one unit of provenance; if it reaches zero it disappears, but the entity survives on chunk 17. +- **Synonym edges are derived, not extracted.** They are recomputed from name embeddings for the entities touched by an insert or delete. No LLM. + +## 4. Indexing pipeline + +```mermaid +flowchart LR + A[Document] --> B[Hash and diff] + B -->|unchanged| Z[skip] + B -->|changed| C[Structure-aware chunking 512 to 800 tokens] + C --> D[Optional GLiNER NER pre-pass, local] + D --> E[One LLM call per chunk, JSON schema] + E --> F[Entities, facts, descriptions, evidence spans] + F --> G[Batch embed: chunks, entity names, fact sentences] + G --> H[Canonicalize entities] + H -->|cos above 0.92 and same type| I[Merge] + H -->|0.80 to 0.92| J[Batched LLM judge, double vote] + H -->|below 0.80| K[New entity] + I --> L[Ledger upsert: increment prov] + J --> L + K --> L + L --> M[Recompute synonym edges for touched entities] + M --> N[Update per-tenant sparse matrix] +``` + +Step by step: + +1. **Hash and diff.** `content_hash` of the whole document, plus a hash per chunk. A re-upload with three changed paragraphs re-extracts only the changed chunks. Unchanged chunks keep their ledger entries. This is GraphRAG-SDK's `update()` idea applied at chunk granularity. +2. **Chunking.** Structure-aware (headings, tables, lists) with a 512 to 800 token target and 10 percent overlap. HippoRAG 2 ships no chunker and treats each document as one chunk, which is why its passage recall is sensitive to document length. Youtu's 5000-token chunks produce prompts that cost more than the extraction they feed. +3. **Optional NER pre-pass.** GLiNER or spaCy on CPU, as in GraphRAG-SDK. It seeds the extraction prompt with candidate spans so a small model misses fewer entities. Cost is CPU only. Measured as an ablation. +4. **One extraction call.** JSON schema with `entities[]` (name, type from a tenant-configurable type list, one-sentence description), `facts[]` (subject, predicate, object, sentence, evidence_span), and nothing else. No gleaning. Model: a 7B to 32B instruction model self-hosted via vLLM, or the cheapest hosted tier. Constrained decoding or JSON mode, never delimiter strings. +5. **Batch embedding.** One embedding request per batch of chunks, entity names and fact sentences. A 384 to 1024 dimension model is enough; HippoRAG's NV-Embed-v2 at 7B is a GPU cost most enterprises will not pay. +6. **Canonicalization.** For each new entity name, HNSW lookup over existing entity name embeddings in the same tenant, filtered by type. Three bands: high similarity merges automatically, a middle band goes to a batched LLM judge that is asked once per pair with both descriptions and votes twice (GraphRAG-SDK's double vote), low similarity creates a new entity. Thresholds are tenant-tunable and reported in the evaluation. +7. **Ledger upsert.** Every touched record gets `prov[chunk_id] += 1`. Mentions, aliases, fact sources all recorded. One transaction per document. +8. **Synonym edges.** Recomputed only for entities whose name embedding is new or whose neighbours changed. k-nearest with cosine at or above 0.80, as in HippoRAG 2. +9. **Sparse matrix update.** The per-tenant PPR matrix (entities, facts, chunks as rows and columns) is updated in place for the touched rows. A full rebuild from the database is available as a background job and takes seconds for a million-edge graph with scipy. + +Index cost target per chunk: 1 LLM call of roughly 1.2k input and 400 output tokens, 1 embedding batch, and on average well under 0.1 LLM judge calls. Compare: LightRAG 2 calls plus summaries, Microsoft about 2 plus one per community, KAG 3 to 4, HyperGraphRAG 3 to 5. + +## 5. Deletion, the point of the design + +``` +DELETE document D: + for chunk c in D: + for record r in ledger where c in r.prov: + r.prov[c] -= 1 + if r.prov is empty: mark r for removal + remove marked Mentions, FactSources, Aliases, Facts, Entities, Synonyms (in that order) + drop rows of removed nodes from the sparse matrix + invalidate TopicCache entries whose chunk_set_hash covered any c + delete chunks and document +commit +``` + +Properties: + +- **Zero model calls.** No re-extraction, no re-summarisation, no re-clustering, no re-embedding. Everything removed was derived only from the deleted chunks; everything kept has other provenance. +- **Bounded cost.** Proportional to the number of ledger records touched by the deleted chunks, which is linear in document size. +- **Exactness.** Because no record was ever produced by combining chunks through an LLM, the post-delete state equals the never-indexed state. The one exception is the LLM judge's merge decision, which is recorded as a Synonym with provenance from both chunks; if one side is deleted the merge is undone and the surviving entity reverts to its own canonical name. +- **Comparison.** Microsoft GraphRAG: no delete. nano-graphrag: no delete. LightRAG: delete by document, but entity descriptions were LLM-summarised, so it must re-run the summary from cached extraction (an LLM call per touched entity when the cache misses). HippoRAG 2: provenance-based delete, but no chunker and in-RAM only. KAG: UPSERT delete through the OpenSPG server. GraphRAG-SDK: delete by document in FalkorDB. R2R: deletes document rows but leaves graph copies. Everything else: none. + +## 6. Query pipeline + +```mermaid +sequenceDiagram + participant U as User + participant Q as Query service + participant V as pgvector + BM25 + participant P as PPR (in-memory) + participant R as Local reranker + participant L as LLM + U->>Q: question + Q->>V: embed question (1 call); dense top-k facts, entities, chunks; BM25 top-k chunks + V-->>Q: seeds with scores + Q->>P: reset vector: facts weighted by similarity, chunks by hybrid score + P-->>Q: PPR scores for all chunks + Q->>R: top 30 chunks by PPR, cross-encoder rerank against question + R-->>Q: top 8 chunks, top facts, top mentions + Q->>Q: confidence gate: max rerank score and seed coverage + alt gate passes + Q->>L: one answer call with chunks, facts, evidence spans, chunk ids + else gate fails + Q->>L: one decomposition call, re-run retrieval per sub-question, merge, one answer call + end + L-->>U: answer with chunk citations +``` + +1. **Hybrid seeding.** Dense similarity against fact sentences, entity names and chunk text, plus BM25 over chunk text. Sparse retrieval catches exact identifiers (part numbers, ticket ids, people's names) that embeddings blur, which matters in enterprise corpora. No framework in the survey combines all four seed sources; LightRAG and HippoRAG use dense only. +2. **Personalized PageRank.** Reset mass goes to seed facts (which spread to their member entities and source chunks), seed entities, and seed chunks. Damping 0.5 as in HippoRAG 2, re-tuned in the evaluation. The walk is a sparse matrix-vector loop in scipy; sub-10 ms on a million-edge graph. +3. **Local reranking.** A cross-encoder (bge-reranker-base or flashrank) over the top 30 chunks. CPU, about 100 ms. Replaces HippoRAG's LLM recognition filter. +4. **Confidence gate.** If the best rerank score is below a threshold, or the seed entities are not all connected to retrieved chunks, escalate to one decomposition call and a second retrieval round, capped at two rounds. This is Youtu's IRCoT loop with a budget. Expected to fire on a minority of questions; the rate is reported in the evaluation. +5. **Context assembly.** Top 8 chunks in document order with chunk ids, the top facts with evidence spans, and the top mentions for seed entities. Token budget 6k by default. +6. **Answer.** One LLM call. Citations are chunk ids, which resolve to document, page and span. + +Query cost target: 1 embedding call, 1 LLM answer call, plus on a minority of queries 1 decomposition call and 1 more embedding call. Compare: LightRAG 2 calls, HippoRAG 2 2 to 3, Microsoft global dozens, KAG 6 to 15. + +## 7. Global questions without index-time reports + +Community reports are the most expensive and least erasable artefact in the Microsoft family. We replace them with lazy topics: + +- **Topic key.** Entities are clustered on their name embeddings with a cheap algorithm (k-means or HDBSCAN) that runs in seconds and needs no LLM. A topic is a cluster id plus the set of chunk ids reachable from its entities. +- **Lazy summary.** The first time a query is classified as global (a cheap heuristic: few or no high-confidence seeds, question words like "overall", "themes", "compare across"), the top topics by seed overlap are summarised by one LLM call each, and the summary is cached under `chunk_set_hash`. +- **Automatic invalidation.** Deleting or adding a chunk changes the hash of every topic it belongs to, so the cached summary is simply not found next time and is regenerated on demand. No background job, no stale reports. +- **Cost.** Zero at index time. At query time, the first global question on a fresh corpus costs k summary calls (k topics, typically 5 to 20); subsequent global questions hit the cache until the corpus changes. + +This gives Microsoft-style global answers on a corpus that is static for days, and degrades gracefully to pay-as-you-ask on a corpus that churns. + +## 8. Storage and deployment + +- **Postgres 16 with pgvector and pg_trgm.** Tables as in section 3, HNSW indexes on the three embedding columns, GIN index on `bm25_tsv`, GIN on the `prov` JSONB. Row-level security by tenant. +- **In-memory PPR matrix per tenant.** scipy CSR, loaded from the database on first query, updated in place on insert and delete, checkpointed to disk. For graphs beyond roughly 50 million edges, shard by tenant or move the walk into the database with a recursive CTE at the cost of latency. +- **Models.** Extraction: a 7B to 32B instruction model on vLLM, or a hosted small model. Embeddings: a 384 to 1024 dimension open model. Reranker: bge-reranker-base on CPU. Answer: any model the tenant chooses. Nothing in the pipeline requires a frontier model. +- **No other services.** No Java, no broker, no clustering microservice, no graph database. A single container plus Postgres. + +## 9. Expected position against the field + +| Dimension | Lightfoot target | Best in survey today | +|---|---|---| +| Index LLM calls per chunk | 1 (+ under 0.1 judge) | fast-graphrag 1, neo4j 1 | +| Query LLM calls | 1 (2 to 3 when gate fails) | RAGFlow 0 to 1, neo4j 1 | +| Delete cost | DB transaction, 0 model calls | HippoRAG 2 (RAM only), GraphRAG-SDK (FalkorDB only) | +| Entity resolution | Embedding bands plus batched judge | GraphRAG-SDK | +| Multi-hop | PPR plus gated second round | HippoRAG 2 | +| Global questions | Lazy cached topics | Microsoft (index-time reports) | +| Infrastructure | Postgres only | LightRAG (Postgres backend) | + +Hypotheses to test, in the order they matter: + +- H1. Index cost per chunk is at or below fast-graphrag and under half of LightRAG at equal model. +- H2. Numbers come from `05-results-all.md` and `04-results-musique.md`; every one was measured in this project. + +## Abstract + +Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation improves multi-hop question answering, but production systems face two costs the research literature rarely measures: building the graph, and removing documents from it. We present Lightfoot, a GraphRAG system in which every entity, fact and synonym edge is a deterministic function of per-passage extractions that carry chunk-level provenance. Indexing makes one language-model call per passage, retrieval makes none, and deleting a document is a database transaction with zero model calls. We verify on the full 11,402-passage MuSiQue corpus that after deleting 10% of documents, the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. We compare against HippoRAG 2, LightRAG and fast-graphrag under identical models, embeddings and answer prompts on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA. Lightfoot builds the cheapest index on all three, 26 to 31% below HippoRAG 2 and 3 to 6 times below LightRAG and fast-graphrag. Its retrieval accuracy is significantly higher than HippoRAG 2's on MuSiQue (+2.8 points recall@5 and +4.3 points recall@10 on a held-out split) and HotpotQA (+1.3 points recall@10, +5.3 points exact match), and significantly lower on 2WikiMultiHopQA at recall@2 (-3.9) and F1 (-8.1). LightRAG needed 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours to delete the same documents; fast-graphrag cannot delete at all. + +## 1. Introduction + +- Enterprises must delete: retention policies, right-to-erasure requests, retracted or superseded documents. A survey of 17 open-source GraphRAG frameworks (`../frameworks/`) found only five with document-level delete, and none that claims the result equals a never-indexed graph. +- Index cost differs by an order of magnitude across frameworks for similar accuracy. Most of it goes to second extraction passes, model-written description summaries and community reports. +- Contributions: + 1. A provenance model in which every derived record is a pure function of the surviving per-passage extractions, so deletion is exact and needs no model calls. + 2. A one-call extraction schema that halves output tokens while doubling facts per passage. + 3. A retrieval pipeline with no model calls: fact-seeded Personalized PageRank fused with a local cross-encoder. + 4. A cost-normalised, deletion-audited comparison against three open-source baselines under identical models and prompts, including two baseline failure modes uncovered along the way. + +## 2. Method + +### 2.1 Extraction + +One call per passage to an open 70B model returns minified JSON: up to 12 entities (name, type, 8-word description) and up to 12 facts as `[subject, predicate, object, evidence]` arrays, with evidence a verbatim quote of up to 12 words. On MuSiQue this averaged 269 output tokens and 7.7 facts per passage. + +### 2.2 Resolution and the erasure invariant + +Each (chunk, name) pair is stored as a *form*. Two forms of the same type are linked when the cosine of their name embeddings is at least 0.92. An entity is a connected component of live forms, identified by its smallest member name, and its canonical name is the alias with the most provenance. Synonym edges join every same-type pair at cosine 0.80 or above, with no top-k cap. Name embeddings are computed in fixed-shape batches so they do not depend on batch composition. + +Every link, entity and synonym edge is therefore a function of the set of live forms alone, independent of insertion order, batching or history. Deleting a document removes its forms and recomputes only the components it touched. The result is, by construction, the graph that would exist had the document never been indexed. + +Two choices were made for exactness: no top-k synonyms, and no model judge for ambiguous name pairs. On a 2,000-passage ablation, neither changed recall beyond noise. + +### 2.3 Retrieval + +1. Embed the question. +2. Seed a Personalized PageRank walk on the entity-passage graph. The subject and object entities of the two most similar facts receive weight equal to the fact score divided by the entity's passage count; the 100 most similar passages receive weight up to 0.05. +3. Walk with damping 0.9 and take the top 30 passages. +4. Score them with a local cross-encoder, and fuse the cross-encoder rank with the PageRank rank by reciprocal rank fusion (k = 60). +5. Send the top 8 passages to one answer call that returns a short span. + +Settings were chosen on MuSiQue questions 1 to 500 only. + +## 3. Experimental setup + +- **Datasets:** MuSiQue (1,000 questions, 11,402 passages), 2WikiMultiHopQA (300 / 2,131) and HotpotQA (300 / 2,957), built following HippoRAG's construction. +- **Models, identical for every system:** Llama 3.3 70B for extraction; gpt-5.6-luna with reasoning off for answers; bge-base-en-v1.5 embeddings; the same short-span, best-guess answer instruction. +- **Answers:** generated for the first 300 questions of each dataset; the remaining MuSiQue questions are scored on retrieval only. +- **Deletion audit:** a seeded random 10% of documents is deleted, then every question is re-queried. Recall is reported separately for questions whose evidence survived and questions whose evidence was deleted. +- **Cost:** every model call is logged, and token counts are priced at one fixed list price per model. +- **Statistics:** 95% paired bootstrap intervals. MuSiQue comparisons use the held-out questions 501 to 1000. + +## 4. Results + +See `05-results-all.md` for the full tables. Summary: + +- **Index cost.** Lightfoot is cheapest on every dataset: $1.64 vs $2.23 (HippoRAG 2), $4.89 (fast-graphrag) and about $9.5 (LightRAG) on MuSiQue. +- **Accuracy.** Across 14 paired comparisons with HippoRAG 2, Lightfoot is significantly better on 5, worse on 2 (both on 2Wiki) and tied on 7. Against LightRAG and fast-graphrag it is better on every dataset at recall@5. +- **Deletion.** Zero model calls on every dataset, and an exact match to a fresh index of the survivors on the full MuSiQue corpus. LightRAG made 2,187 calls and took 3.7 hours on MuSiQue; fast-graphrag has no delete path. +- **Ablations, MuSiQue held-out R@5:** + +| Component | Effect | +|---|---| +| Rerank fused with PageRank, instead of replacing it | about +3.5 points | +| Damping 0.9 vs 0.5 under fusion | +2 to 3 points | +| Seeding from 2 facts vs 5 | about +1 point | +| Entity-only graph vs fact nodes | none | +| Model judge vs none | none | + +## 5. Analysis + +- **Where the graph helps.** The graph finds passages that share no words with the question. In a traced MuSiQue example, the passage naming the album's performer was outside the top 100 by dense similarity but was reached in two hops and ranked fourth after fusion. +- **Where it fails.** Seeding on the two most similar facts sometimes picks trivia, such as a release date or a chart position, over the fact that carries the chain. HippoRAG 2 filters seed facts with a model call; that call is the likely source of its 2Wiki advantage, where questions compare two named entities. +- **Baseline failure modes found during benchmarking:** + - LightRAG aborted most of its first index after an embedding timeout but reported success, leaving 31% of chunks indexed. + - Its default file storage rewrites the full graph and vector files for every document, about 415 MB per document at 3,000 passages. + - HippoRAG 2 aborted its whole index on 24 malformed model outputs. + +## 6. Limitations + +- **One tuned dataset.** Retrieval settings were tuned on half of MuSiQue. The other two datasets are untuned, and one of them is a loss. +- **Small answer sets.** Answer metrics rest on 232 to 300 questions per dataset. +- **Shared embedder.** HippoRAG 2 used the shared bge-base embedder, not its paper's 7B NV-Embed-v2, so its absolute numbers are below those published. +- **Estimated cost.** LightRAG's MuSiQue index cost is estimated from its call count, because its extraction was billed across several runs. +- **Untested erasure.** Exactness was not tested for the baselines' deletes. HippoRAG 2's provenance-based delete may also be exact. +- **No global questions.** Corpus-level summarisation questions were not evaluated; lazy topic summaries exist but fired on only five MuSiQue questions. + +## 7. Pros and cons by family + +### Family A: community-summary graphs (Microsoft GraphRAG, nano-graphrag, R2R) + +**How it works.** Entities and relations are extracted per chunk, merged by name, clustered with hierarchical Leiden, and each community gets an LLM-written report. Global questions are answered by map-reducing over the reports; local questions start from entity vector hits. + +**Pros** +- The only family that can answer corpus-level sensemaking questions such as "what are the main themes" without reading everything at query time. +- Rich provenance tables: every claim traces to text units, entities, and reports. +- Microsoft's implementation has prompt auto-tuning, a CLI, Azure backends, and the best documentation in the set. + +**Cons** +- Indexing is the most expensive in the set: extraction, gleaning, summaries, then one LLM call per community per level. Microsoft's own docs attribute about three quarters of cost to extraction. +- Global search costs dozens of 12k-token map calls per question. +- Incremental updates do not re-cluster, so communities drift stale. nano-graphrag regenerates every report on every insert instead. +- Entity resolution is exact string match. Multi-hop reasoning is one hop in local mode. +- Microsoft GraphRAG is in declared maintenance mode. R2R's graph search is only vector kNN over descriptions, with communities built by an external service. + +### Family B: keyword dual-level graphs (LightRAG, PathRAG, MiniRAG, HyperGraphRAG, RAGFlow) + +**How it works.** Same extraction step, but no clustering or reports. The query is turned into low-level keywords (matched against entity vectors) and high-level keywords (matched against relation vectors). Hits are expanded one hop and the provenance chunks are stitched into a budgeted context. + +**Pros** +- Roughly half the indexing cost of Family A, and two LLM calls per query. +- LightRAG has the most complete lifecycle: queued inserts, delete-by-document with cached rebuild, entity edit and merge, workspaces, 25 storage implementations, REST API and UI. +- Easy to fork, which is why PathRAG, MiniRAG, HyperGraphRAG, and Graph-R1 all start from it. +- RAGFlow puts the graph rows in the existing search index, so there is no extra infrastructure and tenancy and citations come for free. + +**Cons** +- No corpus-level summaries, so global questions degrade to whatever the top relations happen to be. +- Multi-hop is one hop by default. PathRAG fixes this with path enumeration but does it by loading the whole graph into memory and enumerating all simple paths, which is exponential. +- Exact-name entity resolution throughout. +- The forks are research quality: PathRAG has a hard-coded 20-second sleep and an invalid default mode, MiniRAG re-extracts the whole corpus on every insert with no cache, HyperGraphRAG relies on brittle positional parsing and has a broken delete path. +- RAGFlow's graph feature is mid-rewrite. The legacy PageRank and community path needs columns the new compiler never writes. + +### Family C: PageRank over a triple graph (HippoRAG 2, fast-graphrag, KAG's kg_fr retriever) + +**How it works.** Extraction produces entity and fact nodes linked to passages. At query time the query is linked to a few seed nodes and Personalized PageRank spreads activation across the graph; passages are ranked by their resulting score. No LLM reasoning over the graph is needed. + +**Pros** +- Cheapest indexing among graph methods: one to two calls per chunk, no summaries, no communities. +- Multi-hop retrieval is deterministic, milliseconds, and does not depend on an LLM following paths. +- Strongest published multi-hop numbers for the cost. Core idea in one paragraph + +fast-graphrag keeps the LLM-built entity/relationship graph but drops communities and community reports entirely. Retrieval is HippoRAG-style: the LLM extracts named and generic entities from the query, those are matched to graph nodes with an HNSW cosine search, the resulting node weights seed a **personalized PageRank** over the whole igraph graph, and PageRank mass is propagated through two sparse matrices (entities -> relationships -> chunks) to rank relationships and source chunks. The answer is generated from a tabular context of top entities, relationships, and chunks. Index cost is one or two LLM calls per chunk plus occasional description/edge-merge calls; there is no per-community summarization, which is where the "6x cheaper than graphrag" claim comes from. The extraction prompt is "promptable" via a user-supplied `domain`, `example_queries`, and `entity_types`. + +## 3. Indexing pipeline, step by step + +Entry: `GraphRAG.insert(content, metadata)` -> `BaseGraphRAG.async_insert` (`fast_graphrag/_graphrag.py`). `GraphRAG` (`fast_graphrag/__init__.py`) wires the default services through a nested `GraphRAG.Config` dataclass. + +1. **Checkpoint/open**: `state_manager.insert_start()` opens all storages inside `Workspace.with_checkpoints` (`_storage/_namespace.py`); with `n_checkpoints > 0` each insert writes to a new timestamped sub-directory and old ones are pruned. +2. **Chunking** (`_services/_chunk_extraction.py::DefaultChunkingService`): regex split on `DEFAULT_SEPARATORS` (paragraph breaks and CJK/Latin sentence punctuation), merged greedily to `chunk_token_size 800` with `chunk_token_overlap 100`, **measured in characters using `TOKEN_TO_CHAR_RATIO = 4`** (`_utils.py`), not a tokenizer. Chunk id = `xxhash.xxh3_64_intdigest(content) // 2`. Input bytes are sanitized. Chunks carry the document `metadata` dict. +3. **Dedup**: `DefaultStateManagerService.filter_new_chunks` masks chunks whose hash already exists in `chunk_storage` (`PickleIndexedKeyValueStorage`). +4. **Information extraction** (`_services/_information_extraction.py::DefaultInformationExtractionService.extract`), one asyncio task per document: + - Per chunk: `format_and_send_prompt("entity_relationship_extraction", response_model=TGraph)`. The system prompt `entity_relationship_extraction_text` (`_prompt.py`) is parameterized by `{domain}`, `{example_queries}`, `{entity_types}` and asks for strictly valid JSON with `entities[{name,type,desc}]`, `relationships[...]`, `other_relationships[...]`; it also instructs the model to connect isolated entities. The pydantic `TGraph.Model` (`_types.py`) upper-cases names and types and parses JSON via `instructor` (`Mode.JSON`) with `json_repair` as a dependency. + - **Gleaning**: `_gleaning` runs `max_gleaning_steps` rounds (`_services/_base.py` default **0**, so off by default) of `entity_relationship_continue_extraction` plus a `TGleaningStatus` done/continue check. Note: the check compares `gleaning_status.status == Literal["done"]`, which is always false in Python, so when enabled gleaning always runs the full number of steps. + - Entity types not in `entity_types` (after stripping spaces/underscores and upper-casing) are relabelled `UNKNOWN`. Each relationship gets `chunks = [chunk.id]`. + - `_merge`: per-document chunk graphs are upserted into a temporary `IGraphStorage` using the `information_extraction_upsert_policy` = `DefaultGraphUpsertPolicy(NodeUpsertPolicy_SummarizeDescription, EdgeUpsertPolicy_UpsertIfValidNodes)`. +5. **Graph upsert into the main store** (`_services/_state_manager.py::DefaultStateManagerService.upsert`): + - Nodes: `NodeUpsertPolicy_SummarizeDescription` (`_policies/_graph_upsert.py`) groups by name, appends the existing node, joins descriptions with newlines, and if the result exceeds `max_node_description_size` (512 chars) calls the LLM with `PROMPTS["summarize_entity_descriptions"]` (`TEntityDescription`); type = most common. + - Edges: `EdgeUpsertPolicy_UpsertValidAndMergeSimilarByLLM`: edges are grouped by `(source, target)`; if existing + new edges between a pair exceed `edge_merge_threshold` (5), the LLM is asked with `PROMPTS["edges_group_similar"]` (`TEditRelationList`) to group duplicate facts into merged descriptions; chunk lists are unioned, merged-away edges deleted. Otherwise edges are simply inserted (multi-edges between the same pair are allowed). + - **Entity embeddings**: `embedding_service.encode([entity.to_str()])` where `to_str()` = `"[TYPE] NAME\n[DESCRIPTION] desc"`; upserted into `HNSWVectorStorage` keyed by node index. + - **Entity deduplication by similarity**: `entity_storage.get_knn(embeddings, top_k=3)`; pairs with cosine score >= `insert_similarity_score_threshold` (0.9) that are not already neighbours get an **identity edge** with description `"is"` and no chunks. Nodes are not merged, only linked, so PageRank flows between duplicates. + - Chunks are stored (`chunk_storage.upsert`). +6. **Commit** (`insert_done`): builds and pickles two sparse matrices via `PickleBlobStorage`: `map_e2r` (entities x relationships incidence from `IGraphStorage.get_entities_to_relationships_map`) and `map_r2c` (relationships x chunks from edge `chunks` attributes). All storages are flushed (igraph pickle, hnswlib index + metadata, KV pickle). + +```mermaid +flowchart TB + IN[insert text + metadata] --> CH[DefaultChunkingService
separator split, 800 tok as chars/4, overlap 100, xxhash ids] + CH --> NEW[filter_new_chunks] + NEW --> EX[entity_relationship_extraction
domain / example_queries / entity_types
instructor JSON -> TGraph] + EX -. optional max_gleaning_steps .-> GL[continue_extraction] + EX --> DOCG[per-document IGraphStorage merge] + DOCG --> NU[NodeUpsertPolicy_SummarizeDescription

Graph data model + +Defined in `fast_graphrag/_types.py` as dataclasses with paired pydantic `Model`s for LLM I/O. + +- **Node** `TEntity`: `name` (upper-cased, is the node id), `type` (upper-cased, constrained to user `entity_types` or `UNKNOWN`), `description`. Context fields `F_TO_CONTEXT = ["name", "description"]`. No degree, no community, no source chunk list on nodes. +- **Edge** `TRelation`: `source`, `target`, `description`, `chunks: List[THash]` (provenance lives on edges, not nodes). Graph is undirected (`ig.Graph(directed=False)`), multi-edges allowed, plus synthetic identity edges (`description="is"`, `chunks=[]`) between near-duplicate entities. +- **Chunk** `TChunk`: `id` (xxh3 64-bit), `content`, `metadata` dict (surfaced in context via `F_TO_CONTEXT = ["content", "metadata"]`). +- **Derived matrices**: `map_e2r` (entities x relationships), `map_r2c` (relationships x chunks), rebuilt on every `insert_done`. +- **Context/response**: `TContext` holds scored lists of entities, relations, chunks; `TQueryResponse` = `response` + `context`, with `to_dict()` for serialization. +- No communities, reports, claims, or documents table. Document identity is not preserved beyond chunk metadata. + +Working directory layout: `Workspace.make_for(namespace)` creates namespaces `graph`, `entities`, `chunks`, `map_e2r`, `map_r2c` under `working_dir` (or `working_dir//` when `n_checkpoints > 0`). Query / retrieval modes + +There is exactly one retrieval mode. `GraphRAG.query(query, QueryParam, response_model=None)` -> `BaseGraphRAG.async_query` (`_graphrag.py`). `QueryParam`: `with_references` (False), `only_context` (False), `entities_max_tokens` 4000, `relations_max_tokens` 3000, `chunks_max_tokens` 9000 (converted to characters x4 for truncation). + +1. **Query entity extraction** (`DefaultInformationExtractionService.extract_entities_from_query`): 1 LLM call with `PROMPTS["entity_extraction_query"]` returning `TQueryEntities{named: [...], generic: [...]}` (named entities are upper-cased and written as `[TYPE] NAME`; generic concepts such as "film director"). +2. **Embedding**: one `encode` call for `named + "[NONE] " + generic + [query]`. +3. **Vector scoring** (`DefaultStateManagerService.get_context` -> `_score_entities_by_vectordb`): + - named entities: `score_all(top_k=1, threshold=query_similarity_score_threshold=0.7)`; + - generic entities and the raw query: `score_all(top_k=20, threshold=0.5)`; + - each row is normalized to sum 1, rows are max-combined into a single `(1, #entities)` sparse seed vector. Generation / answer synthesis + +- Prompts are entries in `fast_graphrag/_prompt.py::PROMPTS`: `entity_relationship_extraction_system/_prompt`, `entity_relationship_continue_extraction_*`, `entity_relationship_gleaning_done_extraction_*`, `entity_extraction_query`, `summarize_entity_descriptions`, `edges_group_similar`, `generate_response_query_with_references`, `generate_response_query_no_references`, `fail_response`. `format_and_send_prompt` (`_llm/_base.py`) looks up `_system` / `_prompt` pairs or a single key. +- Answer prompt instructs the model to use Entities/Relationships as a map and read Sources for detail, to be concise, and to say no relevant information was found rather than invent. With `with_references=True` it must append `[]` after each sentence, where ids index the `## Sources` list; `TQueryResponse.context.chunks` carries the same order so callers can resolve ids to chunk content and metadata (`examples/query_parameters.ipynb`). +- Structured output: responses are parsed into `TAnswer{answer}` or any pydantic `response_model` passed to `query()`, enabling typed answers. +- Single-shot generation only; no map-reduce, no streaming, no conversation history. + +## 8. LLM and embedding usage, cost profile + +- Default LLM: `OpenAILLMService` (`_llm/_llm_openai.py`) with `model="gpt-4o-mini"`, `instructor.Mode.JSON`, `AsyncOpenAI` (any OpenAI-compatible `base_url`), tenacity retries on rate-limit/connection/timeout. Concurrency: semaphore `max_requests_concurrent` from env `CONCURRENT_TASK_LIMIT` (default 1024), optional `aiolimiter` per-minute/per-second limiters (`rate_limit_per_minute`, `rate_limit_per_second`). Also `GeminiLLMService`/`GeminiEmbeddingService` (`_llm/_llm_genai.py`, google-genai and Vertex AI) and `VoyageAIEmbeddingService` (`_llm/_llm_voyage.py`). +- Default embedder: `OpenAIEmbeddingService` `text-embedding-3-small` (dim 1536), per-minute limiter on by default. +- No response cache in the OSS code (unlike the other two frameworks); repeated inserts of identical chunks are skipped by hash instead. +- Index-time LLM calls: 1 per chunk (gleaning off by default); +1 per entity whose merged description exceeds 512 chars; +1 per entity pair whose edge count exceeds 5 (edge grouping). Embedding calls: one batch per insert over all upserted entities. No community-level calls at all. README: *The Wizard of Oz* costs $0.08 vs $0.48 for graphrag (6x). +- Query-time: 1 LLM call (query entity extraction) + 1 embedding batch + 1 LLM call (answer) = 2 completions per query, plus CPU-side PPR over the full graph (igraph, fast for 10^5-10^6 nodes). +- Chunk sizes are estimated by characters (ratio 4), so actual token counts vary by language. + +Worked example: *A Christmas Carol* (~160k characters) becomes ~55 chunks of 3 200 characters; indexing is ~55 extraction calls with gpt-4o-mini (each roughly 2.5k prompt tokens including the long JSON-example system prompt) plus a handful of summarization/edge-merge calls and one embedding batch for a few hundred entities, which is consistent with the README's $0.08 figure. Querying costs two small completions regardless of corpus size; the graph walk is local CPU. + +## 9. Configuration and extension points + +- Constructor: `GraphRAG(working_dir, domain, example_queries, entity_types, n_checkpoints=0, config=GraphRAG.Config(...))`. `domain`, `example_queries`, `entity_types` are mandatory and are injected into the extraction prompt, which is the primary "tuning" mechanism. +- `GraphRAG.Config` fields (`fast_graphrag/__init__.py`): `chunking_service_cls`, `information_extraction_service_cls`, `information_extraction_upsert_policy`, `state_manager_cls`, `llm_service`, `embedding_service`, `graph_storage`, `entity_storage`, `chunk_storage`, `entity_ranking_policy`, `relation_ranking_policy`, `chunk_ranking_policy`, `node_upsert_policy`, `edge_upsert_policy`. Example in `examples/custom_llm.py`: `config=GraphRAG.Config(llm_service=OpenAILLMService(model=..., base_url=..., api_key=...), embedding_service=OpenAIEmbeddingService(...))`. +- Service/policy tunables: `DefaultChunkingServiceConfig(separators, chunk_token_size, chunk_token_overlap)`; `max_gleaning_steps` on the extraction service; `NodeUpsertPolicy_SummarizeDescription.Config(max_node_description_size, node_summarization_prompt, is_async)`; `EdgeUpsertPolicy_UpsertValidAndMergeSimilarByLLM.Config(edge_merge_threshold)`; `DefaultStateManagerService.insert_similarity_score_threshold` (0.9), `query_similarity_score_threshold` (0.7); `IGraphStorageConfig.ppr_damping`; `HNSWVectorStorageConfig(ef_construction, M, ef_search, num_threads)`; ranking policy configs. +- Prompts: mutate `fast_graphrag._prompt.PROMPTS[...]` before constructing. +- **Incremental updates**: first-class. Each `insert` only extracts new chunks (hash dedup), merges nodes/edges into the persistent igraph graph via the upsert policies, re-embeds only upserted nodes, adds identity edges, and rebuilds the two sparse maps. No global recomputation (no clustering exists), so cost is proportional to the delta. Strengths + +- Lowest indexing cost of the three: one LLM call per 800-token chunk by default, no community summarization, no per-entity summary unless descriptions grow large. +- Query retrieval is graph-native (personalized PageRank from HippoRAG) rather than "embed query, grab neighbours", which is well suited to multi-hop factoid questions; the author benchmark shows large gains on 2WikiMultihopQA multihop queries. +- True incremental updates proportional to the delta, with checkpointing. +- Embedding-based entity deduplication (identity edges) and LLM-based edge fact merging keep the graph from fragmenting as data accumulates. +- Structured-output everywhere (`instructor` + pydantic), typed `response_model` on queries, and an explicit `TContext` with scores returned alongside the answer. +- Domain/example-query/entity-type driven prompt makes the ontology steerable without editing prompt text. +- Small, well-typed code base with unit tests; policies and services are swappable dataclasses. + +## 12. Limitations and known issues + +- No global / summarization mode: without communities or reports it cannot answer "what are the main themes across the corpus" style questions; retrieval always bottoms out in top-8 chunks. +- Single-process file storage only (igraph pickle, hnswlib, pickles); no database backends, no multi-tenant workspaces in OSS, the whole graph and index are loaded into memory per process. +- Chunk sizing by characters/4 rather than tokens; no tokenizer-aware truncation (tiktoken is a dependency but not used for budgeting in the reviewed code). +- Gleaning is off by default and the done-check (`== Literal["done"]`) is a bug, so enabling it always runs all steps. +- `node_specificity` and `RankingPolicy_WithConfidence` are stubs raising `NotImplementedError`. +- No LLM response cache; no per-document delete; document identity is only preserved through chunk `metadata`. +- Citations are chunk indexes within the returned context, not stable ids; nodes have no provenance (only edges carry `chunks`), so entity-only facts are not traceable to sources. +- Identity edges link near-duplicate entities but never merge them, so duplicate nodes persist in the entities table shown to the LLM. +- Version 0.0.5, no documentation site, roadmap unclear; the team's effort is on the managed service. + +## 13. Best fit / when to choose it + +Choose fast-graphrag when you need cheap, incrementally updated graph indexing and precise multi-hop retrieval over facts (QA, agents, support/knowledge bases), you are happy with a single mode of query, and you can run everything in one process on local files. It is a good fit for OpenAI-compatible or Gemini endpoints and for workloads where index cost dominates. Prefer Microsoft GraphRAG when corpus-level summarization (global/DRIFT search) or Azure backends matter, and nano-graphrag when you want a hackable reference GraphRAG with community reports and pluggable graph/vector databases. + +## 14. Core idea in one paragraph + +Graph-R1 treats GraphRAG as a **multi-turn agent problem**: a small policy LLM (Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B-Instruct) repeatedly emits `…{"query": …}`, an external retrieval server answers inside `…`, and the loop ends when the policy emits `……` (or `max_turns` is hit). The knowledge base is HyperGraphRAG's n-ary hypergraph (hyperedge sentences + member entities, extracted once with GPT-4o-mini); retrieval is dual-channel dense matching (BGE-large over entity descriptions and over hyperedge sentences via FAISS) followed by one-hop bipartite expansion and **reciprocal-rank fusion** of the two channels. The policy is trained **end-to-end with GRPO** (also PPO and REINFORCE++ scripts) using a purely outcome-based reward: `-1 + format_reward (0..1) + answer_F1` where the F1 term is only awarded when the format is perfect. Retrieved `` tokens are masked out of the policy-gradient loss, so the model learns *when and what to query* and *how to compose answers*, not to imitate retrieved text. + +## 3. LLM and embedding usage, cost profile + +**Offline (once per corpus)** +* Hypergraph extraction: same as HyperGraphRAG — ~3 (max 5) `gpt-4o-mini` calls per 1200-token chunk plus occasional description summaries. For the six FlashRAG corpora (Wikipedia-derived, tens of thousands of passages each) this is the dominant API cost; the authors distribute pre-built graphs for this reason. +* Embedding: BGE-large-en-v1.5 over every entity (name+description) and every hyperedge sentence (and chunks, unused). Runs on whatever device FlagEmbedding picks (GPU if available at build time; CPU at serve time). + +**Training (per run)** +* GRPO: 128 prompts x 5 samples x up to 10 turns of vLLM generation per step, plus a retrieval HTTP call per active trajectory per turn, plus actor/ref log-prob passes. README: 4 x 48 GB GPUs for 3B; `max_prompt_length=4096` bounds the context (long multi-turn histories are left-truncated, which can drop the question — unclear whether the authors guard against this; I found no guard). +* The retrieval server runs BGE on **CPU** by default, which can bottleneck rollouts; batched calls mitigate this. +* No reward model GPU: rewards are rule-based. + +**Inference (per question)** +* 1 to `max_turns` policy generations (paper reports ~2-3 turns on average after training), each followed by one BGE encode + two FAISS Flat searches + graph lookups. No API LLM needed at inference; the 3B policy fits on one GPU. + +## 9. Configuration and extension points + +* **Hydra config**: `verl/trainer/config/ppo_trainer.yaml` (data lengths, actor/critic/rollout, `algorithm.adv_estimator`, `tool.*`: `max_turns`, `use_batch_tool_calls`, tag strings, `tool_custom_response_template`, `env`). Override on the CLI as in `run_*.sh`. +* **Swap the tool / knowledge source**: implement `agent/tool/tool_base.py::Tool` (`execute`, `batch_execute`, `calculate_reward`, `validate_args`) and register in `agent/tool/tools/__init__.py::_default_tools` (`search` -> hypergraph server, `wikisearch`, `calculator` exist). The policy prompt is fixed in `script_process.py`; changing tags requires editing `tool.*` YAML, `qa_em_and_format.py` regexes and `_create_loss_mask` tag strings together. +* **Swap retrieval behaviour**: `script_api.py` (k per channel = 5, `top_k=10`, embedding model) and `graphr1/operate.py::_build_query_context` (fusion rule). Returning chunk text instead of hyperedge sentences is a two-line change (commented code present). +* **Swap extraction LLM / embeddings for graph building**: `GraphR1(llm_model_func=…, embedding_func=…)` as in HyperGraphRAG (embedding_func is effectively unused because vdbs are KV); dense indexes are built separately by `embed_knowledge()`. +* **Swap reward**: `verl/trainer/main_ppo.py::RewardManager` calls `_default_compute_score_format_answer`; edit `qa_em_and_format.py` or pass a different function. `NaiveRewardManager`/`PrimeRewardManager` in `verl/workers/reward_manager/` are unused. +* **Base policy**: `-p ` in the run scripts; chat template assumptions (`<|im_start|>`, `<|im_end|>`) are Qwen-specific and baked into the reward parser, loss mask and response template — other model families need those strings changed. +* **Incremental update**: none. The hypergraph can be appended via `GraphR1.insert()` (HyperGraphRAG semantics), but `embed_knowledge()` rebuilds all FAISS indexes from scratch and the API server loads indexes once at startup. There is no deletion. Policy retraining is not required for new knowledge (the policy learns a querying behaviour, not the facts), which is the practical upside of the design. + +## 10. Benchmarks reported by the authors + +* **Datasets** (FlashRAG splits, Terabox download): 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, NQ, PopQA, TriviaQA. Training on each dataset's train split; test on its test split; corpus = that dataset's passages. +* **Metrics**: EM, F1 (`evaluation/eval.py`), LLM-judge generation score (`eval_g.py`, 7 rubrics x 0-100 blended with F1), average retrieval turns and response length (README figures `*_turn.png`, `*_res.png`). +* **Reported comparisons** (README figures; numbers from the paper, not in the repo — verify before quoting): (1) RL algorithms — GRPO > REINFORCE++ > PPO on F1/EM with Qwen2.5-3B; (2) across GraphRAG baselines — Graph-R1 (3B, GRPO) is reported to beat NaiveGeneration, StandardRAG, GraphRAG, LightRAG, PathRAG, HippoRAG2 and HyperGraphRAG *as well as* RL-RAG methods Search-R1 and R1-Searcher on average F1, with the abstract citing an average F1 of about 57.8 for the 7B setting (3B around the low 50s) versus roughly 40 or below for prompt-only GraphRAG baselines on the same splits; (3) scaling — 1.5B < 3B < 7B monotonically, with 1.5B sometimes failing to learn the format. Average turns settle around 2-3 and responses get longer than non-RL baselines. +* **Ablations** in the paper (not reproducible from repo scripts alone): removing the hypergraph (plain chunk retrieval), removing multi-turn (single query), and removing the format reward each reduce F1; hypergraph retrieval has higher per-query cost than chunk retrieval but higher answer quality. +* **Third-party**: none found in repo. Note Graph-R1's baseline numbers for HippoRAG2 / LightRAG use the same FlashRAG corpora and their own re-runs, so they are not directly comparable to those methods' own papers. + +## 11. Strengths + +* Clean separation: the **knowledge store is frozen and external** (HTTP), the **policy learns to use it**; new facts do not require retraining, and any retrieval backend speaking the `/search` contract can be swapped in. +* Outcome-only reward with format gating is simple, rule-based (no reward model) and demonstrably teaches small models (3B) a stable think -> query -> knowledge -> answer protocol. +* Loss masking of retrieved tokens (`_create_loss_mask`) is correctly implemented, so the policy is not trained to regurgitate knowledge blocks. +* Multi-turn querying gives genuine multi-hop behaviour without PPR or graph algorithms; the agent decomposes the question itself. +* Hypergraph sentences are a good retrieval unit for an agent: short, self-contained, readable, already de-contextualised by the extractor. +* Full veRL/Ray/vLLM/FSDP training stack vendored with working GRPO, PPO and REINFORCE++ scripts; wandb logging of F1/EM/format/turns. +* Inference needs no API LLM. + +## 12. Limitations and known issues + +* **Heavy and brittle environment**: pinned `torch 2.4 + vllm<=0.6.3 + flash-attn + ray`, 4 x 48 GB GPUs, hard-coded ports/paths, OpenAI key file, Terabox-only datasets and graphs; `verl` is vendored, not pip-installable from upstream. +* Qwen chat-template strings are hard-coded in reward parsing, loss masking and the tool-response template; other model families need code edits in three places. +* Retrieval quality is capped by **5 + 5 FAISS neighbours** and the unbounded one-hop expansion from entities (no token truncation in `_get_node_data`), then RRF to 10; hub entities bias the list toward high-degree hyperedges. Hyperedge FAISS scores are discarded (`rank = weight`). +* `SearchTool.execute` is a stub; only batched execution works. `PENALTY_FOR_INVALID=0` and tool rewards are 0, so all shaping comes from the format regex. +* Format reward counts 0.5 per well-formed query turn but is clamped at 1.0, so after one query there is no incentive difference between 1 and 10 queries other than context length; the paper's "turns" curves show it settles at 2-3 by F1 pressure, but that is emergent, not designed. +* Rollout context is left-truncated to 4096 tokens including the prompt; with 4096-token tool responses a single large `` block can push the question out of context. I found no safeguard. +* No incremental/delete path; FAISS indexes rebuilt wholesale; server loads everything into RAM; BGE runs on CPU at serve time. +* Graph building inherits all HyperGraphRAG issues (positional entity-to-hyperedge parsing, string-keyed nodes, no entity resolution, dead LightRAG code paths). +* No tests, squashed history, Chinese/English mixed comments, evaluation depends on a paid LLM judge. +* Reported gains are on Wikipedia QA with gold short answers; nothing in the repo evaluates long-form or domain corpora. + +## 13. Best fit / when to choose it + +Choose Graph-R1 when you (a) own a GPU training budget and want a **small, self-hosted policy model** that has learned to interrogate a knowledge base over multiple turns, (b) have gold short answers for your domain to drive the F1 reward, and (c) are comfortable running a veRL/Ray/vLLM stack. It is the right reference implementation for "RL-trained agentic GraphRAG" and for reusing its environment/reward/loss-mask code with your own retriever. It is the wrong choice for a drop-in RAG library, for corpora that change often, for long-form answers, or for teams without RL infrastructure — in those cases take the HyperGraphRAG retrieval server idea alone and drive it with a prompted frontier model. + +## 14. Core idea in one paragraph + +GraphRAG-SDK v1 is a single-database GraphRAG framework: FalkorDB holds the lexical layer (Document and Chunk nodes), the knowledge layer (typed entity nodes joined by a single `RELATES` edge type whose original predicate lives in a `rel_type` property), the vector indexes and full-text indexes, and even the ontology itself (stored as a sibling graph `__ontology`). Ingestion is a fixed nine-step strategy pipeline (`ingestion/pipeline.py:IngestionPipeline`) in which a local GLiNER NER model proposes entities, one LLM call per chunk verifies them and extracts relationships, entities are pruned against an ontology and deduplicated, and everything is written with batched `UNWIND ... MERGE`. Retrieval (`retrieval/strategies/multi_path.py:MultiPathRetrieval`) fans a question out over RELATES-edge vector search, entity name/full-text discovery, 1- and 2-hop relationship expansion, four chunk-retrieval paths and an optional text-to-Cypher path, reranks chunks locally with stored embeddings, assembles a sectioned context and asks the LLM to answer from it only. The design thesis stated in the README is that "the retrieval harness matters more than the model", with grounding/abstention (`return_context=True`, `MENTIONED_IN` provenance) as a first-class concern. + +## 3. Indexing pipeline, step by step + +Entry point: `GraphRAG.ingest()` (`api/main.py:1778`), which builds an `IngestionPipeline` with defaults and calls `IngestionPipeline.run()` (`ingestion/pipeline.py:217`). The pipeline docstring says it is "intentionally *not* a generic DAG". + +Defaults chosen by the facade (`api/main.py`, `ingest()` docstring and `_default_extractor` / `_default_ingest_resolver`): +- Loader: picked from extension (`ingestion/loaders/`: `TextLoader`, `pdf_loader.PdfLoader` (pypdf; PyMuPDF optional), `markdown_loader` (structure-preserving, heading breadcrumbs), `record_loader.CsvRecordLoader` for `.csv/.tsv/.psv/.tab`). +- Chunker: `SentenceTokenCapChunking(max_tokens=384, overlap_sentences=2)` (`ingestion/chunking_strategies/sentence_token_cap.py`). 384 is the GLiNER window. Alternatives: `FixedSizeChunking(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=100)`, `ContextualChunking` (one LLM call per chunk to prepend document context, `_CONTEXT_PROMPT`), `StructuralChunking` (Markdown headings), `CallableChunking`. +- Extractor: `GraphExtraction(llm, entity_types=)`. +- Resolver: `ExactMatchResolution` (zero LLM calls). +- `max_concurrency=3` parallel documents. + +Steps as logged in `IngestionPipeline.run()`: + +1. **Load** (`Step 1/9`) - `LoaderStrategy.load(source, ctx)` returns `DocumentOutput(text, document_info, elements)`. A SHA-256 `content_hash` of the text is compared with the stored `DocumentRecord`; unchanged content is skipped (`metadata["skipped_unchanged"]`). +2. **Chunk** - `ChunkingStrategy.chunk_document()` -> `TextChunks`; chunk uids are made deterministic from the document uid (`_assign_deterministic_chunk_uids`). +3. **Lexical graph** - `_build_lexical_graph()` (mixin `LexicalGraphWriter`) MERGEs `Document` and `Chunk` nodes, `PART_OF` and `NEXT_CHUNK` edges. Mandatory, not a strategy. +4. **Extract** - `GraphExtraction.extract(chunks, ontology, ctx)` (`ingestion/extraction_strategies/graph_extraction.py:561`). Two sub-steps: + - 4a. Optional coreference resolution (`coref_resolvers.FastCorefResolver`, extra `fastcoref`). + - 4b. NER via a pluggable `EntityExtractor` (`entity_extractors.py`): `GLiNERExtractor` (default, local model `urchade/gliner_medium-v2.1`, threshold 0.75, sub-threshold band labelled `Unknown`), `LLMExtractor` (uses `NER_PROMPT`, batched through `LLMInterface.abatch_invoke`), `SpacyExtractor`, `CompositeExtractor`. + - 4c. One LLM call per chunk with `VERIFY_EXTRACT_RELS_PROMPT` ("VERIFY the entities ... EXTRACT all relationships"). The prompt lists entity types and, when no ontology relations are declared, offers `DEFAULT_RELATION_TYPES` (31 UPPER_SNAKE_CASE labels such as `LOCATED_IN`, `EMPLOYED_AT`, `AUTHORED`) as a *preferred* vocabulary. A long code comment documents the measurement behind this (447 distinct labels without a default list; +2x triple F1 with one). Output is JSON parsed into `ExtractedEntity` / `ExtractedRelation` / `EntityMention` and aggregated into `GraphData` (`core/models.py`). Entity ids are deterministic: `compute_entity_id(name, type)` -> `"alice__person"`. + - `GraphData.extraction_failed` and per-chunk failure counts are carried into `IngestionResult.metadata["extraction"]`. +5. **Quality filter + Prune** - `_filter_quality()` then `_prune(graph_data, ontology)`: drops entities whose label is not in `Ontology.entities` and relations whose `(source_label, rel_type, target_label)` pattern is not declared in `Ontology.relations[].patterns`. Skipped entirely in open-schema mode (empty `Ontology()`). +6. **Resolve** - `ResolutionStrategy.resolve(graph_data, ctx)` -> `ResolutionResult(nodes, relationships, remap)`. `ExactMatchResolution` groups by `(normalized name, label)`; `LLMVerifiedResolution` (`resolution_strategies/llm_verified_resolution.py:423`) adds embedding-ANN candidate pairs, hard-merges above `hard_threshold`, sends the ambiguous band to a YES/NO LLM batch (`_VERIFY_PROMPT_INTRO`), re-asks cross-label pairs with A/B swapped (`cross_label_vote`), then Union-Find. Strengths + +- Everything lives in one database: graph, vectors, full-text and the ontology. Operationally simple (one Docker container), one connection, one backup. +- Grounding is designed in: `MENTIONED_IN` provenance, document attribution in every passage, `return_context=True`, prompt-injection hardening of the context block, abstention example. +- Mature incremental-update story (hash short-circuit, cached chunk extraction, crash-safe cutover, orphan cleanup, batch API) - rare among GraphRAG frameworks. +- Low extraction cost: local GLiNER NER plus one LLM call per chunk; zero-LLM resolution by default; reranking from stored vectors. +- Serious entity resolution: three-tier within-document resolver, cross-document LLM judge with double-vote, acronym folding, `SAME_AS`/`DISTINCT_FROM` audit edges, near-miss reporting. +- Ontology lifecycle: discovery (LLM or DBpedia-grounded), persistence in the DB, evolution with LLM backfill, structured CSV ingestion with typed columns that feed text-to-Cypher. +- Strict, well-commented code with measurement notes explaining design decisions; `mypy --strict`, Pydantic everywhere. + +## 12. Limitations and known issues + +- **FalkorDB lock-in**: no other graph or vector backend; Cypher dialect specifics (`vecf32`, `db.idx.*`) are baked into `GraphStore`/`VectorStore`. +- **Breaking rewrite**: v1 is API-incompatible with v0.x; the v0.x `KnowledgeGraph`, `ChatSession`, `Orchestrator` and multi-agent features are gone. Projects that depended on them must pin 0.8.2. +- `finalize()` is O(graph size) and must be remembered; skipping it leaves cross-document duplicates and no entity/edge vector indexes (the SDK only warns). +- Text-to-Cypher is explicitly "experimental", off by default, weakest path in isolation (53%), and adds 1-3 LLM calls and ~1.5 s. +- No community detection / global summarisation mode, so corpus-level "what are the main themes" questions rely on vector+fact retrieval alone. +- `gliner` (and therefore torch/transformers) is a *hard* dependency, making the install heavy even if you use `LLMExtractor`. +- Single `RELATES` edge type means native Cypher queries by predicate need property filters rather than typed edges; schema-driven tooling that expects typed relationships will not see them. +- PDF ingestion is described as incomplete on the roadmap ("complete PDF ingestion" 2026-Q3); `pdf-fast` uses AGPL PyMuPDF. +- Facade is large (`api/main.py` ~5,200 lines) and not re-entrant as an async context manager. +- Vendor-reported benchmarks only. + +## 13. Best fit / when to choose it + +Choose GraphRAG-SDK when you want a single-process Python library with one lightweight database, care about provenance/abstention and low per-chunk LLM cost, need documents to be re-synced incrementally (CI-driven doc sites, knowledge bases), or need to join CSV/tabular facts with prose into one graph and ask aggregate questions via text-to-Cypher.
