Graph data model + +There is no fixed entity ontology; the library imposes only the lexical-graph vocabulary and two marker labels. + +**Lexical graph** (`components/types.py:LexicalGraphConfig`, every name overridable): + +| Element | Default | Properties | +|---|---|---| +| Document node | `Document` | `path`, user `document_metadata` | +| Chunk node | `Chunk` | `id` (uid), `index`, `text`, `embedding` | +| Chunk -> Document | `FROM_DOCUMENT` | | +| Chunk -> Chunk | `NEXT_CHUNK` | | +| Entity -> Chunk | `FROM_CHUNK` | | + +**Entity layer**: each extracted node carries the LLM-assigned label from the schema (e.g. `Person`) **plus `__Entity__`** (added in `Neo4jWriter._nodes_to_rows`), with whatever properties the LLM emitted and the schema allowed. Relationships are real typed Neo4j relationships (`apoc.merge.relationship` with `row.type`), so `(:Person)-[:WORKS_FOR]->(:Company)` is native; relationship properties are kept. `__KGBuilder__` and `__tmp_internal_id` are transient write-time scaffolding. + +**Schema model** (`components/schema.py:GraphSchema`, immutable): `node_types: tuple[NodeType(label, description, properties: list[PropertyType(name, type, description)])]`, `relationship_types: tuple[RelationshipType]`, `patterns: tuple[Pattern(source, relationship, target)]` (tuples accepted), `constraints: tuple[ConstraintType(type=KEY|UNIQUENESS|EXISTENCE, entity label, property_names)]` (migrated from the old `required` flag), and the flags `additional_node_types`, `additional_relationship_types`, `additional_patterns`, `additional_properties` (default: True when the corresponding list is empty, False otherwise). Labels may not start with `__`. `GraphSchema.save()/store_as_json()/store_as_yaml()/from_file()` persist it to disk; the schema is **not** stored in Neo4j (although `SchemaFromExistingGraphExtractor` can rebuild one from a populated DB). Passing a plain dict `{"node_types": [...], "relationship_types": [...], "patterns": [...]}` or the deprecated `entities=/relations=/potential_schema=` lists is also accepted. + +**Query-side model**: retrievers are agnostic - they only require a vector index (and optionally a full-text index) on whatever label/property you configured, and return raw `neo4j.Record`s (`node`, `score`) that a `result_formatter` turns into `RetrieverResultItem(content, metadata)`. + +## 5. Storage backends supported + +- **Graph store: Neo4j only** (5.x; version-specific Cypher is generated, e.g. `CALL (vars) {}` subquery syntax for >= 5.23, Cypher 25 `SEARCH` clause support via `neo4j_queries.prefix_cypher_25` and `_build_search_clause_*` builders). Requires **APOC core** for the KG writer and resolvers. Multi-database via the `neo4j_database` argument everywhere. Works against Aura. +- **Vector store: Neo4j native vector indexes** (`db.index.vector.queryNodes` / `queryRelationships`, `db.create.setNodeVectorProperty`), full-text via `db.index.fulltext.queryNodes`. Default similarity `cosine`. +- **External vector databases** (read-only bridges, `retrievers/external/`): `WeaviateNeo4jRetriever`, `PineconeNeo4jRetriever`, `QdrantNeo4jRetriever` - all subclass `ExternalRetriever(id_property_external, id_property_neo4j)`: the external DB returns ids and scores, then a Cypher `MATCH (node) WHERE node. IN $ids` (+ optional `retrieval_query`) hydrates them from Neo4j. Vectors are *not* written to these stores by the library. +- **Parquet** as an offline write target (`ParquetWriter`). +- Chat history: `message_history.py:InMemoryMessageHistory` or `Neo4jMessageHistory` (stores `Session`/`Message` nodes in Neo4j with a window). + +## 6. Query / retrieval modes + +All retrievers derive from `retrievers/base.py:Retriever` (metaclass `RetrieverMetaclass` wraps `search()` with Pydantic validation). `search(...)` -> `get_search_results()` -> `RawSearchResult(records, metadata)` -> `get_result_formatter()` -> `RetrieverResult(items: list[RetrieverResultItem], metadata)`. Every retriever can be exposed as an LLM tool with `convert_to_tool(name, description, parameter_descriptions)` (`tool.py`). + +| Retriever (`retrievers/`) | Query processing | What is retrieved | Ranking | +|---|---|---|---| +| `VectorRetriever(driver, index_name, embedder, return_properties, result_formatter)` | `query_text` is embedded with `embedder.embed_query()` (or `query_vector` given); `top_k=5`, `effective_search_ratio`, metadata `filters` (`filters.py` builds a `WHERE` clause; pre-filtering uses the Cypher 25 `SEARCH` clause or a filtered exact scan) | `node, score` from `db.index.vector.queryNodes` | Index similarity score | +| `VectorCypherRetriever(driver, index_name, retrieval_query, embedder)` | same vector search, then the user's `retrieval_query` Cypher is appended with `node` and `score` in scope for traversal (e.g. `MATCH (node)-[:AUTHORED_BY]->(a) RETURN ...`) | whatever the user's `RETURN` yields | user-defined | +| `HybridRetriever(driver, vector_index_name, fulltext_index_name, embedder)` | embeds query **and** passes `query_text` to full-text; `neo4j_queries._get_hybrid_query` runs both in a `CALL { ... UNION ... }`, normalises each score by its own max, `WITH node, max(score)` (ranker `naive`) or `_get_hybrid_query_linear(alpha)` (`ranker="linear"`, weighted sum) | top_k nodes | normalised max or alpha-weighted | +| `HybridCypherRetriever(..., retrieval_query)` | hybrid + appended traversal Cypher | user-defined | as above | +| `Text2CypherRetriever(driver, llm, neo4j_schema=None, examples=None, custom_prompt=None)` | formats `Text2CypherTemplate` (schema string, examples, question), `llm.invoke(prompt)`, `extract_cypher()`, then **`EXPLAIN`s the query and refuses anything whose `query_type` is not read-only**, then executes with `RoutingControl.READ`; `CypherSyntaxError` -> `Text2CypherRetrievalError` (no automatic retry loop) | raw records of the generated query; `metadata["cypher"]` holds the statement | none | +| `ToolsRetriever(driver, llm, tools: list[Tool])` | one LLM call with tool definitions; the LLM picks zero or more tools (each a wrapped retriever or any `Tool`); selected tools are executed and results concatenated | union of tool outputs | per tool | +| `WeaviateNeo4jRetriever` / `PineconeNeo4jRetriever` / `QdrantNeo4jRetriever` | external ANN search (client objects passed in), ids joined back into Neo4j, optional `retrieval_query` | Neo4j nodes | external score | +| Custom | subclass `Retriever` and implement `get_search_results()` (`docs/source/user_guide_rag.rst` "custom-retriever") | | | + +Relationship vector indexes are supported in query builders (`db.index.vector.queryRelationships`, `upsert_vector_on_relationship`) but no retriever class wraps them directly. + +Default formatting: `VectorRetriever.default_record_formatter` puts `return_properties` (or the whole node minus embeddings) into `content` and `score` into metadata; `HybridRetriever.default_record_formatter` likewise. + +**Metadata filtering** (`filters.py`): `search(..., filters={"year": {"$gte": 2020}, "genre": {"$in": ["scifi", "fantasy"]}})` is compiled into a Cypher `WHERE` clause by `Operator` subclasses (`EqOperator "="`, `NeqOperator "<>"`, `LtOperator`, `GtOperator`, `LteOperator`, `GteOperator`, `InOperator`, `NinOperator`, `LikeOperator`, `ILikeOperator`; operator keys `$eq`, `$ne`, `$lt`, `$lte`, `$gt`, `$gte`, `$between`, `$in`, `$nin`, `$like`, `$ilike`, combined with `$and` / `$or`). On Neo4j versions with the Cypher 25 `SEARCH` clause the filter is pushed into the index query (`_build_search_clause_vector_query`); otherwise `_get_filtered_vector_query` falls back to an exact-scan `vector.similarity.cosine` over nodes matching the filter, which is correct but O(n). `effective_search_ratio` multiplies `top_k` for the ANN candidate pool before post-filtering. Filtered indexes are discussed in `docs/source/user_guide_rag.rst` ("filterable-index-creation"). + +**Tool-based routing**: `ToolsRetriever.get_search_results()` calls `self.llm.invoke_with_tools(query_text, tools=self._tools)`, so the provider must implement tool calling (`OpenAILLM`, `AnthropicLLM`, `VertexAILLM`, ...); the returned `tool_calls` are executed via each `Tool.execute()` and the item lists are concatenated with the tool name in metadata. There is no second LLM pass to reconcile or re-rank tool outputs. + +A typical "retriever + Cypher" pattern from the docstrings: + +```python +retrieval_query = """ +MATCH (node)-[:FROM_DOCUMENT]->(doc:Document) +OPTIONAL MATCH (e:__Entity__)-[:FROM_CHUNK]->(node) +RETURN node.text AS text, doc.path AS source, collect(DISTINCT e.name) AS entities, score +""" +retriever = VectorCypherRetriever(driver, "chunk_embeddings", retrieval_query, embedder=OpenAIEmbeddings()) +rag = GraphRAG(retriever=retriever, llm=OpenAILLM(model_name="gpt-4o")) +rag.search(query_text="...", retriever_config={"top_k": 5}, return_context=True) +``` + +```mermaid +sequenceDiagram + participant U as caller + participant R as GraphRAG.search + participant V as HybridCypherRetriever + participant E as Embedder + participant N as Neo4j + participant L as LLM + U->>R: search(query_text, message_history?, retriever_config, return_context) + opt message_history given + R->>L: summarise history (<=300 words) + R->>R: query = conversation_prompt(summary, query_text) + end + R->>V: search(query_text=query, **retriever_config) + V->>E: embed_query(query_text) + V->>N: CALL { vector index UNION fulltext index } normalised, top_k
+ user retrieval_query traversal + N-->>V: records + V-->>R: RetrieverResult(items) + R->>R: context = "\n".join(item.content) + R->>L: RagTemplate(context, examples, query_text) + system instruction
(+ raw message_history as prior turns) + L-->>R: answer + R-->>U: RagResultModel(answer, retriever_result?) +``` + +## 7. Generation / answer synthesis + +`generation/graphrag.py:GraphRAG(retriever, llm, prompt_template=RagTemplate())`. `search(query_text, message_history=None, examples="", retriever_config=None, return_context=None, response_fallback=None) -> RagResultModel(answer, retriever_result)`: +- `RagTemplate.DEFAULT_SYSTEM_INSTRUCTIONS = "Answer the user question using the provided context."`; `DEFAULT_TEMPLATE` is `Context:\n{context}\n\nExamples:\n{examples}\n\nQuestion:\n{query_text}\n\nAnswer:`. Context is the plain concatenation of `RetrieverResultItem.content` strings - there is no sectioning, no token budgeting, no de-duplication, and no citation markers; attribution has to be carried by the `result_formatter` you write (e.g. include `node.id` or document path in `content`). +- **Chat**: `message_history` (list of `LLMMessage` or a `MessageHistory`) triggers one extra LLM call (`_build_query`) that summarises the history in <= 300 words, and the retrieval query becomes `conversation_prompt(summary, current_query)`; the raw history is also passed to the LLM as prior messages for the final answer. `Neo4jMessageHistory` persists sessions in the graph. +- `response_fallback` returns a canned answer when the retriever returns zero items (cheap abstention). `return_context=True` attaches the `RetrieverResult` (default will flip to True; currently warns). +- The LLM may be an `LLMInterface`, `LLMInterfaceV2`, or any LangChain chat model (`is_langchain_compatible()`), which is how LangChain users plug in. +- **Agent loops**: none built in. `ToolsRetriever` is a single-step tool selection (one LLM call picks tools, no iteration). `Retriever.convert_to_tool()` and `tool.py:Tool` exist so an external agent framework (LangGraph, the Neo4j Agent Framework, MCP servers) can call the retrievers. + +## 8. LLM and embedding usage, cost profile + +**LLM providers** (`llm/`, lazily imported since 1.22): `OpenAILLM`, `AzureOpenAILLM`, `AnthropicLLM`, `CohereLLM`, `MistralAILLM`, `OllamaLLM`, `VertexAILLM`, `GeminiLLM` (google-genai), `BedrockLLM`; base classes `BaseOpenAILLM`, `BaseAnthropicLLM`, `BaseGeminiLLM` for custom endpoints (`base_url`, `http_client`). Interfaces: `LLMInterface` (`invoke(input, message_history, system_instruction)`, `ainvoke`), `LLMInterfaceV2` (message lists, `response_format` structured output; `supports_structured_output` flag), `LLMBase` implements both. `LLMResponse.usage` carries token counts. Rate limiting via `utils/rate_limit.py:RetryRateLimitHandler` (tenacity exponential backoff) applied with `@rate_limit_handler` decorators. + +**Embedders** (`embeddings/`): `OpenAIEmbeddings`, `AzureOpenAIEmbeddings`, `CohereEmbeddings`, `MistralAIEmbeddings`, `OllamaEmbeddings`, `VertexAIEmbeddings`, `GeminiEmbeddings`, `BedrockEmbeddings`, `SentenceTransformerEmbeddings`. Interface `Embedder.embed_query(text)` only - **no batch method**, so `TextChunkEmbedder` issues one embedding request per chunk. + +**Indexing cost per chunk** (default 4000-char chunks): 1 LLM call (`LLMEntityRelationExtractor`), 1 embedding call. Plus 1 LLM call per document when `SchemaFromTextExtractor` is used (it is sent the whole document text). Entity resolution: 0 LLM calls (exact / spaCy / RapidFuzz are local). No LLM-based description summarisation, no community detection, no relationship embeddings by default. + +**Query cost**: `VectorRetriever`/`Hybrid*` = 1 embedding + 1 Cypher; `Text2CypherRetriever` = 1 LLM call + `EXPLAIN` + 1 Cypher (no embedding); `ToolsRetriever` = 1 LLM call + the selected tools; `GraphRAG.search` adds 1 LLM call for the answer and 1 more when `message_history` is given. Typical total: **1 embedding + 1 LLM call per question**. + +## 9. Configuration and extension points + +- **Swap LLM/embedder**: pass any `LLMInterface`/`Embedder` instance; subclass `LLMInterface` for new providers (`docs/source/llm.rst`). LangChain chat models accepted by `GraphRAG` directly. +- **Swap components**: `SimpleKGPipeline(text_splitter=, file_loader=, kg_writer=, prompt_template=, lexical_graph_config=)`; or build your own `Pipeline()` with `add_component(component, name)` / `connect(from, to, input_config={...})` (`examples/pipeline/`, `docs/source/user_guide_pipeline.rst`). Any `Component` subclass with typed `run()` works, including non-KG tasks. +- **Config files**: `experimental/pipeline/config/` lets a whole pipeline be declared in JSON/YAML (`PipelineRunner.from_config_file`), with `ComponentType`/`ObjectConfig` resolving class paths and `ParamResolver` reading env vars (`resolver_: ENV`). `examples/build_graph/from_config_files/simple_kg_pipeline_config.yaml` is the canonical shape: + +```yaml +version_: "1" +template_: SimpleKGPipeline +neo4j_config: + params_: {uri: {resolver_: ENV, var_: NEO4J_URI}, user: {resolver_: ENV, var_: NEO4J_USER}, password: {resolver_: ENV, var_: NEO4J_PASSWORD}} +llm_config: + class_: OpenAILLM + params_: {api_key: {resolver_: ENV, var_: OPENAI_API_KEY}, model_name: gpt-5} +embedder_config: + class_: OpenAIEmbeddings + params_: {api_key: {resolver_: ENV, var_: OPENAI_API_KEY}} +from_file: false +schema: + node_types: + - label: Person + - {label: House, description: Family the person belongs to, properties: [{name: name, type: STRING}]} + relationship_types: + - label: PARENT_OF + - {label: RULES, properties: [{name: fromYear, type: INTEGER}]} + patterns: + - ["Person", "PARENT_OF", "Person"] + - ["House", "RULES", "Planet"] +text_splitter: + class_: text_splitters.fixed_size_splitter.FixedSizeSplitter + params_: {chunk_size: 100, chunk_overlap: 10} +perform_entity_resolution: true +``` + + `template_` selects `SimpleKGPipelineConfig`; a non-template `PipelineConfig` instead lists `component_config` entries and `connection_config` edges explicitly, mirroring `Pipeline.add_component/connect`. +- **Prompts**: `generation/prompts.py:PromptTemplate(template, expected_inputs)` subclasses - `RagTemplate`, `Text2CypherTemplate`, `ERExtractionTemplate`, `SchemaExtractionTemplate`; pass instances or raw strings with `{text}`, `{schema}`, `{examples}`, `{context}`, `{query_text}` placeholders. +- **Schema**: `GraphSchema`/dict/none (auto-extract); `additional_*` flags control strictness; constraints drive pruning of nodes missing mandatory properties. Schema files via `GraphSchema.from_file`. +- **Lexical graph naming**: `LexicalGraphConfig` renames every label/relationship/property so the output can match an existing data model. +- **Error policy**: `on_error=OnError.IGNORE|RAISE` per chunk; `Neo4jWriter` returns `KGWriterModel(status="FAILURE")` rather than raising on `ClientError`. +- **Incremental update**: not modelled. Running `SimpleKGPipeline` again on the same file creates a new `Document` node and new `Chunk`/entity nodes (the writer uses `CREATE` for nodes; entity de-duplication happens only through the post-write resolver, which merges same-label same-name nodes globally). There is no document hash, no delete-document helper, no chunk cache. `components/neo4j_reader.py:Neo4jChunkReader` lets you re-run extraction from chunks already stored. +- **Multi-tenancy**: per-database (`neo4j_database`) or by convention (labels / `filter_query` on resolvers / `filters` on vector search); nothing tenant-aware is built in. +- **Observability**: `Pipeline.stream()` events, `experimental/pipeline/notification.py`, `pipeline/observers.py:LoggingStageObserver` for the new DSL, `utils/logging.py`. + +## 10. Benchmarks + +**Author-reported**: none in the repository. There is no benchmark directory, no accuracy numbers in README, docs or CHANGELOG. The library is positioned as infrastructure; quality depends on the schema, chunking and Cypher the user supplies. + +**Third-party**: Neo4j blog posts and the "GraphRAG manifesto" link from the README describe use cases but do not publish quantitative comparisons from this package. None found in-tree. + +## 11. Strengths + +- First-party, actively maintained by Neo4j with a detailed changelog, deprecation discipline, Pydantic validation on every public entry point and large unit/e2e test suites (`tests/unit`, `tests/e2e`). +- Widest retriever palette of the three frameworks: vector, vector+Cypher, hybrid (two rankers), hybrid+Cypher, text2Cypher with `EXPLAIN` read-only guard, LLM tool routing, and three external vector DB bridges, all with a common `Retriever` contract and `convert_to_tool()`. +- Leverages Neo4j's native capabilities directly (typed relationships, vector + full-text indexes, metadata pre-filtering with the Cypher 25 `SEARCH` clause, multi-database, Aura). +- Broad provider coverage (9 LLM families, 9 embedders) with lazy imports, structured output support, rate-limit retries, and LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters. +- Flexible KG construction: schema-guided or schema-free with LLM schema inference, strict pruning with stats, APOC-based merging, Parquet export, configurable lexical graph vocabulary, JSON/YAML pipeline definitions. +- Small conceptual surface; easy to read and to embed into an existing application. + +## 12. Limitations and known issues + +- **Neo4j lock-in**: every component and retriever takes a `neo4j.Driver`; APOC core is mandatory for writing and resolution (not always available on managed/limited editions). +- The KG builder remains under `experimental/` with an explicit "may change or be removed" warning, and the task-graph `Pipeline` is slated for removal in 2.0 in favour of the new streaming DSL; expect migration work. +- **No retrieval algorithm beyond single-query index lookups**: no multi-hop expansion, no entity-centric retrieval, no reranking, no context budgeting, no community/global summaries. Anything beyond "vector hit + your Cypher" is on you. +- Weak default entity resolution (exact `name` match per label) and no LLM-verified dedup; similarity resolvers are O(n^2) within a label and run over the whole database. +- No incremental-update or deletion story; re-ingesting duplicates documents and chunks. +- Extraction is one prompt per 4000-char chunk with no NER pre-pass, no description aggregation, no relationship embedding; quality is fully dependent on the LLM honouring the JSON format (`fix_invalid_json` mitigates). +- `Embedder` has no batch API (one request per chunk). +- `GraphRAG` context assembly is naive string concatenation; no citations unless you format them in. +- `Text2CypherRetriever` has no self-correction loop; a syntax error surfaces as an exception. + +## 13. Best fit / when to choose it + +Choose neo4j-graphrag-python when Neo4j (self-hosted or Aura) is already the system of record, when you want typed, domain-specific relationships rather than a generic `RELATES` edge, when your team is comfortable writing the Cypher that turns a vector hit into graph context, or when you need many retrieval styles behind one interface to hand to an agent framework. It is a good fit for product teams composing their own RAG stack and a weak fit for anyone wanting a batteries-included GraphRAG algorithm, incremental sync, or a storage-agnostic layer. + +## 14. Core idea in one paragraph + +PathRAG indexes exactly like LightRAG (chunk → LLM entity/relation extraction with gleaning → merge into one entity graph → embed entities, relations, chunks). At query time it also extracts low/high-level keywords and retrieves top-k entities (by low-level keywords) and top-k relations (by high-level keywords). The novelty is in how it turns retrieved *entities* into relational context: instead of dumping all one-hop edges, it enumerates every simple path of length ≤ 3 between each pair of retrieved entities, propagates a "resource" score along the paths with a decay factor `alpha` and pruning `threshold`, keeps the top-15 highest-reliability paths after a hop-balanced cut, verbalises each path as a sentence chain ("The entity A is a person with the description(...) through edge(keywords) to connect to A and B ..."), and places the most reliable paths at the end of the prompt to exploit LLM recency bias. The paper's claim is that this reduces redundant/noisy context compared to LightRAG's flat neighbourhood dump and yields more logical, coherent answers. + +## 3. The demo API passes `QueryParam(mode=chat.search_context)` (`api/features/chats/routes.py:168`). + +### 6.1 Keyword extraction + +`PROMPTS["keywords_extraction"]` (3 few-shot examples, `addon_params["example_number"]` can truncate) → JSON `{high_level_keywords, low_level_keywords}` parsed with a `\{.*\}` regex. If either list is empty the query **fails** with `fail_response` (stricter than LightRAG, which degrades to the other mode). The whole response is cached with `handle_cache` / `save_to_cache` keyed by `compute_args_hash(mode, query)`; an optional embedding-similarity cache (`embedding_cache_config`, `similarity_check` prompt) is off by default. + +### 6.2 Context building (`_build_query_context`, `operate.py:588`) + +Two branches, both run for `hybrid`: + +**Low-level branch — `_get_node_data(ll_keywords)`** (`operate.py:686`) +1. `entities_vdb.query(ll_keywords, top_k=40)` → load nodes and degrees (`rank`). +2. `_find_most_related_text_unit_from_entities()` (`operate.py:753`): collect chunks from each node's `source_id`; for each chunk count how many one-hop neighbours of the entity also cite it (`relation_counts`); sort by `(entity order, -relation_counts)`; truncate to `max_token_for_text_unit`. +3. **Path pruning — `_find_most_related_edges_from_entities3()`** (`operate.py:1107`): + - Rebuild `G = nx.Graph()` from `knowledge_graph_inst.edges()` / `.nodes()`. + - `find_paths_and_edges_with_stats(G, source_nodes)`: for every ordered pair of retrieved entities run a DFS enumerating **all simple paths of depth ≤ 3**, bucketed into `one_hop_paths`, `two_hop_paths`, `three_hop_paths`. + - `bfs_weighted_paths(G, paths, source, target, threshold=0.3, alpha=0.8)`: implements the paper's resource-flow scoring. Starting with 1 unit at the source, each outgoing edge in the path set receives `1/len(successors)`; propagation to the next hop only continues if the accumulated edge weight exceeds `threshold`, and is multiplied by `alpha` per hop. A path's reliability = mean of its edge weights. + - Worked example of `bfs_weighted_paths` with `alpha=0.8`, `threshold=0.3`. Suppose the DFS found two paths from `A` to `D`: `A-B-D` and `A-C-E-D`, so `follow_dict = {A:{B,C}, B:{D}, C:{E}, E:{D}}`. From `A`, each of the two successors receives `1/2 = 0.5`. Edge `(A,B)=0.5 > 0.3`, so flow continues: `(B,D) += 0.5*0.8/1 = 0.4` and `D` is the target, so `[A,B,D]` is recorded. Edge `(A,C)=0.5 > 0.3`, so `(C,E) += 0.4`; `0.4 > 0.3`, so `(E,D) += 0.4*0.8/1 = 0.32`, recording `[A,C,E,D]`. Path reliabilities are the mean edge weight: `A-B-D = (0.5+0.4)/2 = 0.45`, `A-C-E-D = (0.5+0.4+0.32)/3 ≈ 0.41`. Had `A` had five successors, each first edge would start at `0.2 < threshold` and nothing beyond one hop would be explored from `A` — this is how hub nodes get pruned. Note that `threshold` is compared against the *accumulated* weight of an edge, so an edge shared by many enumerated paths can cross the threshold even when each individual contribution is small. + - All scored paths are sorted descending, deduplicated by node set, and cut to `total_edges = min(15, len(hop-balanced subset))`, where the hop-balanced subset keeps the first half of each hop bucket (`length_1 = len(one_hop)/2`, etc.). `threshold`, `alpha` and `total_edges` are hard-coded; the README tells you to edit `operate.py` to change them. + - Each surviving path is **verbalised**: node sentences `"The entity X is a TYPE with the description(...)"` chained with edge sentences `"through edge(keywords) to connect to X and Y."` (2-, 3- or 4-node variants). If any edge lookup fails it prints `边丢失` and skips the path. + - Sentences are truncated to `max_token_for_local_context` and **reversed** (`reversed_relationship = relationship[::-1]`) so the highest-scoring paths sit at the end of the context, per the paper's "path ordering for recency" argument. +4. Output as three CSV tables: entities `(id, entity, type, description, rank)`, relations `(id, context)` where `context` is the path sentence, sources `(id, content)`. + +**High-level branch — `_get_edge_data(hl_keywords)`** (`operate.py:826`): unchanged from LightRAG: `relationships_vdb.query(top_k=40)` → edges with `rank = edge_degree`, sorted by `(rank, weight)`, truncated to `max_token_for_global_context`; endpoint entities via `_find_most_related_entities_from_relationships()` truncated to `max_token_for_local_context`; chunks from edge `source_id`s truncated to `max_token_for_text_unit`. + +**Combination**: `combine_contexts()` → `process_combine_contexts()` merges the CSV tables (deduplicating rows); the final string has `-----global-information-----` (HL entities, HL relations, Sources) and `-----local-information-----` (LL entities, LL path relations). If a branch has no keywords the code mutates `query_param.mode` to `"global"`/`"local"`, but since no code path handles those modes afterwards the combined context variables may be undefined; this is a latent bug in the fallback path. + +### 6.3 Token budget + +No overall budget. Each table is truncated independently with `truncate_list_by_token_size`: chunks ≤ 4000 tokens per branch (so up to ~8000 after combination), HL relations ≤ 3000, LL path sentences ≤ 5000, HL-derived entities ≤ 5000. Generation / answer synthesis + +`PROMPTS["rag_response"]` is the original nano-graphrag/GraphRAG "data tables" prompt: "You are a helpful assistant responding to questions about data in the tables provided... summarizing all information in the input data tables... **incorporating any relevant general knowledge**... If you don't know the answer, just say so." Target length/format is `{response_type}` ("Multiple Paragraphs"). There is **no citation mechanism**: chunks appear as `(id, content)` rows with no document ids, and the answer prompt does not ask for references. The query and system prompt are passed to `llm_model_func(query, system_prompt=..., stream=...)`; the result is post-processed by stripping the prompt text and the literal strings `"user"`, `"model"`, `""` (a crude fix for HF models that echo the prompt) and cached. No conversation history support. + +## 8. LLM and embedding usage, cost profile + +- **Indexing**: 2 LLM calls per chunk (extraction + 1 gleaning); +1 per entity/relation whose merged description exceeds 500 tokens; embeddings for every chunk, entity and relation. Plus a fixed 20 s sleep per `extract_entities` invocation. Note that the LLM bindings in `PathRAG/llm.py` all `kwargs.pop("hashing_kv", None)` and never read or write the cache, so **extraction calls are not cached**; the only cache is the whole-answer cache in `kg_query` (`handle_cache` / `save_to_cache`, keyed by `(mode, query)`). Re-inserting identical text is still cheap because `ainsert` drops chunks whose md5 id already exists in `text_chunks` before extraction. +- **Query**: 1 keyword call + 1 answer call, 2 embedding calls (ll and hl keyword strings), plus CPU cost: full-graph reload into NetworkX and an exhaustive DFS over all simple paths ≤ 3 hops between up to 40×39 entity pairs. On dense graphs this DFS is the dominant latency and is exponential in branching factor; there is no cap on enumerated paths before scoring. +- Default models: `llm_model_func=openai_complete` with `llm_model_name="gpt-4o"`, `embedding_func=openai_embedding` (text-embedding-3-small via `PathRAG/llm.py`). Bindings exist for Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, HuggingFace, Ollama, LMDeploy, Zhipu, NVIDIA, vLLM, ModelScope, local transformers; embeddings for OpenAI, Jina, SiliconCloud, Bedrock, Ollama, HF. +- Small-model friendliness: the extraction prompt and verbalised path context are long; the paper evaluates with GPT-4o-mini. Nothing in the code targets SLMs. + +## 9. Configuration and extension points + +- **LLM/embedding**: `PathRAG(llm_model_func=..., embedding_func=EmbeddingFunc(embedding_dim, max_token_size, func))`; `llm_model_kwargs` forwarded to the binding; `llm_model_max_async=16`, `embedding_func_max_async=16`, `embedding_batch_num=32`. +- **Prompts**: edit `PathRAG/prompt.py` (`PROMPTS` dict). `addon_params` keys: `language`, `entity_types`, `example_number`. +- **Path pruning**: constants `threshold = 0.3`, `alpha = 0.8`, `total_edges = 15`, DFS depth `> 3` cut-off — all hard-coded inside `_find_most_related_edges_from_entities3` / `find_paths_and_edges_with_stats`; change by editing source. +- **Storage**: `kv_storage`, `vector_storage`, `graph_storage` names; `vector_db_storage_cls_kwargs`. Only the three local defaults are present. +- **Incremental insert**: content-hash dedupe of docs and chunks; new chunks are merged into the existing graph (description/source_id union). No document status, no failure recovery, no parallel-insert control beyond the LLM semaphore. +- **Delete**: `adelete_by_entity(name)` removes the entity from the entity VDB, relation VDB and graph. Benchmarks reported by the authors and notable third-party results + +- Dataset: UltraDomain (same as LightRAG) — the README links `TommyChien/UltraDomain`; the paper uses six domains (Agriculture, CS, Legal, Mix, Cooking, Art per the paper) with LLM-generated questions. +- Metric: pairwise LLM-judge win rates on five criteria — Comprehensiveness, Diversity, Logicality, Coherence, Relevance (prompt reproduced in the README). Anecdotally the hard-coded 20 s sleep and exhaustive DFS make it unsuitable for latency-sensitive evaluation without modification. + +## 11. Strengths + +- Genuine multi-hop relational context: paths up to 3 hops between query entities, scored by a principled resource-propagation heuristic, rather than one-hop neighbour dumps. +- Paths are verbalised into readable sentences and ordered for recency, which the paper shows improves answer logicality/coherence under LLM judges. +- Small, readable code base (~1.2k-line `operate.py`): easy to study or lift the path-pruning functions (`find_paths_and_edges_with_stats`, `bfs_weighted_paths`) into another framework. +- Index format is LightRAG-compatible (same GraphML/JSON/NanoVectorDB layout from early 2025), so an existing LightRAG index from that era can be queried with PathRAG's retrieval. + +## 12. Limitations and known issues + +- Prototype quality: `time.sleep(20)` in `extract_entities`; `QueryParam.mode` default is invalid; `insert` wrapper is an `async def` calling `run_until_complete`; Chinese debug prints; README references missing `RAGRunner`/`rag_test.py`; no tests; no `LICENSE` file. +- Only `hybrid` mode; no naive/local/global fallback; empty keyword lists abort the query. +- Path search loads the entire graph into memory and enumerates all simple paths ≤ 3 hops between every pair of up to 40 entities per query — exponential worst case, no cap before scoring. Hyper-parameters are hard-coded. +- Storage: only JSON/NanoVectorDB/NetworkX are implemented; the registry references a non-existent `.kg` package. No doc-status store, no delete-by-document, no workspace isolation, single-process only. +- No citations, no reranking, no global token budget, no conversation history, no streaming beyond passing `stream=` through. +- Entity names are upper-cased and quoted (`"ITRAVEL"`), which hurts readability in context and makes entity resolution case-insensitive but still exact-match. +- Fork is frozen at an early LightRAG snapshot; none of LightRAG's later improvements (map-reduce summarisation, role-specific LLMs, rebuild-on-delete, PostgreSQL backends, REST API with auth) are present. + +## 13. Best fit / when to choose it + +Choose PathRAG when you are doing research on graph-RAG retrieval and want a working reference implementation of relational path pruning to experiment with or port, or when your corpus is small (thousands of entities), questions are genuinely multi-hop, and you can afford to run it offline. Core idea of its GraphRAG mode (one paragraph) + +R2R implements a Microsoft-GraphRAG-style pipeline on top of Postgres + pgvector. Each document's chunks are grouped (`chunk_merge_count`, default 2), sent to one LLM prompt (`graph_extraction`) that returns XML ``/`` elements with descriptions and weights; every entity and relationship description is embedded and stored in `documents_entities` / `documents_relationships`. Duplicate entity names within a document are optionally merged and re-described by the LLM. A collection's graph is materialized by **pulling** (SQL copy) document-level rows into `graphs_entities` / `graphs_relationships`; **communities** are built by sending the relationship edge list to an external Leiden (graspologic `hierarchical_leiden`) microservice and summarizing each cluster with the `graph_communities` prompt into `graphs_communities`. At query time, graph search is a plain pgvector cosine KNN over entity, relationship and community description embeddings (no traversal), whose results are concatenated with chunk results as extra "Source [id]" blocks in the RAG prompt or agent context. + +--- + +## 3. Generation config per request (`rag_generation_config`), including Anthropic extended thinking. + +--- + +## 8. LLM and embedding usage, cost profile + +**Indexing per document (N chunks):** +- Extraction: `ceil(N / chunk_merge_count)` LLM calls (default N/2), each with the full prompt (two long few-shot examples + document summary + ~2k tokens of text) and an XML output that is typically long (full descriptions for every entity). Retries up to 5× on failure. +- Embeddings: one request **per entity and per relationship** (`async_get_embedding` inside the parse loop), i.e. hundreds of small embedding calls per document; the cookbook reports ~120 entities for a short story. +- Description pass: LLM calls only for entities lacking a description (rare) + 1 embedding each. +- Dedup: 1 LLM call + 1 embedding per duplicate-name group. +- Document summary at ingest: 1 LLM call (ingestion, not graph-specific). + +**Per collection:** +- Pull: 0 LLM calls (SQL copy). +- Communities: 2 clustering-service calls (clustering is re-run inside summarization) + 1 LLM call (prompt can be up to 65k chars) + 1 embedding per community; 3 attempts on parse failure. + +**Per query:** 1 embedding (shared by chunk and graph search) + 3 pgvector KNN queries; HyDE/RAG-fusion add 1 LLM call plus per-sub-query searches; RAG answer = 1 LLM call; agent = N tool loops. + +**Providers:** LLM via `litellm` (any litellm-supported model: OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure, Bedrock, Gemini, Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio...), native `openai`, `anthropic`, `azure_foundry`, and `r2r` router (`core/providers/llm/`). Embeddings via `litellm`, `openai`, `ollama` (`core/providers/embeddings/`). Defaults in `r2r.toml`: `openai/gpt-5-2025-08-07` quality, `openai/gpt-5-nano-2025-08-07` fast, `openai/text-embedding-3-small` @ 512 dims. Sample configs for Ollama, LM Studio, Azure, Gemini in `core/configs/`. + +--- + +## 9. Configuration and extension points + +- **Enable per collection:** graph tables always exist; extraction happens per document (automatic via `[ingestion] automatic_extraction` or on demand), the collection graph is filled by `graphs.pull`, communities by `graphs.build`. Graph search is on by default (`GraphSearchSettings.enabled = True`); disable per request with `graph_settings.enabled = false`. +- **Config keys** (`[database.graph_creation_settings]`): `graph_extraction_prompt`, `graph_entity_description_prompt`, `entity_types[]`, `relation_types[]`, `chunk_merge_count` (2), `max_knowledge_relationships` (100, declared but not used by the extraction code), `max_description_input_length` (65536), `generation_config`, `automatic_deduplication`. `[database.graph_enrichment_settings]`: `graph_communities_prompt`, `max_summary_input_length`, `generation_config`, `leiden_params`. Swap LLM/embedding: TOML provider sections + env keys. Clustering service URL via `CLUSTERING_SERVICE_URL`. +- **APIs/SDKs:** Python `r2r` client (`client.documents.extract`, `client.graphs.pull/build/reset`, `client.retrieval.search/rag/agent`), JS SDK in `js/sdk`, OpenAPI from FastAPI. + +--- + +## 10. Benchmarks + +- **Authors:** none for the graph mode in the repo. The README claims "the most advanced AI retrieval system" without published numbers; `docs/cookbooks/graphs.md` only shows a worked example (The Gift of the Magi: ~120 extracted entities, ~20 distinct after dedup). No eval harness for graph quality exists under `py/tests` beyond API/unit tests. +- **Third-party:** none found in the repo. (SciPhi previously published general RAG evaluations on their blog; these did not isolate graph search.) + +--- + +## 11. Strengths + +1. Simple, inspectable storage: four Postgres tables with pgvector columns, plain SQL, CSV export, full CRUD API — easy to audit, back up, or hand-edit. +2. Clean separation of document-level extraction (reusable across collections via `pull`) from collection-level graphs and communities. +3. Explicit, editable prompts (`graph_extraction`, `graph_entity_description`, `graph_communities`) with schema constraints via `entity_types`/`relation_types`; XML output is robustly sanitized. +4. Graph results flow through the same citation and agent machinery as chunks, so RAG answers can cite entities/relationships/communities with short ids. +5. Fully asynchronous with Hatchet orchestration for long-running extraction (per-document child workflows, retries, concurrency limits, failure status tracking). +6. Permissive MIT license; litellm gives wide model coverage. + +--- + +## 12. Limitations and known issues + +1. **Graph search is not graph traversal.** It is three independent vector KNNs; no neighbourhood expansion, no use of `subject_id/object_id`, no PageRank or path scoring; relevance of relationships depends entirely on their description embeddings. +2. **Entity resolution is weak:** exact name match within a single document; `pull` copies rows verbatim so the collection graph accumulates duplicate nodes across documents (and the Leiden graph is built on names, so duplicates collapse there but not in search results). +3. **Communities** require a separate microservice, are rebuilt from scratch (no incremental), ignore the hierarchical `level` when summarizing, re-run clustering twice, and the summary prompt input can be 65k characters, which is expensive and may exceed smaller context windows. +4. **Embedding cost pattern:** one embedding API call per entity/relationship rather than batched; extraction failures after 5 retries silently drop a chunk group. +5. Declared but unused settings (`max_knowledge_relationships`), `graph_search_results_*` naming artifacts from a refactor, and docstring/SQL mismatches (`pull` claims property merging) indicate the module has had less recent attention than retrieval/agent code. +6. Deletion of a document does not clean `graphs_*` copies; stale graph rows persist until `reset` + `pull`. +7. No native pgvector index on graph tables in DDL; KNN on large graphs will scan. +8. Deployment: light mode is `pip install r2r` + Postgres with pgvector; full mode adds Hatchet (engine, dashboard, RabbitMQ, second Postgres), MinIO, Unstructured, clustering service, dashboard (`docker/compose.full.yaml`). +9. Platform coupling: the graph code depends on R2R's providers/handlers and auth model; it is not a standalone library. + +--- + +## 13. Best fit / when to choose it + +Choose R2R when you want an API-first RAG backend on Postgres with users, collections, hybrid search, citations and a tool-using agent, and you want a lightweight "GraphRAG-lite" (entity/relationship/community descriptions as additional vector-searchable context) without running a graph database. It suits teams who are comfortable editing prompts and SQL and who mostly need better recall for entity-centric questions. It is not the right choice if you need multi-hop traversal, robust cross-document entity resolution, hierarchical community-based global summarization with token budgeting, or a storage backend other than Postgres. + +--- + +## 14. Core idea of its GraphRAG mode (one paragraph) + +RAGFlow does not keep a separate graph database. Entities, relations, community reports and RAPTOR summary nodes are stored as *extra chunk rows* in the same per-tenant document-engine index (`ragflow_` in Elasticsearch or Infinity) as ordinary text chunks, discriminated by keyword columns (`type_kwd` / `knowledge_graph_kwd` = `entity` | `relation` | `community_report` | ...; `scope_kwd` = `doc` | `dataset`; `compile_kwd` = template kind). Construction is a two-stage LLM extraction (entities, then relations constrained to the known entities) per token-packed batch of chunks, followed by an LLM-judged merge/dedup, then a dataset-level merge into one graph per knowledge base. Retrieval either (a) in the chat path, prepends one synthetic "Related content in Knowledge Graph" chunk built from entity/relation/community rows ranked by `similarity × pagerank`, or (b) in Agentic RAG, lets the model call a `graph_explore` tool that seeds entities by vector similarity, walks relations for two hops and returns the subgraph plus the source passages behind it. + +--- + +## 3. Indexing pipeline, step by step + +### 3.1 Ingestion pipeline shape + +Knowledge compilation runs as the `Compiler` operator in an Ingestion Pipeline: **Parser → Chunker → Compiler → Indexer** (`docs/guides/knowledge_compilation/overview.md`). Each pipeline component lives in `internal/ingestion/component/`: + +- `parser.go`, `parser_dispatch.go`, `pdf_vision_dispatch*.go` — document parsing (DeepDoc / vision models) +- `chunker/` — template chunkers +- `extractor.go`, `extractor_tag.go` — non-LLM NER/tag extractor (cgo ThincNER, `internal/ingestion/compilation/extractor/ner.go`), separate from the LLM graph +- `knowledge_compiler/` — the Compiler operator (`component.go`, `NewKnowledgeCompilerComponent`, `Invoke`) +- `document_storage.go` — the Indexer + +The Compiler resolves a `CompilationTemplate` (MySQL table `compilation_template`, entity `internal/entity/compilation_template.go` with `Kind` and `Config JSONMap`) via `compilation_template_id` or `compilation_template_group_id` (`component.go:resolveTemplateSpecs`) and dispatches by variant: `structure` (Graph / Timeline / PageIndex / list / set), `tree` (RAPTOR), `mindmap`, `wiki`. + +### 3.2 Graph (structure variant) — `internal/ingestion/component/knowledge_compiler/structure/` + +`structure.Run` (`structure.go`) executes four phases entirely in memory (no ES reads during the run): + +1. **Batch packing.** Chunks are packed into batches by token budget: `structureInputBudget = max(modelContextLen × 0.5 − promptOverhead, 1024)` (fallback 4096 when window unknown); `common.PackBatches`. `PackBatch` renders each chunk as `[CHUNK_ID: ]\n\n[END_CHUNK]` so the LLM can return `source_chunk_ids` per item. Env `STRUCT_MAX_CHUNKS_PER_BATCH` optionally caps chunks per batch. +2. **MAP — two-stage extraction** (`compile.go:extractHypergraph`), batches run concurrently on a process-wide vCPU-sized pool (`SetBatchSubmitter`): + - Stage 1 (node prompt) → `{"items":[{type,name,description,source_chunk_ids,...}]}` + - Stage 2 (edge prompt, with `{known_nodes}` filled from stage-1 names) → `{"items":[{type,source,target,description,source_chunk_ids}]}`; "Only create relations between entities listed in 'Known Entities'". Stage 2 is skipped when no entities or no relation spec. + - Both calls use `temperature 0.1`, `DisableThinking: true`, `common.GenJSON`. + - Prompts are *rendered from the template config*, not hard-coded: `prompt.go:HypergraphPrompts` assembles `# Role and Task` (guideline.target), `## Global Rules` (`global_rules`), `## Entity Extraction Rules`, `## Entity Fields` (from `entity.fields[]` with `type/description/rule`), `## Response Format`. Default entity types shipped in the built-in Graph template: `person, org, product, regulation, location, other`; default relation types: `owns, part_of, caused_by, regulates, located_in, other` (`docs/guides/knowledge_compilation/built_in_templates_and_dedicated_configuration.md`). + - **Evidence gate** (`evidence.go:ValidatePayloadEvidence`, `EvidenceGateMode`): quotes returned by the LLM are located in the batch source text; unsupported items can be dropped depending on mode. +3. **Embedding** (`compile.go:buildRows`): one embedding call per batch over the flattened description of every entity/relation; produces `common.Product` rows with `Meta{kind, name, entity_type | from, to, relation_type, source_chunk_ids, mention_count}` and a stable id `StableRowID(content, docID, templateID)`. Self-loop relations are dropped. +4. **DEDUP** (`merge.go`): `GroupedDeduper` folds rows sequentially in batch order. Entities with the same normalized name merge without an LLM (`mergeEntitiesByName`). Otherwise, if cosine similarity of description embeddings ≥ `SimilarityThreshold`, `LLMMergeDecider` asks the LLM (`mergeSystemPrompt` + `mergeDecisionInstruction`, temperature 0, batched pairs via `DecideBatch` within 20 % of the model window) whether A and B are "the same logical entity/relation" and to return the merged JSON. Aliases are recorded and `RewriteRelations` rewrites relation endpoints to canonical names. +5. **Kind post-processing** (`chain.go`): for `list` / `timeline` kinds, relations must form a strict chain; violations are sent to an LLM correction prompt (`chainCorrectionPrompt`, fail-open) and isolated timeline entities are dropped. + +The output is a list of entity/relation products; the earlier compact `knowledge_graph_kwd="graph"` blob was removed ("saves one embedding call per compile"). + +### 3.3 Dataset-level merge — `internal/ingestion/knowledge_compile/` + +Document-level rows are written with `scope_kwd="doc"`. A separate **Consumer** worker (`consumer.go`, claims per-KB rows in MySQL, heartbeat/TTL, single writer per KB) runs `mergeStructureDataset`: buckets entities by `(template, lower(name), compile_kwd)` and relations by `(template, lower(from), relation type, lower(to), compile_kwd)`, picks a preferred type, unions `source_doc_ids` / `source_chunk_ids`, then `writer.go:WriteMergedStructure` upserts deterministic dataset-level rows (`datasetLevelStructureID`) with `scope_kwd="dataset"`, `doc_id = kb_id`, plus a `knowledge_graph_kwd="kg_build_meta"` marker row. `mergeExistingStructureBuckets` does read-modify-write so a re-run is incremental. Dataset-level structure is only supported on `infinity` and `elasticsearch` (`writer.go:datasetStructureSupported`). + +Note: there is **no PageRank, no Leiden/community detection, and no community report** in the new Graph compile. Those exist only in the legacy pipeline (rows with `rank_flt`, `n_hop_with_weight`, `community_report`, `ty2ents`) that the Go search code still reads. + +### 3.4 Tree (RAPTOR) — `internal/ingestion/component/knowledge_compiler/tree/` + +`tree.Run` (`raptor.go`) is RAGFlow's RAPTOR: +- Optional **claim extraction** per chunk (`claims.go:ExtractClaimsForChunks`, customizable "Claim Extraction Prompt", evidence-gated) and clustering on claim-digest embeddings instead of raw chunk vectors. +- **Clustering** is a 1-D "watershed" over document-ordered embeddings (`watershed.go`): a new cluster starts when the cosine similarity between consecutive chunks drops below a percentile threshold, controlled by `tree_order` (default `DefaultTreeOrder = 4`, range 2–16). There are no entities, relations, or communities; the only structure is parent-child membership between summaries and the chunks they summarise. + +## 2. Core idea in one paragraph + +Split a document into ~100-token leaf chunks, embed them, and then repeatedly: (a) reduce the embeddings with UMAP, (b) soft-cluster them with a Gaussian Mixture Model (a node may land in several clusters), (c) ask an LLM to summarise each cluster's text into a new parent node, (d) embed the parent nodes and recurse on them. The result is a multi-layer tree in which upper layers hold increasingly abstract summaries of larger spans of the document. At query time you either flatten the whole tree and run plain nearest-neighbour search across *all* layers simultaneously ("collapsed tree", the default and best-performing mode in the paper), or walk top-down from the roots picking the top-k children at each layer ("tree traversal"). Retrieved node texts are concatenated and handed to a QA model. The claim is that mixing fine-grained chunks and coarse summaries in one index lets a single retriever answer both detail and "whole-document theme" questions. + +## 3. Indexing pipeline, step by step + +Entry point: `RetrievalAugmentation.add_documents(text)` in `raptor/RetrievalAugmentation.py`, which calls `ClusterTreeBuilder.build_from_text()`. + +1. **Chunking** – `raptor/utils.py::split_text(text, tokenizer, max_tokens, overlap=0)`. Splits on `. ! ? \n` into sentences, packs sentences greedily into chunks of at most `max_tokens` (default `tb_max_tokens=100` cl100k tokens; the paper used 100). Over-long sentences are sub-split on `, ; :`. Overlap defaults to 0. No document boundaries are preserved: `add_documents` takes one string; multiple docs are just concatenated. +2. **Leaf node creation** – `TreeBuilder.create_node(index, text, children=set())` in `raptor/tree_builder.py`. Each node gets an embedding from *every* configured embedding model (`embedding_models` dict, default `{"OpenAI": OpenAIEmbeddingModel("text-embedding-ada-002")}`). `multithreaded_create_leaf_nodes` uses a `ThreadPoolExecutor`. Leaf nodes form `layer_to_nodes[0]`. +3. **Layer loop** – `ClusterTreeBuilder.construct_tree()` in `raptor/cluster_tree_builder.py`, for `layer in range(num_layers)` (default `tb_num_layers=5`). Stops early when the current layer has `<= reduction_dimension + 1` nodes (default 10 → stops at 11 or fewer nodes). +4. **Clustering** – `RAPTOR_Clustering.perform_clustering(nodes, embedding_model_name, max_length_in_cluster=3500, reduction_dimension=10, threshold=0.1)` in `raptor/cluster_utils.py`, which calls `perform_clustering(embeddings, dim, threshold)`: + - **Global step**: `global_cluster_embeddings` runs `umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=int(sqrt(N-1)), n_components=min(dim, N-2), metric="cosine")`; then `GMM_cluster` picks the number of components by minimising BIC over `1..min(50, N)` (`get_optimal_clusters`) and assigns each point to every component with posterior probability `> threshold` (soft assignment). + - **Local step**: for each global cluster with more than `dim+1` members, re-run UMAP (`n_neighbors=10`) + BIC-GMM inside the cluster. Clusters with `<= dim+1` members become a single local cluster. + - Local cluster ids are offset and accumulated so each node ends up with a list of cluster labels (`all_local_clusters`). + - **Size guard**: if the total token length of a cluster's texts exceeds `max_length_in_cluster` (3500), the cluster is recursively re-clustered. + - Note: node identity after local clustering is recovered by matching embedding vectors with `(embeddings == local_cluster_embeddings_[:, None]).all(-1)` – O(N²·d) and fragile if two chunks have identical embeddings. +5. **Summarisation** – `process_cluster` concatenates cluster texts (`utils.get_text`, double-newline separated) and calls `TreeBuilder.summarize(context, max_tokens=summarization_length)` (default `tb_summarization_length=100`). Default model `GPT3TurboSummarizationModel` (`gpt-3.5-turbo`) with the prompt literally: `"Write a summary of the following, including as many key details as possible: {context}:"` (`raptor/SummarizationModels.py`). A new parent `Node` is created with `children = {node.index for node in cluster}` and embedded. Optional `use_multithreading` (default False at this level; and note `next_node_index` is incremented outside the lock, so the parallel path is racy on indices). +6. **Bookkeeping** – new nodes are appended to `all_tree_nodes` and `layer_to_nodes[layer+1]`; the loop recurses on the new layer. Output is a `Tree(all_nodes, root_nodes, leaf_nodes, num_layers, layer_to_nodes)`. +7. **Persistence** – `RetrievalAugmentation.save(path)` pickles the whole `Tree` (text + all embeddings) with `pickle.dump`; `RetrievalAugmentation(tree="path")` loads it. + +```mermaid +flowchart TD + A[Raw text string] --> B[split_text

embed with every embedding model] + C --> D[Layer 0 = leaf nodes] + D --> E{nodes in layer

all_nodes, layer_to_nodes, root_nodes] + E -- yes --> F[UMAP global reduce
n_neighbors = sqrt N, dim=10] + F --> G[GMM, k by BIC,
soft assign prob > 0.1] + G --> H[per global cluster:
UMAP local + GMM again] + H --> I{cluster text
> 3500 tokens?} + I -- yes --> H + I -- no --> J[LLM summarise cluster
gpt-3.5-turbo, 100 tokens] + J --> K[new parent Node
children = cluster ids, embed] + K --> L[Layer n+1] + L --> E + Z --> P[pickle.dump Tree] +``` + +## 4. Graph / tree data model + +`raptor/tree_structures.py` (28 lines total): + +```python +class Node: text: str; index: int; children: Set[int]; embeddings: Dict[str, vector] +class Tree: all_nodes: Dict[int, Node]; root_nodes; leaf_nodes; num_layers: int; layer_to_nodes: Dict[int, List[Node]] +``` + +- **Node types**: only one class. Layer 0 nodes are raw chunks; layer ≥1 nodes are LLM summaries. Layer membership is not stored on the node; it is derived from `layer_to_nodes` (`utils.reverse_mapping` builds `index -> layer` at retrieval time). +- **Edges**: implicit parent→child via `Node.children` (a set of integer indices). Because GMM assignment is soft, a child can have several parents (a DAG, not strictly a tree). There are no child→parent back-pointers, no sibling links, no typed relations. +- **Attributes**: `text`, integer `index`, and a dict of embeddings keyed by embedding-model name (so a node can carry both an OpenAI and an SBERT vector). No metadata (source doc, page, offsets, layer, cluster id, score) is stored. +- **Where stored**: everything in Python memory; persisted only as a single pickle. + +## 5. Query / retrieval modes + +Both modes live in `raptor/tree_retriever.py::TreeRetriever` and are selected by the `collapse_tree` flag on `retrieve()` / `answer_question()` (default `True`). + +### 6.1 Collapsed tree (default; best in the paper) + +`retrieve_information_collapse_tree(query, top_k, max_tokens)`: +1. Embed the query with `TreeRetrieverConfig.embedding_model` (default `OpenAIEmbeddingModel`). +2. Take `get_node_list(tree.all_nodes)` – **every node from every layer**, sorted by index. +3. Compute cosine distance query↔node for all nodes (`context_embedding_model` key, default `"OpenAI"`). +4. Sort ascending; iterate the first `top_k` (default 10) adding nodes while the running cl100k token count stays `<= max_tokens` (default 3500); stop at the first node that would overflow. +5. Context = node texts joined by blank lines (`utils.get_text`). Leaf chunks and summaries are intermixed with no labels indicating layer. + +There is no deduplication of a summary and its own children, no re-ranking, no MMR, no metadata filtering. + +### 6.2 Tree traversal + +`retrieve_information(current_nodes, query, num_layers)` with `start_layer` (default `tree.num_layers`, i.e. the root layer) and `num_layers` (default `tree.num_layers + 1`, i.e. walk all the way down): +1. Start with `layer_to_nodes[start_layer]`. +2. At each layer compute distances for the candidate set; choose by `selection_mode`: `"top_k"` (default 5) or `"threshold"` (keeps nodes with `distance > threshold` – note the comparison direction looks inverted for a cosine *distance*; this is a latent bug if you use threshold mode). +3. Add the selected nodes to the result, then set the next candidate set = union of their `children`. +4. Repeat for `num_layers` layers. All selected nodes from every visited layer are concatenated (no token cap in this mode). + +`return_layer_information=True` returns `[{node_index, layer_number}]` alongside the context – useful for analysing which layers answered. + +```mermaid +sequenceDiagram + participant U as User + participant RA as RetrievalAugmentation + participant TR as TreeRetriever + participant E as EmbeddingModel + participant QA as QAModel (gpt-3.5-turbo) + U->>RA: answer_question(q, top_k=10, max_tokens=3500, collapse_tree=True) + RA->>TR: retrieve(q, ...) + TR->>E: create_embedding(q) + E-->>TR: q_vec + TR->>TR: cosine distance vs ALL nodes (all layers) + TR->>TR: argsort, take top_k under token budget + TR-->>RA: context text (+ layer info) + RA->>QA: answer_question(context, q) + QA-->>U: answer string +``` + +### 6.3 FAISS leaf-only retrieval (baseline) + +`FaissRetriever.retrieve(query)`: inner-product search over leaf embeddings; either `top_k` chunks or fills `max_context_tokens`. Standalone, not combined with the tree. + +## 7. Generation / answer synthesis + +`raptor/QAModels.py`. Default `GPT3TurboQAModel` (`gpt-3.5-turbo`, `temperature=0`) with: + +- system: `"You are Question Answering Portal"` +- user: `"Given Context: {context} Give the best full answer amongst the option to question {question}"` + +Other classes: `GPT4QAModel` (same prompt, `gpt-4`), `GPT3QAModel` (legacy `text-davinci-003` completions endpoint; dead model), `UnifiedQAModel` (local T5 `allenai/unifiedqa-v2-t5-3b-1363200`, used in the paper's small-model experiments). + +There is a single LLM call, no reasoning loop, no self-check, no citations (the context carries no node ids or source metadata, so citations cannot be produced without modifying `get_text`). Exceptions inside `answer_question` are caught and the *exception object itself is returned* as the answer – callers must check types. + +## 8. LLM and embedding usage, cost profile + +**Indexing** (`N` leaf chunks of ~100 tokens): +- Embedding calls: `N` for leaves + one per summary node, times the number of configured embedding models (each `create_node` embeds with all models). Each call is a single-text request (no batching) via `OpenAIEmbeddingModel.create_embedding`. +- LLM calls: one summarisation call per cluster per layer. Empirically the number of nodes shrinks by roughly 3–10× per layer, so total summary calls ≈ `N/3 … N/10` summed over layers, i.e. ~0.1–0.5 calls per chunk; each call's input is up to 3500 tokens (`max_length_in_cluster`) and output 100 tokens. With soft clustering a chunk can be summarised in more than one cluster, inflating input tokens. +- Compute: UMAP + up to 50 GMM fits (BIC search) per clustering step, run twice (global + local) per layer. This is the practical bottleneck for >10k chunks (and UMAP is not deterministic across runs even with the module-level `random.seed(224)`; the GMM uses `random_state=0`). +- Retrieval ranking at query time is a Python loop over all nodes – fine for thousands of nodes, slow for hundreds of thousands. + +**Query**: 1 embedding call + 1 QA LLM call (collapsed or traversal). Context ≤ 3500 tokens by default in collapsed mode; unbounded in traversal mode (`top_k × layers` nodes). + +All OpenAI calls are wrapped in `tenacity.retry(wait_random_exponential(1..20), stop_after_attempt(6))`. + +## 9. Configuration and extension points + +Everything is constructor-injected; there is no config file or env-driven registry. + +- `RetrievalAugmentationConfig(tree_builder_config, tree_retriever_config, qa_model, embedding_model, summarization_model, tree_builder_type="cluster", tr_*, tb_*)` in `raptor/RetrievalAugmentation.py`. Shortcut args: `embedding_model=` sets both builder and retriever models under the key `"EMB"`; `summarization_model=`; `qa_model=`. +- `TreeBuilderConfig` keys: `tokenizer`, `max_tokens` (chunk size), `num_layers`, `threshold`, `top_k`, `selection_mode`, `summarization_length`, `summarization_model`, `embedding_models` (dict), `cluster_embedding_model` (which key to cluster on). `ClusterTreeConfig` adds `reduction_dimension`, `clustering_algorithm` (any class with a static `perform_clustering(nodes, embedding_model_name, ...)`), `clustering_params`. +- `TreeRetrieverConfig` keys: `threshold`, `top_k`, `selection_mode`, `context_embedding_model`, `embedding_model`, `num_layers`, `start_layer`. +- **Swap LLM**: subclass `BaseSummarizationModel.summarize(context, max_tokens)` and `BaseQAModel.answer_question(context, question)`. Benchmarks reported by the authors + +Numbers come from the paper (arXiv:2401.18059), not from anything in the repo (the repo has no evaluation scripts): + +- **QuALITY** (long-document multiple choice): with GPT-4, RAPTOR 82.6% overall / 76.2% on the hard subset, which the paper reports as a new SOTA, +20% absolute over the prior best on the hard subset. With UnifiedQA-3B: 62.4%/56.6% vs 53.4%/48.2% for DPR-style chunk retrieval. +- **QASPER** (F1): RAPTOR+GPT-4 55.7 vs BM25 and DPR baselines in the 50–53 range; RAPTOR+UnifiedQA 36.6 vs 32.7. +- **NarrativeQA**: RAPTOR+UnifiedQA ROUGE-L 30.9 / BLEU-1 23.6 / METEOR 19.1, above the BM25/DPR baselines. +- Ablations: collapsed tree beats tree traversal at equal token budgets; retrieving at ~2000 tokens is roughly the sweet spot; roughly 18–57% of retrieved nodes come from non-leaf layers depending on dataset, with higher layers helping on "theme"-style questions. + +Third-party: LlamaIndex (`RaptorPack`), LangChain cookbook, and several GraphRAG papers (e.g. GraphRAG-Bench, HippoRAG2) use RAPTOR as a baseline; results there typically show it competitive on summarisation-style questions and weaker than entity-graph methods on multi-hop fact questions. These are external and not in the repo. + +## 11. Strengths + +- Conceptually simple and model-agnostic; ~2k lines, easy to read and modify in an afternoon. +- Captures document-level and section-level abstractions that flat chunk RAG misses, which helps "what is this document about / compare the themes" questions. +- Collapsed-tree retrieval needs no special query planning: a single vector search over mixed-granularity nodes. +- No extraction schema, no entity resolution, no graph database – low operational surface. +- Soft clustering lets a chunk contribute to several summaries, which is sensible for sections that bridge topics. +- Permissive MIT license; the idea is widely re-implemented (LlamaIndex, LangChain) if you prefer a maintained host. + +## 12. Limitations and known issues + +- **Research code, effectively unmaintained**: no tests, pinned 2024 dependencies (`openai==1.3.3`, `transformers==4.38.1`, `numpy==1.26.3`), `text-davinci-003` references, `print(e)` error handling that returns exception objects as answers, racy `next_node_index` in multithreaded tree construction, an O(N²) embedding-equality lookup inside clustering, and a probable inverted comparison in `threshold` selection mode. +- **No incremental indexing**: any corpus change is a full rebuild including all summarisation calls. +- **Single-document mindset**: `add_documents(text)` takes one string; no document ids, no metadata, no per-document boundaries, no filtering at query time, no citations. +- **Scalability**: brute-force cosine in Python at query time, pickled embeddings, and UMAP+BIC-GMM sweeps (up to 50 GMM fits per step) make tens of thousands of chunks slow and memory-heavy. Nothing is persisted to a vector DB. +- **Non-determinism**: UMAP is stochastic; two builds of the same corpus yield different trees and therefore different summaries. +- **Summary hallucination risk**: upper layers are LLM-written; errors propagate upward and are retrieved as if they were source text, with no provenance back to the originating chunks in the context given to the QA model. +- **No multi-hop reasoning**: a single retrieve-then-answer step; no decomposition, no iteration, no graph traversal between entities. +- The FAISS retriever is leaf-only and separate; there is no ANN index for the tree itself. + +## 13. Best fit / when to choose it + +- Long single documents or small homogeneous corpora (books, manuals, reports, transcripts) where questions mix fine detail with "big picture" summarisation. +- Teams that want a hierarchical-summary index without the cost and complexity of entity extraction and a graph store. +- As a component inside a larger stack (e.g. use the tree builder to produce summary nodes that you then store in your own vector DB), rather than as a turnkey system. +- Not a fit for: frequently changing corpora, multi-hop entity questions, provenance/citation requirements, >100k chunks, or production services needing a maintained library. In those cases take the idea and use a maintained re-implementation or a GraphRAG framework. + +## 14. Core idea in one paragraph + +TrustGraph is a distributed knowledge-engineering platform rather than a GraphRAG library: every function (PDF decoding, chunking, each kind of extraction, embeddings, each store writer and reader, each LLM provider, prompt templating, Graph RAG, Document RAG, agents, SPARQL, GraphQL, the API gateway) is a separate long-running processor that consumes and produces typed dataclass messages over Apache Pulsar (or RabbitMQ / Kafka). Knowledge is modelled as **RDF 1.2 quads** (`B/schema/core/primitives.py:Triple(s, p, o, g)` with `Term` supporting IRI / blank / literal / quoted-triple terms) stored in Cassandra (or Neo4j, FalkorDB, Memgraph) with entity-level and chunk-level embeddings in Qdrant (or Pinecone, Milvus). Extraction can be ontology-guided ("OntoRAG": OWL classes/properties are embedded and the relevant subset is retrieved per chunk to steer the LLM), and provenance of every extraction and every query is itself written as W3C PROV-O triples into named graphs. "Flows" (`docs/tech-specs/flow-blueprint-definition.md`) are JSON blueprints that instantiate a wired set of processors and queues per workspace; the API gateway and CLI expose them to applications and agents, and a ReAct / plan / supervisor agent runtime with tool filtering and explainability sits on top. + +## 3. Message types are plain dataclasses in `B/schema/` serialised by the backend (`B/base/async_pulsar_backend.py`, `async_rabbitmq_backend.py`, `async_kafka_backend.py`; selected by `pubsub_backend` in `B/base/pubsub.py:get_async_pubsub`). Topic naming follows `persistent://tg/flow/{workspace}::{id}` for fire-and-forget data and `non-persistent://tg/request|response/{workspace}::{class}` for request/response services. + +1. **Submit** - `T/librarian/` (`librarian` script) stores the blob in S3-compatible storage (Garage/MinIO, path `doc/{object_id}`) and metadata in Cassandra (`T/tables/library.py`: `document`, `processing`, `upload_session`); `add-processing(document_id, flow, collection)` publishes a `Document` (`B/schema/knowledge/document.py`) to the flow's `document-load` (PDF) or `text-load` (text) interface. Graph data model + +- **Primitive**: `Triple(s: Term, p: Term, o: Term, g: str|None)` - an RDF 1.2 quad; `Term(type=IRI|BLANK|LITERAL|TRIPLE, iri, id, value, datatype, language, triple)` so literals carry XSD datatypes or language tags and quoted triples (RDF-star style reification) are first-class. Batched as `Triples(metadata: Metadata(id, root, collection), triples[])`. +- **Vocabulary used by extractors** (`B/rdf.py`): `rdf:type`, `rdfs:label`, `skos:definition`; entity IRIs under `http://trustgraph.ai/e/`; predicates from free-text extraction are also minted as IRIs with `rdfs:label`. With OntoRAG the classes and properties of the loaded OWL ontology are used instead (prefix map in `extract/kg/ontology/extract.py:URI_PREFIXES` covers rdf, rdfs, owl, skos, schema.org, xsd). +- **Named graphs**: `g` separates source knowledge, provenance (`GRAPH_SOURCE`), retrieval explainability (`GRAPH_RETRIEVAL`) and agent traces; `B/provenance/uris.py` mints question / grounding / exploration / focus / synthesis / agent-session URIs. +- **Entity contexts & embeddings**: `EntityContext(entity: Term, context: str, chunk_id)`; `EntityEmbeddings(entity, vector, chunk_id)`; chunk embeddings keyed by librarian `chunk_id`. Entities are therefore addressable both as graph nodes and as vectors. +- **Structured rows**: `RowSchema(name, fields: [Field(name, type, size, primary, required, enum_values, indexed)])` stored in Cassandra tables with GraphQL query (`docs/tech-specs/graphql-query.md`). +- **Ontology handling**: OWL/Turtle ontologies are workspace configuration (`config type "ontology"`, Ontology Workbench in the UI, `T/query/ontology/` answers ontology questions incl. `query_explanation.py`); SHACL is mentioned in README but no SHACL validation processor was found in `trustgraph-flow`. There is no schema enforcement in the free-text extractors; OntoRAG constrains the prompt and normalises entities to ontology terms (`entity_normalizer.py`). +- **Where stored**: triples in the quad store, entity vectors in the vector store, chunk text/pages/documents in S3 via the librarian, document/processing metadata, config, flows, IAM and knowledge-core snapshots in Cassandra keyspaces, keyword index in SQLite FTS5. + +Cassandra quad layout (`T/direct/cassandra_kg.py`): a 7-table scheme, e.g. `spog(collection, s, p, o, g) PRIMARY KEY ((collection, s), p, o, g)`, `posg`, `ospg` for wildcard-graph queries and `gspo`, ... with `g` in the partition key, so every triple-pattern shape resolves to a partition read. `docs/tech-specs/cassandra-consolidation.md`, `cassandra-performance-refactor.md`, `neo4j-user-collection-isolation.md` cover keyspace/collection isolation. + +## 5.
