Query / retrieval modes + +All query services are request/response processors reachable through the API gateway (`T/gateway/dispatch/*.py`: `graph_rag`, `document_rag`, `agent`, `triples_query`, `graph_embeddings_query`, `document_embeddings_query`, `sparql_query`, `structured_query`, `nlp_query`, `rows_query`, `text_completion`, `prompt`, `embeddings`, `reranker`, `mcp_tool`, import/export of triples, embeddings and cores, librarian, flow, config, iam, ...) over REST and WebSocket (`docs/README.api-docs.md`, `specs/api`, `specs/websocket`), or via the Python API (`docs/python-api.md`) and `tg-*` CLI. + +**(a) Graph RAG** - `T/retrieval/graph_rag/graph_rag.py:GraphRag.query(query, collection, entity_limit=50, triple_limit=30, max_subgraph_size=1000, max_path_length=2, edge_limit=25, max_reranker_input=350, max_reranker_text_length=240, streaming, chunk_callback, explain_callback, save_answer_callback)`: +1. `Query.extract_concepts()` - prompt `extract-concepts` (one LLM call) returns one concept per line; falls back to the raw query. +2. `get_vectors()` - embed each concept (embeddings service). +3. `get_entities()` - for each concept vector, `graph_embeddings_client.query(vector, limit=entity_limit // n_concepts, collection)` against the entity vector index; de-duplicated seed entity IRIs. +4. `hop_and_filter()` - up to `max_path_length` hops: fetch all edges from the frontier via batched triple-pattern queries (`execute_batch_triple_queries`, `triple_limit` per entity, LRU+TTL caches), resolve `rdfs:label`s (`resolve_labels_batch`), render each edge as `"{p} {o}"` text (truncated to 240 chars, at most 350 candidates), score them with the **cross-encoder reranker service** (`reranker-flashrank`, default `ms-marco-MiniLM-L-12-v2`) against the concepts, keep `edge_limit` top edges, and use their targets as the next frontier. This replaced an LLM 1-10 "semantic filter" prompt (`docs/tech-specs/graph-rag-semantic-filter.md` explains why). +5. `trace_source_documents()` - follow PROV-O edges from selected triples back to chunks/documents so the answer can cite sources. +6. Synthesis - prompt `kg-synthesis` with the labelled edge list and question (streaming supported). Token usage from all prompt calls is accumulated. +7. Explainability - at each stage (`question`, `grounding`, `exploration`, `focus`, `synthesis`) PROV-O triples are emitted through `explain_callback` into `GRAPH_RETRIEVAL` (`docs/tech-specs/query-time-explainability.md`), which the UI renders as a DAG. + +**(b) Document RAG** - `T/retrieval/document_rag/document_rag.py:DocumentRag.query(query, collection, doc_limit=20, fetch_limit=0, ...)`: `extract-concepts` prompt -> per-concept vector search over chunk embeddings (and/or FTS5 keyword search; `retrieval_mode` dense / keyword / hybrid fused with `rrf_fuse()` reciprocal-rank fusion), over-fetch `OVERFETCH_FACTOR x doc_limit` when a reranker is wired, optional cross-encoder rerank with MMR diversity (`rerank.py`, `rerank_diversity_mode="mmr"`), then prompt `document-prompt` (`prompt_client.document_prompt(query, documents)`) for synthesis. + +**(c) Structured / NL-to-GraphQL** - `structured-query` (`T/retrieval/structured_query/service.py`) -> `nlp-query` (`T/retrieval/nlp_query/service.py`: phase 1 prompt `schema-selection`, phase 2 GraphQL generation) -> `rows-query-cassandra`. `structured-diag` diagnoses CSV/JSON samples and proposes a `RowSchema`. + +**(d) SPARQL** - `sparql-query` (`T/query/sparql/service.py`) parses SPARQL, decomposes it into triple-pattern lookups against the triples query service and performs joins/filters/projections in memory - works on any backend, at the cost of pulling data client-side. + +**(e) Raw services** - `triples-query` (pattern match `s?/p?/o?/g?` with limits), `graph-embeddings-query`, `document-embeddings-query`, `row-embeddings-query`, `embeddings`, `reranker`, `text-completion`, `prompt`. + +**(f) Agents** - see section 7; the agent's `knowledge-query` tool wraps Graph RAG. + +**API surface.** `api-gateway` (`T/gateway/service.py`) registers one dispatcher per service in `T/gateway/dispatch/` and exposes them as REST (`/api/v1/...`) and WebSocket endpoints; request/response calls are multiplexed over the broker with correlation ids (`dispatch/requestor.py`, `mux.py`), streaming responses are forwarded chunk by chunk, and the gateway enforces IAM (`gateway/auth.py`, bearer API keys or signed tokens, or `no-auth-svc` for development) and audit (`gateway/audit.py`). Import/export endpoints (`triples_import`/`_export`, `graph_embeddings_*`, `document_embeddings_*`, `entity_contexts_*`, `core_import`/`core_export`, `rows_import`) move bulk data without going through extraction. The Python client (`trustgraph-base/trustgraph/api`, `docs/python-api.md`) and every `tg-invoke-*` CLI call the same endpoints, so anything the UI does is scriptable. + +```mermaid +sequenceDiagram + participant Cl as client / gateway + participant GR as graph-rag processor + participant PR as prompt-template -> text-completion + participant EM as embeddings + participant GEQ as graph-embeddings-query (Qdrant) + participant TQ as triples-query (Cassandra) + participant RR as reranker-flashrank + Cl->>GR: GraphRagQuery(question, collection, limits) + GR->>PR: prompt "extract-concepts" + PR-->>GR: concept lines + GR->>EM: embed(concepts) + GR->>GEQ: query(vector, limit) per concept + GEQ-->>GR: seed entity IRIs + loop hop 1..max_path_length + GR->>TQ: batched triple patterns from frontier + GR->>TQ: resolve rdfs:label for new terms + GR->>RR: rerank("{p} {o}" texts vs concepts) + RR-->>GR: top edge_limit edges -> next frontier + end + GR->>TQ: PROV-O trace to source chunks/documents + GR->>PR: prompt "kg-synthesis" (streaming) + PR-->>GR: answer tokens + GR-->>Cl: answer + explainability triples (GRAPH_RETRIEVAL) +``` + +## 7. Generation / answer synthesis + +- **Prompts are data, not code.** `T/prompt/template/service.py` holds per-workspace `PromptManager`s loaded from config type `prompt`; every prompt (`extract-definitions`, `extract-relationships`, `extract-rows`, `extract-with-ontologies`, `agent-kg-extract`, `extract-concepts`, `kg-synthesis`, `document-prompt`, `schema-selection`, `agent-react`, `question`, ...) is a Jinja-style template with a declared response type (text / JSON with schema / JSONL). The default template texts ship in the external seed JSON consumed by `bootstrap/initialisers/template_seed.py` (populating the reserved `__template__` workspace) and are editable at runtime through the Prompt Editor UI or `tg-set-prompt`; they are **not** in this repository, so exact wording cannot be cited here. +- **Citations**: Graph RAG passes labelled edges plus traced source documents to `kg-synthesis`; Document RAG passes chunk texts to `document-prompt`. Whether the answer contains inline citations depends on the template. Structured provenance is delivered separately as explainability triples and, when `save_answer_callback` is set, the answer is saved into the librarian as a `document_type: "answer"` child of the question. +- **Agent loops** (`T/agent/`): + - `agent-manager-react` (`react/service.py`, `agent_manager.py`): classic ReAct - prompt `agent-react` renders question, history and tool list; `streaming_parser.py` parses Thought / Action / Observation / Final Answer; `max_iterations=10`; tools built from config type `tool`/`tool-service` with implementations `KnowledgeQueryImpl` (Graph RAG), `TextCompletionImpl`, `PromptImpl`, `McpToolImpl` (MCP servers via `mcp-tool` processor, bearer-token support), `StructuredQueryImpl`, `RowEmbeddingsQueryImpl`, `ToolServiceImpl` (`docs/tech-specs/tool-services.md`); `tool_filter.py` applies tool groups and state machines (`docs/tech-specs/tool-group.md`). Each thought/observation is streamed to the client and recorded as explainability triples (`agent_iteration_uri`, `docs/tech-specs/agent-explainability.md`). + - `agent-orchestrator` (`orchestrator/service.py`, "drop-in replacement" on the same queues): `meta_router.py` asks the LLM to classify the question and pick `ReactPattern`, `PlanThenExecutePattern` (`plan_pattern.py`: plan once, execute each step as a single-shot tool call) or `SupervisorPattern` (`supervisor_pattern.py`: decompose into sub-goals, fan out as child `AgentRequest`s with `correlation_id`, `aggregator.py` waits for all, then synthesise). `docs/tech-specs/agent-orchestration.md`. + - The README's "policy runtime" (authority / scope / risk checks before execution) is reflected in IAM, audit events (`B/base/audit_publisher.py`, `docs/tech-specs/audit-events.md`) and tool gating; no general policy-evaluation engine (e.g. SHACL/OPA) was found in this tree. +- Streaming LLM responses are supported end to end (`docs/tech-specs/streaming-llm-responses.md`, `rag-streaming-support.md`). + +## 8. LLM and embedding usage, cost profile + +**LLM services** (`T/model/text_completion/*`): `openai`, `azure`, `azure_openai`, `claude` (Anthropic), `cohere`, `mistral`, `ollama`, `llamafile`, `lmstudio`, `tgi`, `vllm`; plus `trustgraph-vertexai` and `trustgraph-bedrock` packages. Image-to-text via `image-to-text-openai`. Models are per-flow-class settings (`{workspace}:{class}` service queues), so several flows can share one LLM service or run different ones. `metering` tracks tokens; `LLMResponse`-style results carry `in_token`/`out_token`/`model` which Graph RAG aggregates. + +**Embeddings**: `embeddings-fastembed` (ONNX, default `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, batched - `docs/tech-specs/embeddings-batch-processing.md`), `embeddings-ollama`, `trustgraph-embeddings-hf`. Reranker: `reranker-flashrank` (local cross-encoder). Both default to CPU-local models, so the only paid calls by default are LLM completions. + +**Indexing cost per chunk** (default flow with definitions + relationships extractors): 2 LLM calls (`extract-definitions`, `extract-relationships`); +1 with OntoRAG (`extract-with-ontologies`, with a larger prompt carrying the ontology subset); the agent extractor costs a whole ReAct loop per chunk (several LLM calls). Embeddings: one batch per `EntityContexts` message and one per chunk (local by default). No LLM-based entity resolution or description summarisation; no community detection. + +**Query cost**: Graph RAG = 1 LLM call (`extract-concepts`) + N concept embeddings + up to `max_path_length` rerank batches (local) + 1 LLM call (`kg-synthesis`) = **2 LLM calls**. Document RAG = 2 LLM calls (`extract-concepts`, `document-prompt`). ReAct agent = up to `max_iterations` LLM calls plus any Graph RAG calls inside tools. SPARQL/GraphQL paths use 0-2 LLM calls (`nlp-query` uses 2). + +## 9. Benchmarks + +**Author-reported**: none. No accuracy, latency or cost benchmarks were found in `README.md`, `docs/`, or `docs/tech-specs/` (the only quantitative material is design reasoning, e.g. why the LLM semantic filter was replaced by a cross-encoder). **Third-party**: none found in-tree. The project's claims about reduced hallucination are architectural (ontology grounding, provenance), not measured. + +## 11. Strengths + +- True platform: ingestion, storage, retrieval, agents, IAM, metering, UI, CLI and API gateway in one deployable stack with no mandatory SaaS dependencies ("No API keys required" except LLM providers). +- Standards-based knowledge model: RDF 1.2 quads with datatypes/language tags/quoted triples, OWL ontologies, PROV-O provenance for both extraction and retrieval, Turtle import/export - portable to any RDF system and auditable by design. +- Pluggable everything via pub/sub: 4 triple stores, 3 vector stores, 3 brokers, ~11 LLM back-ends (including self-hosted vLLM/TGI/Ollama/llamafile/LM Studio), multiple decoders and embedders, all selectable per flow. +- Retrieval designed for explainability: concept extraction -> entity vector seeding -> hop-and-filter with a local cross-encoder -> source tracing -> explainability DAG visible in the UI. +- Multiple extraction strategies, including ontology-guided (OntoRAG) and agentic extraction, plus structured-data ingestion with GraphQL/NL query. +- Horizontal scalability and isolation: each processor scales independently, flows are isolated per workspace, Cassandra/Qdrant scale out. +- Rich agent runtime (ReAct, plan-then-execute, supervisor fan-out, MCP tools, tool groups/state machines) with per-step provenance. + +## 12. Limitations and known issues + +- **Deployment weight**: minimum stack is Pulsar (plus ZooKeeper/BookKeeper), Cassandra, Qdrant, Garage/MinIO, the gateway, config/flow/IAM services and a dozen processors - heavy for a single developer or small corpus; local development relies on process groups and the dev installer. +- The platform is only configurable through the external `@trustgraph/config` generator and seed files; default flow blueprints and prompt texts are not in the main repository, which makes auditing defaults harder. +- **Knowledge quality controls are thin**: no entity resolution/deduplication beyond identical IRIs minted from the entity string (`to_uri` URL-quotes the surface form, so "Acme" and "Acme Corp" are different nodes), no description merging, no confidence/weights on edges, no schema pruning outside OntoRAG. +- No incremental re-sync or fact retraction; collection-level deletion only. +- SPARQL is executed by client-side decomposition and in-memory joins, which will not scale to analytical queries; GraphQL covers structured rows only. +- No community/global summarisation mode; Graph RAG is entity-seeded local traversal with bounded hops. +- Rapid architectural churn (legacy `ConsumerProducer` processors such as topics extraction still present but unwired; multiple migration specs); API gateway and CLI changed incompatibly between 1.8 and 2.1 (`docs/api-gateway-changes-v1.8-to-v2.1.md`, `cli-changes-v1.8-to-v2.1.md`). +- Python code is largely untyped at the message boundary (dataclasses, hand-rolled serialisation), and many processors share near-duplicate boilerplate. +- No benchmarks; the "policy runtime" marketed in the README is only partially visible in code (IAM, audit, tool gating). + +## 13. Best fit / when to choose it + +Choose TrustGraph when you need an on-prem, multi-tenant knowledge platform rather than a library: regulated environments that require RDF/OWL interoperability and PROV-O-grade provenance for every answer, teams that want to self-host open-weight models end to end, or organisations running agent workloads that must be traced and gated. It is also the only one of the three that ingests office formats, images and structured data into the same graph. Avoid it for prototypes, single-tenant apps with a modest corpus, or when your team is standardised on a property-graph database and wants to write Cypher - the operational cost of the broker-and-processor architecture only pays off at platform scale. + +## 14. Core idea in one paragraph + +Youtu-GraphRAG threads one **graph schema** (a JSON with `Nodes`, `Relations`, `Attributes` type lists) through every stage. At build time an LLM extracts, per chunk, entity attributes, `[s, r, o]` triples and entity types that conform to the schema (and, in "agent" mode, may propose new schema types that get written back to the schema file). The result is a NetworkX graph organised into four levels: attributes (L1), entities/relations (L2), keywords (L3) and LLM-named communities (L4), where communities come from a custom "Tree-Comm" clustering that mixes sentence-embedding similarity of each node's one-hop triples with Jaccard structural similarity. At query time an LLM decomposer reads the same schema to split the question into sub-questions and to predict which schema types are involved; each sub-question is run in parallel through a multi-path FAISS retriever (node/relation/triple/community indices plus chunk embeddings, keyword and path search), results are merged into "Triples + Chunks" context, an initial answer is produced, and an IRCoT loop then alternates LLM reasoning and new retrieval until the model emits "So the answer is:". The pitch is that schema-bounded extraction gives cheaper, cleaner graphs and that schema-aware decomposition plus community/keyword levels give better multi-hop accuracy per token than LightRAG/HippoRAG-style baselines. + +## 3. Indexing pipeline, step by step + +Entry: `main.py::graph_construction()` → `KTBuilder(dataset, schema_path, mode, config).build_knowledge_graph(corpus_path)` (`models/constructor/kt_gen.py`). The web backend (`backend.py::/api/construct-graph`) calls the same builder after turning uploads into a corpus JSON via `utils/document_parser.py`. + +1. **Load schema** – `KTBuilder.load_schema()` reads `schemas/.json` (e.g. `schemas/demo.json`: 10 node types `person, location, organization, event, object, concept, time_period, creative_work, biological_entity, natural_phenomenon`; 12 relations; 11 attribute names). Missing file → empty dict (extraction then runs schema-free). +2. **Load corpus** – `json_repair.load` of a list of docs (`{title, text}` dicts or strings). +3. **Chunking** – `KTBuilder.chunk_text()`. Datasets listed in `construction.datasets_no_chunk` (hotpot, 2wiki, musique, graphrag-bench, demo, ...) are *not* chunked: each doc is one chunk. Otherwise `_split_text_with_overlap()` does fixed token windows (cl100k) with `construction.chunk_size` (default **5000**) and `overlap` 200, merging tails shorter than `min_tail_tokens` 100. Chunk ids are 8-char `nanoid`s; `all_chunks` is later dumped to `output/chunks/.txt` as `id: \tChunk: ` lines – this file is the chunk store used at query time. +4. **Per-chunk LLM extraction** – `process_document()` runs `process_level1_level2_agent()` (mode `agent`, default) or `process_level1_level2()` (mode `noagent`). Prompt selection in `_get_construction_prompt()`: `prompts.construction.general` / `general_agent` (or `novel`, `novel_eng` variants) from `config/base_config.yaml`, formatted with `{schema}` and `{chunk}`. One `LLMCompletionCall.call_api()` call per chunk (`utils/call_llm_api.py`, OpenAI-compatible chat, `temperature=0.3`). Output JSON (`json_repair`-parsed) has `attributes: {entity: ["k: v", ...]}`, `triples: [[s, r, o], ...]`, `entity_types: {entity: type}` and, in agent mode, `new_schema_types: {nodes, relations, attributes}`. +5. **Schema evolution (agent mode only)** – `_update_schema_with_new_types()` appends unseen types to `schemas/.json` on disk and in memory. Note the hard-coded `schema_paths` map only covers `hotpot, 2wiki, musique, novel, graphrag-bench`; for other datasets (including `demo` and user uploads) the function silently returns, so schema evolution does not happen for custom datasets unless you edit that map. +6. **Graph assembly** – `_process_attributes[_agent]` creates one `attribute` node (`attr_`, level 1, `properties={name: "k: v", "chunk id": id}`) per attribute string and an edge `entity --has_attribute--> attr`. `_process_triples[_agent]` creates/looks up `entity` nodes (`entity_`, level 2, `properties={name, "chunk id", schema_type}`) and adds edge `subj ----> obj` on a `nx.MultiDiGraph`. Entity resolution is **exact name match** (`_find_or_create_entity` scans all nodes linearly under a lock – O(V) per lookup). Only the *first* chunk id is kept on an entity. +7. **Concurrency** – `process_all_documents()` uses a `ThreadPoolExecutor` (`construction.max_workers` 32, capped at `cpu_count+4`), one future per document; progress/ETA logging. +8. **Triple dedup** – `triple_deduplicate()` rebuilds the MultiDiGraph keeping one edge per `(u, v, relation)`. +9. **Level 4: communities** – `process_level4()` instantiates `utils/tree_comm.py::FastTreeComm(graph, embedding_model=all-MiniLM-L6-v2, struct_weight=0.3)` and calls `detect_communities(level2_nodes)`: + - Node representation: the concatenation of its one-hop triple strings `"name rel neighbor"` (`_get_triple_strings`), embedded with SentenceTransformer in batches (`get_triple_embeddings_batch`). + - `_fast_clustering`: KMeans with `n_clusters = clamp(N//10, 2, min(N//2, 200))`. + - Clusters larger than 3 are refined (`_refine_cluster`): KMeans again inside, then centres (the top "keyword" node of each sub-cluster) are compared with a fused similarity `0.3 * Jaccard(neighbour sets) + 0.7 * cosine(triple embeddings)` (`_compute_sim_matrix`) and merged greedily when `>= merge_threshold 0.5` and merged size `<= 100`, for `max_iter=1` pass. + - Global cap `tree_comm.max_total_communities` (default 100) – once reached, remaining KMeans clusters are emitted as communities without refinement. + - This is the "dually-perceived community detection" from the paper; it is KMeans + one merge pass, not Leiden/Louvain. +10. **Community naming + Level 3 keywords** – `create_super_nodes_with_keywords(comm_to_nodes, level=4)`: communities with ≥2 members are batched 5 at a time into one LLM prompt (`_build_batch_prompt`: centre name, first 10 member names, size) that returns `{id, name, summary}` per community. A `community` node `comm_4_` (level 4, `properties={name, description, members:[names]}`) is added with `member --member_of--> community` edges. Then `extract_keywords_from_community()` picks top-5 members by `0.3*normalised degree + 0.7*cosine(node, community mean embedding)` and creates `keyword` nodes `kw__` (level 3) with edges `entity --represented_by--> keyword`, `keyword --keyword_of--> community`, and `entity --kw_filter_by--> keyword`. Keywords are therefore *entity names promoted to keywords*, not separately extracted terms. +11. **Serialisation** – `format_output()` flattens to a list of `{start_node:{label, properties}, relation, end_node:{label, properties}}` written to `output/graphs/_new.json` (importable to Neo4j per README). `utils/graph_processor.load_graph_from_json()` rebuilds the MultiDiGraph at query time; GraphML save/load helpers also exist. +12. **Index build (lazy, at first query)** – `KTRetriever.build_indices()` → `DualFAISSRetriever.build_indices()` creates four `faiss.IndexFlatIP` indices with L2-normalised MiniLM vectors under `retriever/faiss_cache_new//`: `node.index` (text = `"name,description"` of every node incl. attributes/keywords/communities), `relation.index` (unique relation strings), `triple.index` (`"head_text,rel,tail_text"` per edge), `comm.index` (`"name,description"` of community nodes), plus `*_map.json` id maps, `node_embeddings.pt/.npy`, `node_embedding_cache.pt`, `dim_transform.pt` (a random `torch.nn.Linear(model_dim, 384)` projection applied only if the embedding model is not 384-d – untrained, so swapping to a larger model degrades search). `KTRetriever` additionally builds a chunk FAISS index (`_precompute_chunk_embeddings`, cached in `chunk_embedding_cache.pt`), a node-text keyword inverted index (`_build_node_text_index` → `node_text_index.pkl`), and a node-text cache. Graph / tree data model + +NetworkX `MultiDiGraph`; every node has `label`, `level`, `properties` (a dict). + +| Level | `label` | id pattern | `properties` | Created by | +|---|---|---|---|---| +| 1 | `attribute` | `attr_` | `name` ("key: value" string), `chunk id` | `_process_attributes` | +| 2 | `entity` | `entity_` | `name`, `chunk id` (first only), `schema_type` | `_find_or_create_entity` | +| 3 | `keyword` | `kw__` | `name` (= an entity's name) | `create_super_nodes_with_keywords` | +| 4 | `community` | `comm_4_` | `name`, `description` (LLM summary), `members` (list of entity names) | `create_super_nodes` | + +Edges (`relation` attribute on the edge): `has_attribute` (entity→attribute), free-text predicates from extraction (entity→entity), `member_of` (entity→community), `represented_by` (entity→keyword), `keyword_of` (keyword→community), `kw_filter_by` (entity→keyword). Communities are flat (one level of L4; no hierarchy of communities despite the "tree" naming). Chunks are **not** nodes: provenance is the `chunk id` property and the sidecar `output/chunks/.txt`. There are no embeddings on the graph itself; vectors live in the FAISS cache directory. No entity descriptions are generated (the `description` field read by `_get_node_text` is only present on community nodes). + +## 5. Query / retrieval modes + +Entry points: CLI `main.py::retrieval()` chooses `no_agent_retrieval` or `agent_retrieval` by `triggers.mode`; the web endpoint `/api/ask-question` always forces agent mode. Both start from `initial_question_decomposition()`. + +### 6.1 Stage A – schema-aware decomposition (`models/retriever/agentic_decomposer.py::GraphQ`) + +One LLM call with `prompts.decomposition.general` (ontology = raw schema file text, question) returning `{"sub_questions": [{"sub-question": ...}], "involved_types": {"nodes": [...], "relations": [...], "attributes": [...]}}`. Simple questions are returned as a single sub-question. On parse/LLM failure the original question is used with empty types. + +### 6.2 Stage B – per-sub-question retrieval (`KTRetriever.process_retrieval_results`) + +If >1 sub-question, `process_subquestions_parallel` runs them in a thread pool (`retrieval.faiss.max_workers` 4). For each: + +- `retrieve_with_type_filtering(question, involved_types)`: if `involved_types.nodes` is non-empty, `_filter_nodes_by_schema_type` restricts candidate entity nodes to those `schema_type`s and runs cosine search on that subset (`_similarity_search_on_filtered_nodes`), then 1-hop triples; otherwise falls back to `retrieve()`. +- `retrieve()` with `recall_paths=2` (default) → `_parallel_dual_path_retrieval`: + - **Path 1 – node/relation retrieval** (`_node_relation_retrieval`), itself parallel: FAISS node search (`search_k = min(3*top_k, 50)`) → re-score candidates with cosine to the question (`_batch_calculate_entity_similarities`); spaCy keyword extraction (`_extract_query_keywords`: NER + NOUN/PROPN/ADJ/VERB tokens) → exact-match lookup in the node-text inverted index (`_keyword_based_node_search`) → same re-scoring, threshold 0.05; FAISS relation search; **chunk FAISS search** (`_chunk_embedding_retrieval`, top_k); merge candidates, keep top `top_k` nodes; expand with `_optimized_neighbor_expansion` (1-hop triples re-scored), `_path_based_search` (DFS to depth 2 from top nodes toward keyword-matching nodes) and `_get_relation_matched_triples` (triples from top nodes whose relation is among the FAISS-matched relations). + - **Path 2 – triple/community retrieval** (`_triple_only_retrieval` → `DualFAISSRetriever.dual_path_retrieval`): FAISS triple search (top_k) → for each hit also collect triples around the 3-hop neighbourhood of head and tail (`_collect_neighbor_triples`, `_get_3hop_neighbors`) → dedupe → `_calculate_triple_relevance_scores` (cosine, threshold 0.1, top_k). Community search (`retrieve_via_communities`: FAISS over community name+summary → expand to member entity ids via `properties.members` and `name_to_id`) also runs here, but **only `scored_triples` is consumed** by `_triple_only_retrieval`; `comm_nodes` are computed and dropped. The L4 community level therefore influences retrieval only indirectly (community nodes are in `node.index` and their keyword nodes are in the node index). +- Chunk ids are gathered from top nodes' `chunk id`, from triple endpoints and from the chunk FAISS hits, capped at `top_k`. +- `process_retrieval_results` then: reranks chunk hits (`_process_chunk_results` → `_rerank_chunks_by_relevance`, average of FAISS score and fresh cosine), collects and scores all triples from both paths (`_collect_all_scored_triples`, `_rerank_triples_by_relevance`), keeps `top_k` (`retrieval.top_k_filter` 20), formats triples as strings (`_format_scored_triples`), and resolves chunk texts from `chunk2id`. + +### 6.3 Stage C – context assembly and initial answer (`main.py::initial_question_decomposition`) + +Union of all sub-question triples and chunks; if more than 20 triples, keep the 20 with most question-word overlap; if more than `top_k_filter` chunks, `rerank_chunks_by_keywords` (keyword overlap). Context string = `"=== Triples ===\n...\n=== Chunks ===\n..."`. One LLM call with `prompts.retrieval.general` → `initial_answer` (retried up to 20 times on empty output). + +### 6.4 Mode `noagent` + +Stops after Stage C; the initial answer is the final answer. `utils/eval.py::Eval` (LLM-as-judge returning "1"/"0") scores against gold when running benchmarks. + +### 6.5 Mode `agent` (IRCoT loop, `main.py::agent_retrieval`) + +Starting from Stage C's triples/chunks/answer (added as "Initial analysis (noagent mode): ..." thought), for `step in 1..retrieval.agent.max_steps` (5): +1. Build context from all accumulated triples/chunks; prompt is the inline IRCoT template in `agent_retrieval` (the YAML `prompts.retrieval.ircot` key exists but the CLI uses its own inline copy that also mentions the initial analysis) with `Previous Thoughts` = all prior thoughts. +2. One LLM call. If the response contains `"So the answer is:"` → stop. Else parse `"The new query is:"` (fallback: the whole response), and if it differs from the current query run `process_retrieval_results(new_query)` (no type filtering here) and merge new triples/chunks. +3. After the loop, one more LLM call with `prompts.retrieval.general` over the final merged context produces the answer. + +"Reflection" in the README maps to this thought-then-requery loop; there is no explicit answer-verification or self-critique prompt beyond the IRCoT instruction text. + +```mermaid +sequenceDiagram + participant U as User + participant D as GraphQ decomposer (LLM) + participant R as KTRetriever + participant F as DualFAISSRetriever / FAISS + participant L as LLM + U->>D: question + schema + D-->>R: sub_questions[], involved_types + par per sub-question (thread pool) + R->>F: node/relation/triple/chunk FAISS search + F-->>R: candidates + R->>R: keyword + path + 1-hop expansion, rerank triples/chunks + end + R-->>L: "=== Triples === ... === Chunks ===" + prompts.retrieval.general + L-->>R: initial_answer + loop IRCoT, max_steps=5 + R->>L: ircot prompt (context + previous thoughts) + alt "So the answer is:" + L-->>R: stop + else "The new query is: q'" + R->>F: process_retrieval_results(q') + F-->>R: new triples/chunks merged + end + end + R->>L: final prompt over merged context + L-->>U: answer (+ sub-questions, reasoning steps, retrieved triples for UI) +``` + +## 7. Generation / answer synthesis + +- Prompts are plain strings in `config/base_config.yaml` under `prompts.construction.*`, `prompts.decomposition.*`, `prompts.retrieval.{general, ircot, novel, novel_eng}`; resolved by `ConfigManager.get_prompt_formatted(section, name, **kwargs)`. Dataset names `novel`/`novel_eng`/`anony_chs` switch to Chinese or novel-specific variants. +- The answer prompt (`retrieval.general`) instructs: use only the provided context, "If the knowledge is insufficient, reject to answer", be concise, give specific entity/date. The novel variants instead allow falling back to model knowledge. +- Reasoning loop: IRCoT as described above, max 5 steps, stop token phrases `So the answer is:` / `The new query is:`. +- Citations: none. Context triples carry entity names but no chunk ids; chunks are inserted as raw text without ids. The web UI returns `sub_questions`, `reasoning_steps`, and `retrieved_triples` for visualisation (`backend.py::prepare_subquery_visualization`, `prepare_retrieved_graph_visualization`), which is the only provenance surface. +- Every generation call is `temperature=0.3` via `LLMCompletionCall.call_api`, with a wrapper that strips code fences; retries are implemented as `for retry in range(20)` loops in `main.py`. + +## 8. LLM and embedding usage, cost profile + +**Indexing** +- LLM: exactly **1 call per chunk** for extraction (attributes + triples + types + optional schema delta in one shot) plus **1 call per 5 communities** for naming/summaries. With `chunk_size=5000` tokens that is few, large calls; with benchmark datasets (no chunking) it is one call per document. The repo's `token_cal` logs total prompt+response tokens. The README claims 33.6% lower token cost than SOTA baselines, attributable to single-pass extraction and no per-entity description generation. +- Embeddings: local MiniLM, no API cost: all nodes (incl. attribute/keyword/community nodes), all unique relations, all triples, all communities, all chunks, plus triple-string embeddings for Tree-Comm. CPU is the default; this is the wall-clock bottleneck for large graphs. +- Also: KMeans/refinement, O(V) linear scans for entity dedup during extraction (quadratic overall in entity count, under a lock – throughput drops on big corpora). + +**Query** (agent mode, `max_steps=5`) +- 1 decomposition call + 1 initial answer call + 1–5 IRCoT calls + 1 final answer call ≈ **4–8 LLM calls** per question (plus 1 judge call when evaluating). Noagent mode: 2 calls. +- Embedding: question (cached per text) and sub-questions; chunk reranking re-encodes each candidate chunk with MiniLM per call. +- Context size: up to 20 triples + up to 20 chunks; with 5000-token chunks the prompt can reach ~100k tokens – `top_k_filter` should be reduced for large-chunk corpora. +- FAISS searches are memoised per (query vector, k) in `faiss_search_cache`. + +## 9. Configuration and extension points + +- **Single YAML**: `config/base_config.yaml`, loaded by `config/config_loader.py::ConfigManager` / `get_config(path)`; `main.py --config` and `--override '{"retrieval.top_k": 10}'` (dotted-key JSON) for runtime overrides. Sections: `construction` (`chunk_size`, `overlap`, `datasets_no_chunk`, `max_workers`, `mode: agent|noagent`, `tree_comm.{embedding_model, struct_weight, max_total_communities, enable_fast_mode}`), `datasets..{corpus_path, qa_path, schema_path, graph_output}`, `embeddings.{model_name, device, batch_size, max_length}`, `nlp.spacy_model`, `retrieval.{top_k, top_k_filter, recall_paths (1|2), similarity_threshold, enable_reranking, enable_query_enhancement, enable_high_recall, enable_caching, cache_dir, faiss.{device, max_workers, search_k}, agent.{enable_ircot, enable_parallel_subquestions, max_steps}}`, `triggers.{constructor_trigger, retrieve_trigger, mode}`, `prompts.*`. +- **LLM**: `.env` only (`LLM_MODEL`, `LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_API_KEY`, optional Azure vars). One model for everything; no per-stage model choice without editing `LLMCompletionCall`. +- **Embedding model**: `embeddings.model_name` (any SentenceTransformer). Non-384-d models trigger the untrained `dim_transform` linear layer – effectively you should stay with 384-d models or fix the projection. +- **Schema**: add `schemas/.json` with `Nodes/Relations/Attributes` lists and a `datasets.` entry; the UI exposes `/api/datasets/{name}/schema` upload. Schema evolution write-back is limited to the hard-coded dataset map in `_update_schema_with_new_types`. +- **Prompts**: edit YAML; dataset-name-based routing in `_get_construction_prompt`, `GraphQ.prompt_format`, `KTRetriever.generate_prompt`. +- **Retrieval knobs**: `recall_paths=1` disables Path 2; `involved_types` filtering is automatic from decomposition; `top_k_filter` caps triples/chunks. +- **Document ingestion**: `utils/document_parser.py` (PDF via MinerU/pypdf, DOCX, RTF, Tika fallback) feeding `/api/upload`; CLI expects pre-built corpus JSON. +- **Incremental update**: **not supported.** `graph_construction` calls `clear_cache_files(dataset)` and rebuilds from the corpus; `KTBuilder.save_chunks_to_file` overwrites the chunk file ("fresh start"); the backend's `/api/datasets/{name}/reconstruct` is a full rebuild; FAISS caches are invalidated whenever the node set changes. Adding documents means re-extracting everything (and re-running Tree-Comm, which re-ids communities). +- **Extension**: no plugin registry; swap components by editing `main.py`/`backend.py` wiring (`constructor.KTBuilder`, `decomposer.GraphQ`, `retriever.KTRetriever`). + +## 10. Benchmarks reported by the authors + +From README/paper (the repo has no results tables; `utils/eval.py` is an LLM judge, and `main.py` prints accuracy): + +- Evaluated on six benchmarks including **HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, GraphRAG-Bench** and the authors' new **AnonyRAG** (Chinese + English; entity names anonymised to defeat pretraining leakage; https://huggingface.co/datasets/Youtu-Graph/AnonyRAG). +- Headline: "33.6% lower token cost and 16.62% higher accuracy over state-of-the-art baselines", presented as moving the accuracy/cost Pareto frontier (figures `assets/performance.png`, `assets/pareto.png`, `assets/radar.png`). Per-dataset numbers are only in the paper (arXiv:2508.19855); they are not reproduced in the repo. +- Tree-Comm is claimed to beat Leiden/Louvain community structure for retrieval, again only in the paper. +- Accuracy is judged by an LLM ("reasonable, not too strict or too lenient"), not EM/F1, which makes cross-paper comparison loose. + +No independent third-party reproductions were found in the repo or its docs. + +## 11. Strengths + +- **Schema-in-the-loop design**: one JSON schema bounds extraction, drives `involved_types` filtering at query time, and (in agent mode) grows itself – a cheap way to adapt to a new domain. +- **Cheap graph construction**: one LLM call per chunk covering attributes, triples and types; no per-entity description generation, no gleaning passes; community summaries are batched 5 per call. +- **Multi-path, parallel retrieval** with many complementary signals (dense nodes/relations/triples/chunks, keyword inverted index, 2-hop path search, 3-hop triple neighbourhoods) and sub-question parallelism. +- **IRCoT loop** gives genuine iterative retrieval for multi-hop questions, with transparent reasoning traces surfaced in the UI. +- **Local, dependency-light storage**: NetworkX + FAISS files + a text file; no graph database or vector DB to operate; Docker image and web UI with upload, build, and graph visualisation. +- Bilingual (EN/CN) prompts and datasets; Azure support. + +## 12. Limitations and known issues + +- **Research-code status**: no tests, no packaging, 2.7k-line retriever with many near-duplicate/legacy methods (`_keyword_based_node_search_original`, `_execute_retrieval_strategies_parallel` vs `_node_relation_retrieval`), commented-out code paths, 20-iteration retry loops, `threading.Lock()` created inline per use (ineffective), and `debug_mode = True` hard-coded. +- **Community level is mostly unused at query time**: `retrieve_via_communities` results are discarded by `_triple_only_retrieval`; the L3/L4 levels mainly add nodes to the node index. The "top-down filtering" the README describes is not wired into the default path. +- **Entity resolution is exact string match** with no normalisation/aliasing and an O(V) scan per lookup under a global lock – both quality (duplicates like "T.I." vs "T.I") and throughput degrade with corpus size. +- **Untrained dimension projection** (`torch.nn.Linear` random init) when using non-384-d embedding models. +- **Schema evolution only for hard-coded datasets**; for uploads the LLM is asked for `new_schema_types` that are then thrown away. +- **No incremental indexing**; full rebuild and cache invalidation on any change. No document-level deletion. +- **No citations / provenance in answers**; chunk ids are stripped from context. +- **Scalability**: in-memory NetworkX graph, flat FAISS indices (`IndexFlatIP`, no ANN), CPU MiniLM; the FULLGUIDE documents FAISS segfault workarounds for large datasets. Chunk default of 5000 tokens makes contexts very large. +- **Single global LLM**; no small-model routing for extraction vs reasoning. +- Spacy `en_core_web_lg` and English-centric keyword extraction; Chinese keyword path depends on the same pipeline. +- License text is MIT-like but bespoke ("Youtu-GraphRAG License"); check with legal if that matters. + +## 13. Best fit / when to choose it + +- Teams with a known domain ontology (or willing to write a short type list) who want a schema-guided, relatively cheap graph build and multi-hop QA with visible reasoning traces, at corpus sizes of thousands (not millions) of chunks. +- Researchers benchmarking against HotpotQA/MuSiQue/2Wiki/GraphRAG-Bench/AnonyRAG with an agentic decomposition + IRCoT baseline. +- Prototyping a self-hosted GraphRAG demo quickly (Docker + UI) without standing up Neo4j/Milvus. +- Not a fit for: production services needing incremental updates, provenance, multi-tenant storage, or a maintained SDK; very large corpora; non-English/Chinese text without re-prompting. For enterprise use the authors point to Tencent Cloud ADP's closed Enterprise Edition. + +## 14. After a deletion, the graph is identical to a fresh index of the remaining documents, verified on the full 11,402-passage MuSiQue corpus. + +This repository holds the reference implementation, the benchmark harness used for the paper, per-question results for every run, and the paper source. + +Paper: [paper/main.pdf](paper/main.pdf) + +## Results + +Recall@5 is the share of gold evidence passages in the top 5 retrieved. EM is exact-match answer accuracy. Index cost is normalised to list prices. + +| System | MuSiQue R@5 | 2Wiki R@5 | HotpotQA R@5 | HotpotQA EM | MuSiQue index cost | Delete 10% of docs | +|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| +| **Lightfoot** | **0.646** | 0.884 | **0.943** | **0.630** | **$1.64** | 0 model calls, exact | +| HippoRAG 2 | 0.616 | **0.905** | 0.930 | 0.553 | $2.23 | 0 model calls | +| LightRAG | 0.480 | 0.722 | 0.902 | 0.543 | ≈$9.5 | 2,187 model calls, 3.7 h | +| fast-graphrag | 0.412 | 0.838 | 0.732 | 0.517 | $4.89 | not supported | + +Against HippoRAG 2, Lightfoot is significantly better on 5 of 15 paired comparisons, significantly worse on 2 (both on 2WikiMultiHopQA), and tied on 8. Full tables, intervals and caveats are in the paper and in [docs/design/05-results-all.md](docs/design/05-results-all.md). + +## How it works + +```mermaid +flowchart LR + subgraph Index + P[Passage] --> X[One LLM call:
entities + facts as JSON] + X --> F[Per-chunk name forms
with provenance] + F --> E[Entities = linked groups of forms
cosine >= 0.92] + E --> G[Graph: entities + passages
fact and synonym edges] + end + subgraph Query + Q[Question] --> S[Seed from top-2 matching facts
+ top-100 dense passages] + S --> W[Personalized PageRank
damping 0.9] + W --> R[Cross-encoder rerank of top 30,
fused with PageRank rank] + R --> A[One answer call
top 10 passages + facts] + end + subgraph Delete + D[Document] --> DF[Remove its forms and fact assertions] + DF --> DR[Recompute only touched groups
no model calls] + end +``` + +Every stored record is a function of the live per-chunk forms only, never of insertion order, batching or history. That is what makes deletion exact. The design and how it changed during benchmarking are in [docs/design/01-architecture.md](docs/design/01-architecture.md), section 11. + +## Repository layout + +| Path | Contents | +|---|---| +| `lightfoot/` | The Lightfoot package: extraction, resolution, provenance ledger, graph, retrieval, answering, stores (SQLite, PostgreSQL), optional Elasticsearch channel | +| `harness/` | Benchmark harness: dataset builders, metrics, cost ledger, runner, answer-only rerun, LiteLLM proxy config, adapters and subprocess workers for each baseline | +| `tests/` | 82 tests, including the exact-erasure tests | +| `runs/` | One YAML per benchmark run | +| `data/` | The question and passage subsets used in the paper (parquet), built from the public datasets | +| `results/` | Per-question predictions, scores, cost ledgers and summaries for every reported run (index stores are not included) | +| `scripts/` | Diagnostics and validation scripts, plus dataset download | +| `docs/design/` | Architecture, evaluation plan, results write-ups, paper draft notes | +| `docs/frameworks/` | Source-code reviews of 17 open-source GraphRAG frameworks | +| `paper/` | LaTeX source and PDF | + +## Setup + +Tested on macOS 14 (Apple M3 Pro, 18 GB) with Python 3.14 for Lightfoot and 3.12 for two baselines. + +```bash +python3 -m venv .venv +.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt +cp .env.example .env # then put your OpenRouter key in .env +``` + +Lightfoot's tests need no API key: + +```bash +.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests +``` + +### Datasets + +The `data/` folder already holds the exact subsets used in the paper. To rebuild them, or build other sizes, download the raw datasets into a sibling `datasets/` folder: + +```bash +./scripts/download_datasets.sh +.venv/bin/python -m harness.datasets build musique 1000 +``` + +### Baselines + +Each baseline runs in its own virtual environment under `envs/`, driven by a worker process: + +```bash +./envs/setup_baselines.sh +``` + +This installs LightRAG (lightrag-hku 1.5.7), HippoRAG 2 (2.0.0a5) and fast-graphrag (0.0.5, commit 23b3a1b). LightRAG runs on PostgreSQL with pgvector; see the script for the database setup. + +## Running the benchmark + +Lightfoot alone (calls OpenRouter directly): + +```bash +./lf_v2.sh lightfoot_v5a_musique_1000 +``` + +Baselines (start a local LiteLLM proxy and embedding server, then run each system): + +```bash +DATASETS="musique_1000" ./run_all.sh lightrag hipporag2 fastgraphrag +``` + +Summary tables from saved results: + +```bash +.venv/bin/python -m harness.report musique_1000 +``` + +Models used in the paper, set in `.env` and `harness/proxy.yaml`: + +| Role | Model | +|---|---| +| Graph building (extraction) | meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct | +| Answers | openai/gpt-5.6-luna, reasoning off | +| Embeddings (local) | BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5 | +| Reranker (local) | BAAI/bge-reranker-base | + +The MuSiQue benchmark for all four systems cost about $35 at list prices on OpenRouter. Expect actual bills to run about 1.45 times list price, depending on provider routing. + +## Citation + +```bibtex +@article{allu2026lightfoot, + title = {Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion}, + author = {Allu, Uday}, + year = {2026}, + note = {arXiv preprint} +} +``` + +## License + +MIT for the code in this repository. Light to build, light to run, and it leaves no footprint when a document is removed. + +Status: design proposal, 2026-10-17. Nothing here has been benchmarked yet. Every performance claim is a hypothesis to be tested under `02-evaluation-plan.md`. + +## 1. What the 17 frameworks taught us + +The survey in `../frameworks/` gives us a short list of mechanisms that demonstrably buy accuracy per dollar, and a short list of mechanisms that burn money without paying for themselves. + +| Keep, because it pays | Evidence | +|---|---| +| One structured extraction call per chunk, no gleaning | fast-graphrag indexes in minutes at 1 call per chunk and still outscores nano-graphrag on 2Wiki retrieval. Microsoft's own docs attribute about three quarters of cost to extraction, and gleaning doubles it. | +| Facts (triples) as first-class retrieval units, not just entities | HippoRAG 2's largest gain over HippoRAG 1 comes from matching the query against fact embeddings and seeding the walk from facts. | +| Personalized PageRank from query seeds to passages | HippoRAG 2 and fast-graphrag get multi-hop retrieval in milliseconds with no LLM in the loop. Planner-based systems (KAG, Youtu) need 6 to 15 calls to do the same job. | +| Original chunks as the answer payload, graph as the router | 16 of 17 frameworks do this. Summaries hallucinate and cannot be erased. | +| Provenance counts on every node and edge | LightRAG's delete-by-document works only because it stores which chunk produced each entity. HippoRAG 2's delete works because facts carry source counts. | +| Content-hash sync at document level | GraphRAG-SDK's update path is the only one that is crash-safe and proportional to the change. | +| Embedding-based entity canonicalization with an LLM judge only in the ambiguous band | fast-graphrag's identity edges and GraphRAG-SDK's double-vote judge are the only resolution strategies better than string equality. 14 of 17 use string equality. | +| Local cross-encoder reranker instead of an LLM filter | TrustGraph uses flashrank; HippoRAG's DSPy filter is an LLM call per query that mostly drops facts. | + +| Drop, because it does not pay | Evidence | +|---|---| +| Leiden communities plus LLM report per community at index time | Microsoft and nano-graphrag spend one LLM call per community per level, then either never re-cluster (stale) or re-cluster everything on insert. Youtu builds communities and discards them at query time. | +| Map-reduce global search over all reports | Dozens of 12k-token calls per question. | +| LLM summarisation of merged entity descriptions | LightRAG, Microsoft, nano all do this. It is an extra call that produces text you cannot attribute to a chunk, so it cannot be erased when a chunk is deleted. | +| LLM query planner by default | KAG and Youtu pay 4 to 15 calls per question. Use it only as an escalation path. | +| Exact-string entity resolution | Universal weak spot. | +| Research-code shortcuts | Hard-coded sleeps, whole-corpus re-extraction, positional parsing of delimiter strings. Use JSON mode or constrained decoding. | + +## 2. Design goals, in priority order + +1. **Erasable.** Deleting a document is a database transaction: zero LLM calls, zero embedding calls, bounded by the number of chunks in that document. The graph after deleting document D must be byte-identical to the graph that would exist had D never been indexed. This is the invariant that makes the system enterprise-safe (GDPR erasure, contract expiry, retracted documents). +2. **Cheap to index.** Target one LLM call and one embedding batch per chunk, with a small model. No second pass, no summaries, no community reports. +3. **At least as accurate as HippoRAG 2 on multi-hop QA, and better than LightRAG on domain QA.** The accuracy levers are facts as retrieval units, hybrid dense plus sparse seeding, entity canonicalization, PPR, and a local reranker. +4. **Cheap to query.** One embedding call, one PPR, one local reranker pass, one answer call. An optional second retrieval round only when a confidence gate fails. +5. **One database.** Postgres with pgvector for truth. An in-memory sparse matrix per tenant for PPR, rebuilt incrementally from the database. No Java server, no message broker, no separate clustering service. +6. **Global questions without index-time cost.** Topic summaries are built lazily at query time and cached with a content hash of the chunk set they cover, so they invalidate automatically on delete. + +## 3. Data model: the ledger + +Three node kinds and four edge kinds. Every node and edge carries `prov`, a map from chunk id to count. A record exists if and only if its `prov` is non-empty. + +``` +Document(doc_id, content_hash, tenant, metadata, created_at) +Chunk(chunk_id, doc_id, ordinal, text, tokens, embedding, bm25_tsv) + +Entity(entity_id, canonical_name, type, name_embedding, prov) + Alias(alias_text, entity_id, prov) -- every surface form ever seen + Mention(chunk_id, entity_id, description, prov) -- per-chunk description, never merged by LLM + +Fact(fact_id, subject_entity_id, predicate, object_entity_id, sentence, embedding, prov) + FactSource(fact_id, chunk_id, evidence_span, prov) + +Synonym(entity_a, entity_b, score, prov) -- embedding-derived, recomputed from Mentions + +TopicCache(topic_key, chunk_set_hash, summary, created_at) -- lazy, invalidated by hash +``` + +Why this shape: + +- **Mentions instead of merged descriptions.** LightRAG joins all descriptions with a separator and asks an LLM to summarise once there are eight. That summary cannot be attributed to a chunk. We keep one description per chunk per entity. At query time we show the top-k mentions by PPR score. Nothing to summarise, nothing to un-summarise. +- **Facts carry their sentence and evidence span.** This is what gets embedded and matched against the query, following HippoRAG 2. The evidence span lets the answer prompt quote exact text and lets a reviewer verify the extraction. +- **Aliases are kept forever while they have provenance.** When chunk 17 called the entity "IBM" and chunk 42 called it "International Business Machines", both aliases point to one entity. Delete chunk 42 and the alias loses one unit of provenance; if it reaches zero it disappears, but the entity survives on chunk 17. +- **Synonym edges are derived, not extracted.** They are recomputed from name embeddings for the entities touched by an insert or delete. No LLM. + +## 4. Indexing pipeline + +```mermaid +flowchart LR + A[Document] --> B[Hash and diff] + B -->|unchanged| Z[skip] + B -->|changed| C[Structure-aware chunking 512 to 800 tokens] + C --> D[Optional GLiNER NER pre-pass, local] + D --> E[One LLM call per chunk, JSON schema] + E --> F[Entities, facts, descriptions, evidence spans] + F --> G[Batch embed: chunks, entity names, fact sentences] + G --> H[Canonicalize entities] + H -->|cos above 0.92 and same type| I[Merge] + H -->|0.80 to 0.92| J[Batched LLM judge, double vote] + H -->|below 0.80| K[New entity] + I --> L[Ledger upsert: increment prov] + J --> L + K --> L + L --> M[Recompute synonym edges for touched entities] + M --> N[Update per-tenant sparse matrix] +``` + +Step by step: + +1. **Hash and diff.** `content_hash` of the whole document, plus a hash per chunk. A re-upload with three changed paragraphs re-extracts only the changed chunks. Unchanged chunks keep their ledger entries. This is GraphRAG-SDK's `update()` idea applied at chunk granularity. +2. **Chunking.** Structure-aware (headings, tables, lists) with a 512 to 800 token target and 10 percent overlap. HippoRAG 2 ships no chunker and treats each document as one chunk, which is why its passage recall is sensitive to document length. Youtu's 5000-token chunks produce prompts that cost more than the extraction they feed. +3. **Optional NER pre-pass.** GLiNER or spaCy on CPU, as in GraphRAG-SDK. It seeds the extraction prompt with candidate spans so a small model misses fewer entities. Cost is CPU only. Measured as an ablation. +4. **One extraction call.** JSON schema with `entities[]` (name, type from a tenant-configurable type list, one-sentence description), `facts[]` (subject, predicate, object, sentence, evidence_span), and nothing else. No gleaning. Model: a 7B to 32B instruction model self-hosted via vLLM, or the cheapest hosted tier. Constrained decoding or JSON mode, never delimiter strings. +5. **Batch embedding.** One embedding request per batch of chunks, entity names and fact sentences. A 384 to 1024 dimension model is enough; HippoRAG's NV-Embed-v2 at 7B is a GPU cost most enterprises will not pay. +6. **Canonicalization.** For each new entity name, HNSW lookup over existing entity name embeddings in the same tenant, filtered by type. Three bands: high similarity merges automatically, a middle band goes to a batched LLM judge that is asked once per pair with both descriptions and votes twice (GraphRAG-SDK's double vote), low similarity creates a new entity. Thresholds are tenant-tunable and reported in the evaluation. +7. **Ledger upsert.** Every touched record gets `prov[chunk_id] += 1`. Mentions, aliases, fact sources all recorded. One transaction per document. +8. **Synonym edges.** Recomputed only for entities whose name embedding is new or whose neighbours changed. k-nearest with cosine at or above 0.80, as in HippoRAG 2. +9. **Sparse matrix update.** The per-tenant PPR matrix (entities, facts, chunks as rows and columns) is updated in place for the touched rows. A full rebuild from the database is available as a background job and takes seconds for a million-edge graph with scipy. + +Index cost target per chunk: 1 LLM call of roughly 1.2k input and 400 output tokens, 1 embedding batch, and on average well under 0.1 LLM judge calls. Compare: LightRAG 2 calls plus summaries, Microsoft about 2 plus one per community, KAG 3 to 4, HyperGraphRAG 3 to 5. + +## 5. Deletion, the point of the design + +``` +DELETE document D: + for chunk c in D: + for record r in ledger where c in r.prov: + r.prov[c] -= 1 + if r.prov is empty: mark r for removal + remove marked Mentions, FactSources, Aliases, Facts, Entities, Synonyms (in that order) + drop rows of removed nodes from the sparse matrix + invalidate TopicCache entries whose chunk_set_hash covered any c + delete chunks and document +commit +``` + +Properties: + +- **Zero model calls.** No re-extraction, no re-summarisation, no re-clustering, no re-embedding. Everything removed was derived only from the deleted chunks; everything kept has other provenance. +- **Bounded cost.** Proportional to the number of ledger records touched by the deleted chunks, which is linear in document size. +- **Exactness.** Because no record was ever produced by combining chunks through an LLM, the post-delete state equals the never-indexed state. The one exception is the LLM judge's merge decision, which is recorded as a Synonym with provenance from both chunks; if one side is deleted the merge is undone and the surviving entity reverts to its own canonical name. +- **Comparison.** Microsoft GraphRAG: no delete. nano-graphrag: no delete. LightRAG: delete by document, but entity descriptions were LLM-summarised, so it must re-run the summary from cached extraction (an LLM call per touched entity when the cache misses). HippoRAG 2: provenance-based delete, but no chunker and in-RAM only. KAG: UPSERT delete through the OpenSPG server. GraphRAG-SDK: delete by document in FalkorDB. R2R: deletes document rows but leaves graph copies. Everything else: none. + +## 6. Query pipeline + +```mermaid +sequenceDiagram + participant U as User + participant Q as Query service + participant V as pgvector + BM25 + participant P as PPR (in-memory) + participant R as Local reranker + participant L as LLM + U->>Q: question + Q->>V: embed question (1 call); dense top-k facts, entities, chunks; BM25 top-k chunks + V-->>Q: seeds with scores + Q->>P: reset vector: facts weighted by similarity, chunks by hybrid score + P-->>Q: PPR scores for all chunks + Q->>R: top 30 chunks by PPR, cross-encoder rerank against question + R-->>Q: top 8 chunks, top facts, top mentions + Q->>Q: confidence gate: max rerank score and seed coverage + alt gate passes + Q->>L: one answer call with chunks, facts, evidence spans, chunk ids + else gate fails + Q->>L: one decomposition call, re-run retrieval per sub-question, merge, one answer call + end + L-->>U: answer with chunk citations +``` + +1. **Hybrid seeding.** Dense similarity against fact sentences, entity names and chunk text, plus BM25 over chunk text. Sparse retrieval catches exact identifiers (part numbers, ticket ids, people's names) that embeddings blur, which matters in enterprise corpora. No framework in the survey combines all four seed sources; LightRAG and HippoRAG use dense only. +2. **Personalized PageRank.** Reset mass goes to seed facts (which spread to their member entities and source chunks), seed entities, and seed chunks. Damping 0.5 as in HippoRAG 2, re-tuned in the evaluation. The walk is a sparse matrix-vector loop in scipy; sub-10 ms on a million-edge graph. +3. **Local reranking.** A cross-encoder (bge-reranker-base or flashrank) over the top 30 chunks. CPU, about 100 ms. Replaces HippoRAG's LLM recognition filter. +4. **Confidence gate.** If the best rerank score is below a threshold, or the seed entities are not all connected to retrieved chunks, escalate to one decomposition call and a second retrieval round, capped at two rounds. This is Youtu's IRCoT loop with a budget. Expected to fire on a minority of questions; the rate is reported in the evaluation. +5. **Context assembly.** Top 8 chunks in document order with chunk ids, the top facts with evidence spans, and the top mentions for seed entities. Token budget 6k by default. +6. **Answer.** One LLM call. Citations are chunk ids, which resolve to document, page and span. + +Query cost target: 1 embedding call, 1 LLM answer call, plus on a minority of queries 1 decomposition call and 1 more embedding call. Compare: LightRAG 2 calls, HippoRAG 2 2 to 3, Microsoft global dozens, KAG 6 to 15. + +## 7. Global questions without index-time reports + +Community reports are the most expensive and least erasable artefact in the Microsoft family. We replace them with lazy topics: + +- **Topic key.** Entities are clustered on their name embeddings with a cheap algorithm (k-means or HDBSCAN) that runs in seconds and needs no LLM. A topic is a cluster id plus the set of chunk ids reachable from its entities. +- **Lazy summary.** The first time a query is classified as global (a cheap heuristic: few or no high-confidence seeds, question words like "overall", "themes", "compare across"), the top topics by seed overlap are summarised by one LLM call each, and the summary is cached under `chunk_set_hash`. +- **Automatic invalidation.** Deleting or adding a chunk changes the hash of every topic it belongs to, so the cached summary is simply not found next time and is regenerated on demand. No background job, no stale reports. +- **Cost.** Zero at index time. At query time, the first global question on a fresh corpus costs k summary calls (k topics, typically 5 to 20); subsequent global questions hit the cache until the corpus changes. + +This gives Microsoft-style global answers on a corpus that is static for days, and degrades gracefully to pay-as-you-ask on a corpus that churns. + +## 8. Storage and deployment + +- **Postgres 16 with pgvector and pg_trgm.** Tables as in section 3, HNSW indexes on the three embedding columns, GIN index on `bm25_tsv`, GIN on the `prov` JSONB. Row-level security by tenant. +- **In-memory PPR matrix per tenant.** scipy CSR, loaded from the database on first query, updated in place on insert and delete, checkpointed to disk. For graphs beyond roughly 50 million edges, shard by tenant or move the walk into the database with a recursive CTE at the cost of latency. +- **Models.** Extraction: a 7B to 32B instruction model on vLLM, or a hosted small model. Embeddings: a 384 to 1024 dimension open model. Reranker: bge-reranker-base on CPU. Answer: any model the tenant chooses. Nothing in the pipeline requires a frontier model. +- **No other services.** No Java, no broker, no clustering microservice, no graph database. A single container plus Postgres. + +## 9. Expected position against the field + +| Dimension | Lightfoot target | Best in survey today | +|---|---|---| +| Index LLM calls per chunk | 1 (+ under 0.1 judge) | fast-graphrag 1, neo4j 1 | +| Query LLM calls | 1 (2 to 3 when gate fails) | RAGFlow 0 to 1, neo4j 1 | +| Delete cost | DB transaction, 0 model calls | HippoRAG 2 (RAM only), GraphRAG-SDK (FalkorDB only) | +| Entity resolution | Embedding bands plus batched judge | GraphRAG-SDK | +| Multi-hop | PPR plus gated second round | HippoRAG 2 | +| Global questions | Lazy cached topics | Microsoft (index-time reports) | +| Infrastructure | Postgres only | LightRAG (Postgres backend) | + +Hypotheses to test, in the order they matter: + +- H1. Index cost per chunk is at or below fast-graphrag and under half of LightRAG at equal model. +- H2. Numbers come from `05-results-all.md` and `04-results-musique.md`; every one was measured in this project. + +## Abstract + +Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation improves multi-hop question answering, but production systems face two costs the research literature rarely measures: building the graph, and removing documents from it. We present Lightfoot, a GraphRAG system in which every entity, fact and synonym edge is a deterministic function of per-passage extractions that carry chunk-level provenance. Indexing makes one language-model call per passage, retrieval makes none, and deleting a document is a database transaction with zero model calls. We verify on the full 11,402-passage MuSiQue corpus that after deleting 10% of documents, the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. We compare against HippoRAG 2, LightRAG and fast-graphrag under identical models, embeddings and answer prompts on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA. Lightfoot builds the cheapest index on all three, 26 to 31% below HippoRAG 2 and 3 to 6 times below LightRAG and fast-graphrag. Its retrieval accuracy is significantly higher than HippoRAG 2's on MuSiQue (+2.8 points recall@5 and +4.3 points recall@10 on a held-out split) and HotpotQA (+1.3 points recall@10, +5.3 points exact match), and significantly lower on 2WikiMultiHopQA at recall@2 (-3.9) and F1 (-8.1). LightRAG needed 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours to delete the same documents; fast-graphrag cannot delete at all. + +## 1. Introduction + +- Enterprises must delete: retention policies, right-to-erasure requests, retracted or superseded documents. A survey of 17 open-source GraphRAG frameworks (`../frameworks/`) found only five with document-level delete, and none that claims the result equals a never-indexed graph. +- Index cost differs by an order of magnitude across frameworks for similar accuracy. Most of it goes to second extraction passes, model-written description summaries and community reports. +- Contributions: + 1. A provenance model in which every derived record is a pure function of the surviving per-passage extractions, so deletion is exact and needs no model calls. + 2. A one-call extraction schema that halves output tokens while doubling facts per passage. + 3. A retrieval pipeline with no model calls: fact-seeded Personalized PageRank fused with a local cross-encoder. + 4. A cost-normalised, deletion-audited comparison against three open-source baselines under identical models and prompts, including two baseline failure modes uncovered along the way. + +## 2. Method + +### 2.1 Extraction + +One call per passage to an open 70B model returns minified JSON: up to 12 entities (name, type, 8-word description) and up to 12 facts as `[subject, predicate, object, evidence]` arrays, with evidence a verbatim quote of up to 12 words. On MuSiQue this averaged 269 output tokens and 7.7 facts per passage. + +### 2.2 Resolution and the erasure invariant + +Each (chunk, name) pair is stored as a *form*. Two forms of the same type are linked when the cosine of their name embeddings is at least 0.92. An entity is a connected component of live forms, identified by its smallest member name, and its canonical name is the alias with the most provenance. Synonym edges join every same-type pair at cosine 0.80 or above, with no top-k cap. Name embeddings are computed in fixed-shape batches so they do not depend on batch composition. + +Every link, entity and synonym edge is therefore a function of the set of live forms alone, independent of insertion order, batching or history. Deleting a document removes its forms and recomputes only the components it touched. The result is, by construction, the graph that would exist had the document never been indexed. + +Two choices were made for exactness: no top-k synonyms, and no model judge for ambiguous name pairs. On a 2,000-passage ablation, neither changed recall beyond noise. + +### 2.3 Retrieval + +1. Embed the question. +2. Seed a Personalized PageRank walk on the entity-passage graph. The subject and object entities of the two most similar facts receive weight equal to the fact score divided by the entity's passage count; the 100 most similar passages receive weight up to 0.05. +3. Walk with damping 0.9 and take the top 30 passages. +4. Score them with a local cross-encoder, and fuse the cross-encoder rank with the PageRank rank by reciprocal rank fusion (k = 60). +5. Send the top 8 passages to one answer call that returns a short span. + +Settings were chosen on MuSiQue questions 1 to 500 only. + +## 3. Experimental setup + +- **Datasets:** MuSiQue (1,000 questions, 11,402 passages), 2WikiMultiHopQA (300 / 2,131) and HotpotQA (300 / 2,957), built following HippoRAG's construction. +- **Models, identical for every system:** Llama 3.3 70B for extraction; gpt-5.6-luna with reasoning off for answers; bge-base-en-v1.5 embeddings; the same short-span, best-guess answer instruction. +- **Answers:** generated for the first 300 questions of each dataset; the remaining MuSiQue questions are scored on retrieval only. +- **Deletion audit:** a seeded random 10% of documents is deleted, then every question is re-queried. Recall is reported separately for questions whose evidence survived and questions whose evidence was deleted. +- **Cost:** every model call is logged, and token counts are priced at one fixed list price per model. +- **Statistics:** 95% paired bootstrap intervals. MuSiQue comparisons use the held-out questions 501 to 1000. + +## 4. Results + +See `05-results-all.md` for the full tables. Summary: + +- **Index cost.** Lightfoot is cheapest on every dataset: $1.64 vs $2.23 (HippoRAG 2), $4.89 (fast-graphrag) and about $9.5 (LightRAG) on MuSiQue. +- **Accuracy.** Across 14 paired comparisons with HippoRAG 2, Lightfoot is significantly better on 5, worse on 2 (both on 2Wiki) and tied on 7. Against LightRAG and fast-graphrag it is better on every dataset at recall@5. +- **Deletion.** Zero model calls on every dataset, and an exact match to a fresh index of the survivors on the full MuSiQue corpus. LightRAG made 2,187 calls and took 3.7 hours on MuSiQue; fast-graphrag has no delete path. +- **Ablations, MuSiQue held-out R@5:** + +| Component | Effect | +|---|---| +| Rerank fused with PageRank, instead of replacing it | about +3.5 points | +| Damping 0.9 vs 0.5 under fusion | +2 to 3 points | +| Seeding from 2 facts vs 5 | about +1 point | +| Entity-only graph vs fact nodes | none | +| Model judge vs none | none | + +## 5. Analysis + +- **Where the graph helps.** The graph finds passages that share no words with the question. In a traced MuSiQue example, the passage naming the album's performer was outside the top 100 by dense similarity but was reached in two hops and ranked fourth after fusion. +- **Where it fails.** Seeding on the two most similar facts sometimes picks trivia, such as a release date or a chart position, over the fact that carries the chain. HippoRAG 2 filters seed facts with a model call; that call is the likely source of its 2Wiki advantage, where questions compare two named entities. +- **Baseline failure modes found during benchmarking:** + - LightRAG aborted most of its first index after an embedding timeout but reported success, leaving 31% of chunks indexed. + - Its default file storage rewrites the full graph and vector files for every document, about 415 MB per document at 3,000 passages. + - HippoRAG 2 aborted its whole index on 24 malformed model outputs. + +## 6. Limitations + +- **One tuned dataset.** Retrieval settings were tuned on half of MuSiQue. The other two datasets are untuned, and one of them is a loss. +- **Small answer sets.** Answer metrics rest on 232 to 300 questions per dataset. +- **Shared embedder.** HippoRAG 2 used the shared bge-base embedder, not its paper's 7B NV-Embed-v2, so its absolute numbers are below those published. +- **Estimated cost.** LightRAG's MuSiQue index cost is estimated from its call count, because its extraction was billed across several runs. +- **Untested erasure.** Exactness was not tested for the baselines' deletes. HippoRAG 2's provenance-based delete may also be exact. +- **No global questions.** Corpus-level summarisation questions were not evaluated; lazy topic summaries exist but fired on only five MuSiQue questions. + +## 7. Pros and cons by family + +### Family A: community-summary graphs (Microsoft GraphRAG, nano-graphrag, R2R) + +**How it works.** Entities and relations are extracted per chunk, merged by name, clustered with hierarchical Leiden, and each community gets an LLM-written report. Global questions are answered by map-reducing over the reports; local questions start from entity vector hits. + +**Pros** +- The only family that can answer corpus-level sensemaking questions such as "what are the main themes" without reading everything at query time. +- Rich provenance tables: every claim traces to text units, entities, and reports. +- Microsoft's implementation has prompt auto-tuning, a CLI, Azure backends, and the best documentation in the set. + +**Cons** +- Indexing is the most expensive in the set: extraction, gleaning, summaries, then one LLM call per community per level. Microsoft's own docs attribute about three quarters of cost to extraction. +- Global search costs dozens of 12k-token map calls per question. +- Incremental updates do not re-cluster, so communities drift stale. nano-graphrag regenerates every report on every insert instead. +- Entity resolution is exact string match. Multi-hop reasoning is one hop in local mode. +- Microsoft GraphRAG is in declared maintenance mode. R2R's graph search is only vector kNN over descriptions, with communities built by an external service. + +### Family B: keyword dual-level graphs (LightRAG, PathRAG, MiniRAG, HyperGraphRAG, RAGFlow) + +**How it works.** Same extraction step, but no clustering or reports. The query is turned into low-level keywords (matched against entity vectors) and high-level keywords (matched against relation vectors). Hits are expanded one hop and the provenance chunks are stitched into a budgeted context. + +**Pros** +- Roughly half the indexing cost of Family A, and two LLM calls per query. +- LightRAG has the most complete lifecycle: queued inserts, delete-by-document with cached rebuild, entity edit and merge, workspaces, 25 storage implementations, REST API and UI. +- Easy to fork, which is why PathRAG, MiniRAG, HyperGraphRAG, and Graph-R1 all start from it. +- RAGFlow puts the graph rows in the existing search index, so there is no extra infrastructure and tenancy and citations come for free. + +**Cons** +- No corpus-level summaries, so global questions degrade to whatever the top relations happen to be. +- Multi-hop is one hop by default. PathRAG fixes this with path enumeration but does it by loading the whole graph into memory and enumerating all simple paths, which is exponential. +- Exact-name entity resolution throughout. +- The forks are research quality: PathRAG has a hard-coded 20-second sleep and an invalid default mode, MiniRAG re-extracts the whole corpus on every insert with no cache, HyperGraphRAG relies on brittle positional parsing and has a broken delete path. +- RAGFlow's graph feature is mid-rewrite. The legacy PageRank and community path needs columns the new compiler never writes. + +### Family C: PageRank over a triple graph (HippoRAG 2, fast-graphrag, KAG's kg_fr retriever) + +**How it works.** Extraction produces entity and fact nodes linked to passages. At query time the query is linked to a few seed nodes and Personalized PageRank spreads activation across the graph; passages are ranked by their resulting score. No LLM reasoning over the graph is needed. + +**Pros** +- Cheapest indexing among graph methods: one to two calls per chunk, no summaries, no communities. +- Multi-hop retrieval is deterministic, milliseconds, and does not depend on an LLM following paths. +- Strongest published multi-hop numbers for the cost.
